nodes.label: PPARα
nodes.description:
PPARα (Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Alpha) is a nuclear receptor transcription factor that regulates Lipid Metabolism, Fatty acid oxidation, Ketogenesis, and Inflammation. It is activated by Fibrate drugs (e.g., Fenofibrate, Gemfibrozil) and endogenous Fatty Acids and their derivatives. PPARα heterodimerizes with RXR and binds to PPRE (PPAR Response Elements) in target gene promoters. It is highly expressed in Liver, Kidney, Heart, and Skeletal Muscle. PPARα activation improves Lipid Profile, reduces Triglycerides, and has Anti-inflammatory effects. It also interacts with SIRT1 and AMPK to coordinate metabolic adaptation during Fasting.

nodes.label: LXRα
nodes.description:
Liver X receptor alpha (LXRα) is a nuclear receptor that plays a central role in the regulation of Cholesterol, fatty acid, and glucose homeostasis. It works in conjunction with other receptors like PPARγ to regulate the expression of ABCA1, which is vital for cholesterol efflux.

## Oxidative Stress and LXRα Regulation

### Oxysterol Ligands and Redox-Dependent Activation
LXRα is activated by specific Oxysterols ligands, including 22(R)-hydroxycholesterol, 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol, and 27-hydroxycholesterol — all generated through enzymatic or non-enzymatic Cholesterol oxidation. The production of these ligands is directly tied to cellular Oxidative Stress: increased ROS drive cholesterol oxidation, generating oxysterols that activate LXRα. Upon ligand binding, LXRα forms a heterodimer with Retinoid X Receptor (RXRα) and binds to LXR response elements (LXREs) in the promoter regions of target genes. The transcriptional activity of the LXRα/RXR heterodimer is further modulated by redox-dependent Coactivator recruitment (e.g., SRC-1, PGC-1α) and Corepressor (NCoR, SMRT) release.

### Regulation of Cholesterol Efflux and Reverse Cholesterol Transport
LXRα transcriptional targets constitute a coordinated cholesterol efflux program. The most well-characterized target — ABCA1 — encodes the ATP-binding cassette transporter A1, which mediates the rate-limiting step of apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I) lipidation to form nascent HDL. nodes.label: Retrograde Response
nodes.description: Retrograde Response is a biological_process. The retrograde response is a conserved signaling program by which mitochondrial dysfunction communicates to the nucleus to induce stress-responsive nuclear genes. In yeast it is mediated by Rtg1 or Rtg3 and orchestrates metabolic remodeling; in metazoans it overlaps with mitochondrial UPR and integrated stress responses. It reallocates metabolism to compensate for impaired respiration.

nodes.label: Rtg1
nodes.description:
Rtg1 is a basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor in the budding yeast S. cerevisiae and a core component of the retrograde response (RTG) pathway. It forms a heterodimer with the bHLH/leucine-zipper protein Rtg3; in healthy cells the complex is phosphorylated and sequestered in the cytoplasm by the 14-3-3 proteins Bmh1/2. When mitochondrial function is compromised — by loss of mitochondrial DNA, respiratory-chain inhibition, or nutrient shifts — the kinases that maintain cytoplasmic retention are inactivated, Rtg1–Rtg3 translocates to the nucleus, and the heterodimer drives expression of nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial and peroxisomal proteins, including the citrate–isocitrate shuttle enzymes (CIT2, ACO1, IDH1/2).

The RTG pathway thus reconfigures intermediary metabolism so that the cell can compensate for lost mitochondrial capacity, a yeast analog of the UPRmt and of mammalian Mitohormesis. The shared logic — a mitonuclear retrograde signal that reprograms nuclear transcription toward stress resistance and metabolic flexibility — is conserved from yeast to humans and is a cornerstone of longevity research in S. cerevisiae.

The connection to Adrenochrome and redox biology is the general principle that mitochondrial stress signals induce cytoprotective, antioxidant programs that limit reactive oxygen species leakage. nodes.label: Rtg3
nodes.description:
Rtg3 is a basic helix-loop-helix/leucine-zipper (bHLH/ZIP) transcription factor in S. cerevisiae and the DNA-binding engine of the retrograde (RTG) response. In healthy cells it is phosphorylated by the conserved kinase cascade (Mks1–Ptc1 axis) and held in the cytoplasm bound to 14-3-3 proteins alongside its partner Rtg1. When mitochondrial respiration is impaired — loss of mitochondrial DNA, respiratory-chain poisons, or carbon-source shifts — the retention signal is lost, and the Rtg1–Rtg3 heterodimer enters the nucleus to activate a battery of nuclear-encoded genes, prominently the citrate–isocitrate shuttle enzymes (CIT2, ACO1, IDH1/IDH2) that sustain anaplerotic metabolism without functional mitochondria.

The RTG pathway is the yeast counterpart of mammalian mitonuclear stress signaling, conceptually aligned with the UPRmt and Mitohormesis. Rtg3 thus integrates mitochondrial state with nuclear transcription to restore metabolic flexibility, a conserved longevity mechanism studied extensively in yeast as a Model Organisms system.

Its relevance to adrenochrome and redox biology lies in metabolic reprogramming that influences the cellular reducing environment. By sustaining citrate flux and α-ketoglutarate/glutathione precursor supply, the Rtg3 program supports antioxidant capacity, buffering the Oxidative Stress that otherwise drives catecholamine autoxidation — the conversion of Epinephrine to Adrenochrome. nodes.label: PERK
nodes.description:
Protein kinase RNA-activated-like ER kinase (encoded by the EIF2AK3 gene). PERK is a key sensor of the integrated stress response that phosphorylates EIF2A, leading to a global reduction in protein synthesis while selectively increasing the translation of ATF4.
Protein kinase RNA-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase, an ER transmembrane protein that senses misfolded proteins and activates the Unfolded Protein Response.
## Mechanism
PERK (EIF2AK3) is a type I transmembrane ER-resident kinase that senses unfolded proteins via its luminal domain. Upon ER stress, PERK dimerizes and autophosphorylates, then phosphorylates eIF2α at Ser51, attenuating global translation while selectively upregulating ATF4 translation.
## Role in Autophagy
PERK-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation induces Autophagy as a cytoprotective response to ER Stress. ATF4 and CHOP downstream of PERK transactivate autophagy genes. In cancer, PERK-dependent autophagy supports tumor survival under hypoxia and nutrient deprivation.
## Pathological Implications
Chronic PERK activation is linked to Neurodegenerative Diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, prion disorders), Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (β-cell loss), and Cancer (tumor adaptation to microenvironmental stress). PERK inhibitors are being explored as cancer therapeutics.

nodes.label: SARM1
nodes.description: SARM1 is a enzyme. SARM1 is a mitochondrial NADase that executes axonal degeneration after injury by depleting axonal NAD+ and ATP. Its ARM domains sense NAD+ loss and activate a TIR-domain NADase, making it a key target for neuroprotective drugs. SARM1 thereby couples mitochondrial or metabolic stress to programmed axon destruction.

nodes.label: NMNAT2
nodes.description:
NMNAT2 (Nicotinamide Mononucleotide Adenylyl Transferase 2) is a neuronal enzyme that synthesizes NAD+ from NMN. It is the central brake on SARM1-mediated axonal degeneration.

## Mechanism

NMNAT2 is continuously delivered from the neuronal soma to the axon, where it converts NMN → NAD⁺, maintaining axonal NAD⁺ at ~400 μM and keeping SARM1 in its autoinhibited state. NMNAT2 has a short half-life (~30 min) and is degraded by the proteasome upon axonal injury (transection severs soma-axon transport). Its loss causes NMN accumulation; the rising NMN/NAD⁺ ratio is the primary metabolic trigger that relieves SARM1 autoinhibition and initiates the NAD⁺ catastrophe of Wallerian Degeneration.

## Significance

- NMNAT2 is the most injury-sensitive node in the axonal NAD⁺ economy — its decline is both necessary and sufficient to license SARM1 activation.
- Therapeutic strategies that preserve NMNAT2 (or bypass it with NAD⁺ precursors) protect axons.
- Part of the broader NAD⁺ consumer network alongside CD38, PARP1, and sirtuins.

## Connections

- NAD+ — product synthesized from NMN
- NMN — substrate; its accumulation triggers SARM1
- SARM1 — suppressed by NMNAT2-derived NAD⁺; released on NMNAT2 loss
- Wallerian Degeneration, Axon Degeneration — pathological outcomes of NMNAT2 loss
- CD38, PARP1 — competing NAD⁺ consumers

## Linking Summary

- New links added: NAD+, NMN, SARM1, Wallerian Degeneration, Axon Degeneration, CD38, PARP1

nodes.label: PARP1
nodes.description:
PARP1 (Poly [ADP-ribose] polymerase 1, 116 kDa) is the founding member of the PARP family, which comprises 17 members in humans. It is a nuclear zinc-finger enzyme that detects DNA strand breaks and catalyzes the transfer of ADP-ribose units from NAD+ onto target proteins, forming poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) chains. This PARylation modifies histones, transcription factors, and DNA repair proteins to facilitate the DNA damage response. PARP1 is the most abundant nuclear protein—approximately one copy per 1,000 nucleosomes—and the primary sensor of DNA single-strand breaks (SSBs) and double-strand breaks (DSBs). By rapidly synthesizing negatively charged PAR polymers, PARP1 initiates a signaling cascade that recruits downstream repair factors and remodels chromatin to provide access to damaged DNA.

## Structure & Domains

PARP1 is organized into three functional regions. The N-terminal DNA-binding domain contains three zinc finger motifs: Zn1 directly detects DNA strand breaks by recognizing disrupted base pairing, Zn2 mediates allosteric activation of the catalytic domain upon DNA binding, and Zn3 serves as an automodification site where PARP1 attaches PAR chains to itself. The central auto-modification domain harbors BRCT (BRCA1 C-terminus) repeats that mediate protein–protein interactions, a WGR motif involved in DNA binding, and glutamate-rich automodification sites that are targets for self-PARylation. The C-terminal catalytic domain comprises a helical autoinhibitory module—h

nodes.label: CZ-48
nodes.description:
CZ-48 (sulfo-ara-F-NMN) is a synthetic, cell-permeant analog of NMN that is the only molecule known to have opposite effects on the two principal NAD⁺ glycohydrolases: it activates SARM1 while inhibiting CD38 (Zhao et al. 2019, _iScience_).

## Mechanism

- SARM1: CZ-48 acts as an NMN mimetic that binds the SARM1 ARM domain, relieving autoinhibition and driving NADase activation. Activated SARM1 produces cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR), depletes NAD+ and ATP, and induces non-apoptotic cell death.
- CD38: CZ-48 inhibits CD38 ecto-enzymatic NADase activity, reducing extracellular NAD⁺/NMN consumption.

## Significance

CZ-48 is a pharmacological proof-of-concept that the two NADases — despite sharing substrate (NAD⁺) and products (nicotinamide, ADP-ribose, cADPR) — can be pharmacologically separated. This divergence underpins the NMN-sensitization paradox: raising NMN/NAD⁺ precursors (to inhibit CD38 and feed sirtuins) could, in principle, sensitize SARM1 — the exact tension addressed by combined CD38 + SARM1 inhibition.

## Connections

- SARM1 — activated by CZ-48 (NMN-mimetic allosteric trigger)
- CD38 — inhibited by CZ-48
- NAD+ — substrate consumed (SARM1) / spared (CD38)
- NMN — structural analog and bridging metabolite

- New links added: SARM1, CD38, NAD+, NMN

- Strong connections to strengthen: SARM1 ↔ CD38 (pharmacological divergence probe)

nodes.label: Disulfiram
nodes.description:
Disulfiram (brand name Antabuse) is an FDA-approved drug originally used as an alcohol-aversion therapy. It was repurposed as the first-in-class SARM1 inhibitor.

## Mechanism

Disulfiram covalently modifies a cysteine residue in the SARM1 TIR domain, irreversibly blocking its NAD+ glycohydrolase (NADase) activity. By preventing SARM1-mediated NAD⁺ depletion, it protects axons from Wallerian degeneration in preclinical injury models.

## Therapeutic Context

- Repurposed from its established alcohol-aversion indication due to the conserved TIR-domain cysteine targeted by disulfiram.
- Limitation: Disulfiram is pharmacologically promiscuous (it inhibits multiple cysteine-dependent enzymes, including aldehyde dehydrogenase), which restricts its utility as a selective SARM1 inhibitor and drives the development of more selective next-generation molecules (DSRM-3716, GSK-428, NB-4746).
- Shares the adduct-forming uncompetitive inhibitor mechanism class with the CD38 inhibitor 78c — a conserved NAD-dependent strategy across NAD hydrolases (Bratkowski et al. 2022, _Neuron_).

## Connections

- SARM1 — covalent TIR-domain inhibitor; blocks NADase, prevents axonal NAD⁺ catastrophe
- CD38 — parallel NAD⁺ glycohydrolase; shares adduct-forming inhibitor logic (78c)
- NAD+ — substrate whose hydrolysis is blocked
- Wallerian Degeneration — pathology prevented by SARM1 inhibition

## Linking Summary

- New links added: SARM1, CD38, NAD+, Wallerian Degeneration

nodes.label: NB-4746
nodes.description:
NB-4746 is a brain-penetrant, clinical-stage SARM1 inhibitor developed by Nura Bio. It is among the most advanced SARM1-directed therapeutics in clinical development.

## Mechanism

NB-4746 blocks the SARM1 TIR-domain NAD+ glycohydrolase, preventing the axonal NAD⁺ catastrophe that drives Wallerian degeneration. Its brain-penetrant profile distinguishes it from earlier peripherally-restricted candidates, enabling central nervous system indications.

## Clinical Status

- Completed Phase 1 in healthy volunteers (2024) with targeted plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) exposure and no serious adverse events.
- Advanced to Phase 1b/2 in 2025.
- Primary indications: chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), traumatic brain injury (Traumatic Brain Injury), and chronic peripheral neuropathy.
- Therapeutic hypothesis: pharmacologically blocking SARM1 during acute injury windows halts axonal degeneration before it becomes irreversible, permitting regeneration and functional recovery.

## Connections

- SARM1 — brain-penetrant clinical-stage inhibitor
- CD38 — parallel NAD⁺ glycohydrolase; shared inhibitor logic (78c)
- NAD+ — substrate protected from hydrolysis
- Traumatic Brain Injury — CNS acute-injury indication

## Linking Summary

- Strong connections to strengthen: SARM1 ↔ CD38 (combined-inhibition synergy hypothesis in CNS)

nodes.label: SASP-Remodeling Aminochrome Complex
nodes.description:
The SASP-Remodeling Aminochrome Complex (SRAC) is an emerging conceptual entity describing the interplay between Aminochrome — the oxidized, cyclized quinone derived from Adrenochrome and catecholamine autoxidation — and the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP). It frames how redox-active indolequinones propagate cellular Senescence by feeding reactive oxygen species (ROS) into stress-transcription circuits.

Adrenochrome forms when Adrenaline and Dopamine undergo autoxidation through o-quinone and semiquinone intermediates (Adrenochrome Semiquinone Radical), ultimately generating Aminochrome. Aminochrome is electrophilic and redox-cycling; it depletes Glutathione, promotes protein carbonylation, and perturbs mitochondrial potential. These redox insults activate NF-κB and NLRP3 Inflammasome, master regulators of the SASP. The "remodeling" aspect denotes positive feedback: SASP factors (Interleukin 1β, Cathepsins) and the senescent microenvironment further oxidize catecholamines, amplifying aminochrome load in a self-sustaining loop.

SRAC is positioned as a ligand-conjugatable scaffold for targeted delivery to senescent cells, leveraging senescent cell surface markers to concentrate redox-modulating payloads. Therapeutic strategies pair aminochrome scavengers or quinone-trapping agents with Senomorphics to blunt the SASP while sparing proliferative tissue.

nodes.label: Senescence
nodes.description:
Senescence, or cellular senescence, is a state of permanent, proliferation-competent cell-cycle arrest that cells enter when exposed to potentially oncogenic or damaging stresses, including DNA Damage, Oxidative Stress, telomere dysfunction, and oncogene activation. First described by Hayflick and Moorhead as replicative exhaustion of human fibroblasts, senescence is now recognized as a pleiotropic program with physiological roles in tumour suppression, embryonic development, and wound healing, but pathological roles in Aging and age-related disease through the accumulation of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype. It is characterized by profound and dynamic remodeling of the Chromatin landscape and Epigenetics state (Gorgoulis et al., 2019, Cell 179:813–827; PMID 30595488; a consensus "Hallmarks of Senescence").

## Types of Senescence

- Replicative senescence (RS): Driven by progressive telomere shortening with each cell division until a DNA-damage-like response is triggered (the Hayflick limit).
- Stress-induced senescence (SIS): Provoked by non-telomeric genotoxic or oxidative insults, including radiation, chemotherapeutics, and Reactive Oxygen Species.
- Oncogene-induced senescence (OIS): Triggered by activated oncogenes (e.g., RAS, BRAF), which generate replicative stress and DDR signaling (Courtois-Cox et al., 2008).

nodes.label: SKN-1
nodes.description:
SKN-1 is the Caenorhabditis elegans ortholog of mammalian NRF2 (NF-E2-related factor 2), a cap'n'collar basic leucine zipper transcription factor that governs the conserved antioxidant and detoxification response. Under basal conditions SKN-1 is retained in the cytoplasm through association with the BTB–Kelch repressor WDR-23 (the homolog of Keap1); upon electrophilic or oxidative insult, the repressor is inactivated and SKN-1 translocates to the nucleus to induce phase-II enzymes, xenobiotic transporters, and proteostasis genes.

SKN-1 is a central node in the Mitohormesis framework: mild mitochondrial dysfunction or low-level Oxidative Stress — including the modest Superoxide anion leak from compromised respiration — activates SKN-1, driving a cytoprotective transcriptional program that extends Lifespan. Genetic studies show that SKN-1 activity is required for the longevity conferred by mitochondrial mutants (e.g., isp-1, clk-1) and by dietary restriction, placing it downstream of the redox signal that links mitochondrial state to systemic stress resistance.

The adrenochrome/redox relevance is direct: SKN-1/NRF2 target genes include glutathione biosynthesis, glutathione-dependent reductases, and quinone reductases that detoxify aminochromes and limit the autoxidation of catecholamines such as Epinephrine to Adrenochrome. nodes.label: Synovial Fluid
nodes.description:
Synovial fluid is the transparent, viscoelastic fluid filling the cavities of synovial (diarthrodial) joints. Secreted mainly by the synovial membrane and enriched in hyaluronic acid and lubricin, it provides boundary and hydrodynamic lubrication, supplies chondrocytes with nutrients (cartilage is avascular), and cushions load. Its low-friction, high-cohesion properties depend on the integrity of matrix macromolecules in the joint.

In chronic joint disease, especially Rheumatoid Arthritis, the composition and redox state of synovial fluid are altered. Persistent Inflammation and the turnover of long-lived matrix proteins favor the accumulation of AGEs within cartilage and the synovial milieu. AGEs crosslink collagen, stiffen the matrix, and engage RAGE on synovial fibroblasts, macrophages, and chondrocytes, amplifying inflammatory cytokine release and proteolytic cartilage degradation — a feed-forward loop of glycative and oxidative damage.

The adrenochrome/redox relevance is the shared glycative–oxidative burden. AGE accumulation in synovial fluid parallels the carbonyl and aminochrome chemistry seen systemically: just as AGEs and their dicarbonyl precursors drive Oxidative Stress and inflammation in joints, catecholamines such as Epinephrine undergo autoxidation under oxidative stress to form Adrenochrome elsewhere. nodes.label: TRAF6
nodes.description:
TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) is a member of the TRAF family of cytoplasmic adaptor proteins with intrinsic E3 ubiquitin ligase activity. Unlike most TRAFs, TRAF6 assembles Lys63-linked and linear ubiquitin chains via its RING domain in collaboration with the Ubc13/Uev1A E2 complex. It sits at a convergence point for multiple upstream receptors: the interleukin-1/Toll-like receptor adaptor MyD88–IRAK axis, the RIG-I/MDA5–MAVS antiviral pathway (where it partners with TRAF2), CD40, RANK, and TNFR superfamily members.

The downstream consequences of TRAF6 activation are broad. K63-linked ubiquitin serves as a scaffold recruiting the TAK1 complex and the IKK and TBK1 kinases, activating NF-κB and MAP kinases (including c-Jun N-terminal kinase) and thus driving Inflammation, interferon responses, and osteoclastogenesis. TRAF6-mediated ubiquitin signaling is also integrated with cellular stress and redox circuits: it modulates autophagy and mitophagy through ubiquitin tags that recruit autophagic receptors, linking innate immunity to the quality-control programs relevant to Mitochondria and Oxidative Stress.

In the adrenochrome/redox frame, chronic TRAF6-driven NF-κB activation is a major source of inflammatory oxidants — activated myeloid cells produce superoxide, Nitric Oxide, and downstream peroxynitrite that accelerate the autoxidation of catecholamines such as Epinephrine into Adrenochrome and related aminochromes. nodes.label: Transcription factor EB
nodes.description:
Transcription factor EB (TFEB) is a basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-Zip) transcription factor belonging to the MITF/TFE3 family. It functions as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and Autophagy, governing the expression of genes required for lysosomal function, autophagic flux, and cellular clearance. TFEB is encoded by the TFEB gene on chromosome 6p21 and drives the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network, a coordinated transcriptional program that controls the expression of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins, and autophagy components.

TFEB was initially identified as a fusion partner in a subset of renal cell carcinomas and was later recognized as the central transcriptional node coupling lysosomal function to nutrient sensing. The protein contains an N-terminal transactivation domain, a bHLH-Zip DNA-binding domain, a nuclear localization signal, and a C-terminal nuclear export signal. This modular architecture enables TFEB to rapidly shuttle between compartments in response to cellular signals.

TFEB subcellular localization is the primary determinant of its activity. Under nutrient-rich conditions, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB at Ser142 and Ser211, creating a docking site for 14-3-3 proteins, which retain TFEB in the cytoplasm. 14-3-3 proteins are a family of highly conserved acidic regulatory molecules found across all eukaryotic lineages, first identified in 1967 based on their migration position (14th fraction on gel No. 3-3) during bovine brain extract fractionation. In humans, seven genes encode distinct isoforms — YWHAB (β), YWHAG (γ), YWHAE (ε), YWHAZ (ζ), YWHAH (η), YWHAQ (θ/τ), and SFN (σ) — each sharing >70% amino acid identity. These proteins function as phosphoserine/phosphothreonine-binding adapters that recognize the consensus motifs RXXpS/TXP or modes 1 and 2 binding motifs on >200 known partner proteins. By forming constitutive homo- and heterodimers, 14-3-3 proteins create a flexible scaffold that sequesters, translocates, or allosterically modulates client proteins, making them central hubs in signal transduction networks governing Apoptosis, Cell Cycle, MAPK signaling, Insulin signaling, Autophagy, and the DNA damage response. Dysregulation of 14-3-3 activity is implicated in multiple pathologies, including Cancer, Alzheimer's Disease, and Cardiovascular Disease.

Each 14-3-3 monomer is a ~30 kDa protein composed of nine antiparallel α-helices (α1–α9), with helices α3, α5, α7, and α9 forming a deep, conserved amphipathic groove that constitutes the phosphopeptide-binding site. nodes.label: CLEAR Element
nodes.description:
The CLEAR Element (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) is a 10-bp E-box-like consensus motif (5′-GTCACGTGAC-3′) enriched in the promoters and enhancers of lysosomal and autophagic genes. It serves as the cognate binding site for the MiT/TFE transcription factors TFEB and TFE3, coordinating a genome-wide program of Lysosome biogenesis, autophagosome component expression, and Autophagic Flux. The discovery of CLEAR provided the molecular explanation for how a small set of transcription factors can orchestrate hundreds of degradative-organelle genes in a coordinated, nutrient-responsive manner.

## Sequence & Genomic Organization

CLEAR is a variation of the canonical E-box (CANNTG), with the central CACGTG (E-box core) embedded in a CLEAR-specific flanking context. Bioinformatic mapping in mammalian genomes identified thousands of CLEAR sites near lysosomal hydrolase genes (e.g., LAMP1, LAMP2, cathepsins), v-ATPase subunits, and autophagy genes (LC3B, Atg family members). The number and affinity of CLEAR sites correlate with the strength of TFEB responsiveness of a given target.

## Mechanism of Action

Under starvation or lysosomal stress, mTORC1 is inhibited and TFEB/TFE3 are dephosphorylated, dissociating from 14-3-3 protein and entering the nucleus. There they bind CLEAR elements and recruit co-activators (e.g., EBF1, MEF2, CREB) and chromatin remodelers to drive transcription. nodes.label: Huntingtin
nodes.description:
Huntingtin (HTT) is a large scaffold protein (~350 kDa) encoded by the HTT gene located on chromosome 4p16.3. It is essential for embryonic development — constitutive HTT knockout in mice is embryonic lethal, with death occurring around embryonic day 7.5 due to defective gastrulation and impaired transcriptional regulation. In the adult nervous system, HTT functions as a multifunctional scaffold that orchestrates vesicular transport, autophagy, endocytosis, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) transport, and transcriptional regulation. The protein contains a polymorphic CAG trinucleotide repeat in exon 1 that encodes a polyglutamine (polyQ) tract. In healthy individuals, this repeat ranges from 6 to 35 CAGs; repeats of 36 or more cause Huntington's Disease with full penetrance at ≥40 CAGs. Wild-type HTT is subject to extensive post-translational modification — phosphorylation at Ser13, Ser16, and Ser421, among other sites — which modulates its subcellular localization, protein–protein interactions, and propensity to aggregate.

nodes.label: Transcriptome
nodes.description:
A transcriptome is the complete set of RNA transcripts (including mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, and non-coding RNA) produced by the genome at a specific time or under a specific condition.

## Transcriptomic Analysis

Transcriptomic analysis (e.g., via RNA-seq) is used to measure the expression levels of thousands of genes simultaneously. In the study of Mitohormesis, transcriptomic analysis is essential for identifying the coordinated changes in nuclear gene expression that occur in response to mitochondrial stress.

nodes.label: aak-2
nodes.description:
aak-2 is the principal catalytic (α) subunit of the C. elegans AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) complex, the conserved cellular energy sensor that monitors the AMP/ATP ratio. When bioenergetic stress (low glucose, exercise, mitochondrial dysfunction) raises AMP, AMPK phosphorylates targets that suppress anabolic processes (protein/lipid synthesis) and stimulate catabolic, repair, and recycling pathways (Autophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis).

Aak-2 is required for several longevity paradigms. Genetic loss of aak-2 abolishes the lifespan extension produced by glucose restriction and by mitochondrial stress-induced Mitohormesis, placing AMPK downstream of the energy-surfeit signal that triggers adaptive reprogramming. Aak-2 also cooperates with Sirtuins (e.g., sir-2.1) and the insulin/IGF-1 signaling axis, integrating nutrient and redox cues into a coordinated longevity response.

> [!info] Conserved geroscience node
> Mammalian AMPK is a major target of metformin and exercise mimetics; aak-2 therefore models the same energy-sensing rheostat that links calorie restriction to healthspan in humans.

Because AMPK activation improves glucose disposal, aak-2 biology is directly relevant to Insulin Resistance and diabetic vascular aging.

## Documents

- Mitohormesis (2014)
- Establishes aak-2/AMPK as required for glucose-restriction and mitohormetic longevity.

## Connections

nodes.label: c-Jun N-terminal kinase
nodes.description:
c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) is a member of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) family that phosphorylates the transcription factor c-Jun (and other substrates) on Ser/Thr residues. Three genes encode JNK isoforms (JNK1/2/3); JNK is activated by MAPK kinases MKK4 and MKK7 in response to cytokines, UV, osmotic shock, and — most relevant here — Oxidative Stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.

JNK occupies a pivotal position in stress signaling. In the mammalian retrograde response, mitochondrial stress (ROS, calcium, bioenergetic crisis) activates JNK, which phosphorylates and modulates transcription factors (AP-1, FOXO, p53) that reprogram nuclear gene expression toward antioxidant defense and mitochondrial biogenesis. JNK also balances life/death decisions: transient activation promotes adaptation and Autophagy, whereas sustained activation drives apoptosis via Bim and mitochondrial permeabilization.

> [!info] Longevity duality
> Like many stress kinases, JNK exerts dose-dependent effects — mild activation supports stress resistance and lifespan, while chronic activation (as in obesity/insulin resistance) fuels inflammation and degeneration.

In muscle, JNK intersects with urolithin A–mediated mitophagy pathways, and in cancer it is co-opted to evade apoptosis, illustrating its context-dependent biology.

nodes.label: cco-1
nodes.description:
cco-1 encodes the C. elegans ortholog of cytochrome c oxidase subunit V (COX5, complex IV of the electron-transport chain). As a structural and regulatory subunit of cytochrome c oxidase, cco-1 is required for efficient mitochondrial respiration and the final reduction of oxygen to water.

Tissue-specific knockdown of cco-1 (classically in body-wall muscle or neurons) produces a localized respiratory deficiency that, rather than remaining cell-autonomous, triggers a cell-non-autonomous stress signal. Stressed cells release Mitokines — secreted factors, notably the mitochondrial-derived peptide humanin and the small protein HPO (FGF21-like in mammals) — that travel to distal tissues and activate the Mitochondrial Unfolded Protein Response (UPRmt) systemically. This inter-tissue communication extends Lifespan and enhances stress resistance organism-wide.

> [!info] Systemic mitohormesis
> cco-1 knockdown is a canonical demonstration that mitochondrial stress in one tissue can be broadcast to others via mitokines, a key mechanism of systemic Mitohormesis.

Because complex IV sits downstream of the redox chain, cco-1 perturbation also perturbs Superoxide anion handling, linking respiratory architecture to redox set-point.

## Documents

- Mitohormesis (2014)
- Describes cco-1 knockdown as a model of cell-non-autonomous UPRmt activation via mitokines.

## Connections

- Mitochondrial Unfolded Protein Response: The systemic stress program activated by cco-1 knockdown.

nodes.label: indoline-5,6-dione
nodes.description: indoline-5,6-dione is a chemical. Indoline-5,6-dione is a reduced indole-dione structural relative of adrenochrome that can serve as an analytical reference and a redox intermediate in adrenochrome chemistry. Its 5,6-dione ring mirrors the quinone moiety of adrenochrome and participates in the same redox and nucleophilic-addition reactions. It is useful for distinguishing the oxidized quinone state from reduced leuco forms in chromatographic assays.

nodes.label: o-quinone
nodes.description: o-quinone is a chemical. Ortho-quinones are six-membered ring diketones with adjacent carbonyls that are highly electrophilic and redox-active. Catecholamines oxidize to ortho-quinone or aminochrome forms, which adduct nucleophilic protein residues and redox-cycle to superoxide. Adrenochrome and adrenolutin are examples of indole-derived ortho-quinone species.

nodes.label: Diabetes Mellitus
nodes.description:
Diabetes Mellitus is a group of metabolic diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels (Hyperglycemia) over a prolonged period. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to increased production of Reactive Oxygen Species in the Mitochondria, resulting in systemic Oxidative Stress and micro/macrovascular complications.
Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by high blood glucose levels. In the context of Aging and Epigenetics, diabetes is often viewed as a condition that accelerates the biological aging process through systemic inflammation and metabolic stress.
## 1. Epigenetic Mechanisms
Research has shown that chronic hyperglycemia can lead to lasting changes in the Epigenome, a phenomenon sometimes called "metabolic memory."
   DNA Methylation: Diabetic individuals often show altered DNA methylation patterns in genes related to insulin signaling and glucose metabolism.
   Histone Modifications: High glucose levels can alter histone acetylation and methylation, particularly affecting genes involved in inflammation and oxidative stress (e.g., through the activity of SIRT1 or mTOR).
## 2. Links to Aging
Diabetes and aging share many biological hallmarks:
   Senescence: Elevated glucose promotes the accumulation of senescent cells, particularly in the vasculature and kidneys.
   Epigenetic Clock: Studies using epigenetic clocks (like DNAmGrimAge) have shown that individuals with type 2 diabetes often have a higher biological age than their chronological age.

nodes.label: DNA
nodes.description:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the macromolecule that stores genetic information in nearly all organisms. Its sequence encodes the proteins and regulatory RNAs that govern cellular function, including the enzymes of catecholamine synthesis and the pigmentation pathways that produce Neuromelanin. While neuromelanin research emphasizes biochemistry, DNA provides the heritable framework that determines pigment-cell fate and PD susceptibility.

## Structure & Function

DNA is a double helix of nucleotide base pairs (A–T, G–C) organized into chromosomes and packaged with histones into chromatin. Genes are transcribed to RNA and translated to protein; regulatory elements control when and where expression occurs. In neurons, DNA must be protected from damage because post-mitotic cells cannot dilute lesions by division.

## Genetic Contributions to Neuromelanin & Parkinson's Disease

Several genes influence whether and how dopaminergic neurons synthesize and handle pigment. Tyrosinase-related enzymes (Tyrosinase, Dopachrome tautomerase) are encoded in the genome, as are the melanogenesis regulators (MITF, MC1R) linking cutaneous and neural pigment. PD risk is shaped by DNA variants in SNCA (e.g., A53T), LRRK2, PARKIN, PINK1, and GBA1, the last connecting pigment-cell lysosomal biology to Lysosomal Dysfunction. Mitochondrial DNA mutations affecting Complex I further modulate vulnerability.

## DNA Damage and Selective Vulnerability

nodes.label: MAPK
nodes.description:
The MAPK (Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase) pathway is a series of proteins in the cell that communicates a signal from a receptor on the surface of the cell to the DNA in the nucleus. It is a critical regulator of cell growth, survival, and stress response.
Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways are a chain of proteins in the cell that communicates a signal from a receptor on the surface of the cell to the DNA in the nucleus of the cell.
## 1. MAPK and Aging
The MAPK pathway becomes increasingly dysregulated during the aging process:
   Stress Response: p38 MAPK is activated in response to cellular stresses like DNA damage and oxidative stress, which accumulate with age.
   Senescence: Chronic activation of the p38 MAPK pathway is a key driver of the entry into senescence. Inhibition of p38 has been shown to delay senescence in human cells.
## 2. Regulation of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype
The MAPK pathway is one of the primary regulators of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype. It controls the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and proteases that senescent cells secrete, which can damage neighboring healthy cells and promote "inflammaging."
## 3. Interplay with Epigenetics

nodes.label: NADPH Oxidase
nodes.description:
NADPH oxidase (NOX) is a family of membrane-bound enzyme complexes whose primary physiological function is the deliberate production of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), specifically Superoxide Radicals.

## Biological Role
- Function: Catalyzes the transfer of electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen to form superoxide.
- Isoforms: Includes NOX1 through NOX5 and the dual oxidases (DUOX1/2).
- Immunity: NOX2 (gp91phox) is essential for the "respiratory burst" in phagocytes to kill bacteria.
- Signaling: Produces low levels of ROS for intracellular signaling cascades.

## Impact on Health
- Oxidative Stress: Overactivity is a major driver of tissue damage in Cardiovascular Disease, Diabetes Mellitus, and neurodegenerative disorders.
- Inflammation: ROS produced by NOX enzymes activate pro-inflammatory transcription factors like NF-κB.

## Structural Organization and Catalytic Mechanism
All NOX isoforms share a conserved catalytic core: the NOX (gp91phox) transmembrane subunit, which contains six transmembrane α-helices, two heme groups (coordinated by four histidine residues in helices III and V), and a cytoplasmic C-terminal NADPH- and FAD-binding domain. The electron transfer proceeds in a linear chain: NADPH → FAD → heme1 (inner) → heme2 (outer) → O₂ on the extracellular/luminal side, producing superoxide. The overall reaction is: $NADPH + 2O_2 \rightarrow NADP^+ + 2O_2^{\bullet-} + H^+$.

nodes.label: Superoxide
nodes.description:
Biochemical properties: Superoxide is an endogenous metabolite involved in cellular energy metabolism, redox reactions, or biosynthetic pathways. Its cellular concentration reflects metabolic flux and energy status.

Metabolic role: Superoxide participates as a substrate, intermediate, or product in key metabolic pathways including glycolysis, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, or one-carbon metabolism.

Regulation: Intracellular levels of Superoxide are maintained through biosynthesis, catabolism, and transport mechanisms. Its concentration serves as a metabolic signal that regulates enzyme activity and gene expression.

Clinical significance: Altered levels of Superoxide are observed in metabolic disorders, mitochondrial diseases, and nutritional deficiencies. Supplementation or pharmacological modulation of this metabolite has therapeutic potential.

nodes.label: Nitric Oxide
nodes.description:
Nitric Oxide ($NO^{\bullet}$) is a gaseous signaling molecule that plays critical roles in the cardiovascular, nervous, and immune systems. It is also a key player in the development of "nitrative stress."
## Biological Role
- Vasodilation: Relaxes vascular smooth muscle to regulate blood flow and pressure.
- Neurotransmission: Acts as a gaseous messenger in the brain.
- Immunity: Produced by macrophages to help kill bacteria and tumor cells.
## Interaction with Oxidative Stress
- Peroxynitrite Formation: Nitric oxide reacts nearly instantly with Superoxide anion to form Peroxynitrite, a highly reactive and damaging oxidant.
- Endothelial Dysfunction: In states of high oxidative stress, NO is "scavenged" by superoxide, reducing its bioavailability and leading to vascular disease.
## Medical Applications and Risks
- Therapy: Used as an inhaled medication to treat respiratory failure.
- Risk: High levels or prolonged exposure can lead to the formation of Methemoglobin, potentially causing Methemoglobinemia.

#

List of documents that mention this entity

nodes.label: eNOS
nodes.description:
eNOS (Endothelial Nitric Oxide Synthase, NOS3) is a constitutively expressed, calcium/calmodulin-dependent isoform of Nitric Oxide Synthase that produces low, pulsatile fluxes of Nitric Oxide critical for vascular homeostasis.
## Structure & Regulation
eNOS is a multidomain enzyme with an N-terminal oxygenase domain (containing heme, tetrahydrobiopterin/BH4, and L-arginine binding sites), a C-terminal reductase domain (binding NADPH, FAD, and FMN), and a calmodulin-binding hinge region. Its activity is tightly regulated by:
- Ca²⁺/Calmodulin: Transient increases in intracellular Ca²⁺ trigger calmodulin binding, enabling electron flow from the reductase to oxygenase domain.
- Phosphorylation: Activating phosphorylation at Ser1177 (by Akt/PKB, AMPK, PKA) increases electron flux; inhibitory phosphorylation at Thr495 decreases activity.
- Subcellular Localization: eNOS is targeted to plasma membrane caveolae via N-myristoylation and palmitoylation, where interaction with Caveolin-1 maintains it in an inactive state; Ca²⁺/calmodulin binding displaces caveolin.
- Protein Interactions: Hsp90 and Dynamin-2 enhance activity.
## Physiological Functions
- Vasodilation: eNOS produces NO that activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) in vascular smooth muscle, raising cGMP → vasorelaxation.
- Platelet Inhibition: NO inhibits platelet adhesion and aggregation.
- Leukocyte Adhesion: NO suppresses VCAM-1 and MCP-1 expression, reducing leukocyte recruitment.

nodes.label: Cardiac Hypertrophy
nodes.description:
Cardiac Hypertrophy is an adaptive enlargement of cardiomyocytes in response to increased workload, neurohumoral stimulation (e.g., Angiotensin II, endothelin-1), or mechanical stress. While initially compensatory—preserving stroke volume—sustained pathological hypertrophy progresses to heart failure, cardiomyopathy, and increased risk of arrhythmias. Distinguishing physiological hypertrophy (exercise-induced, reversible, benign) from pathological hypertrophy (pressure overload, maladaptive) is central to cardiovascular medicine.

## Mechanisms of Hypertrophic Growth

Pathological hypertrophy is driven by neurohumoral axes (renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, sympathetic) and mechanical stretch, activating signaling nodes including calcineurin–NFAT, MAPKs, and AKT–mTOR. These converge on transcription factors (e.g., GATA4, NFAT, MEF2) that induce fetal gene reprogramming (atrial natriuretic peptide, β-myosin heavy chain). Concurrently, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased ROS, and impaired autophagy worsen contractile and energetic reserve.

## Sirtuin Connections

Multiple sirtuins oppose pathological remodeling:

- SIRT1 protects against Cardiac Hypertrophy by deacetylating FoxO1 and FOXO3a, suppressing pathological gene expression programs, and activating PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis; it also promotes cardiac autophagy.

nodes.description: Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Aging discusses CML. It links high-AGE diets to insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and accelerated aging phenotypes. Carboxymethyllysine (CML) is one of the best-characterized advanced glycation end-products, formed from glycoxidation of lysine residues. It is a sensitive marker of AGE burden in diabetes, diet, and aging and binds RAGE to stimulate inflammation.

nodes.label: Malondialdehyde
nodes.description:
Malondialdehyde (MDA) is a reactive dialdehyde end-product of Lipid Peroxidation and a widely used Biomarker of chronic Oxidative Stress and oxidative damage to lipids, proteins, and DNA.

## Formation Chemistry and Sources

MDA is generated primarily from peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) with ≥3 double bonds—arachidonic acid (20:4, n-6), eicosapentaenoic acid (22:5, n-3), and docosahexaenoic acid (22:6, n-3). During Lipid Peroxidation, bicyclic endoperoxide intermediates cyclize and fragment to yield MDA as a three-carbon dialdehyde (CH₂(CHO)₂). The yield is non-stoichiometric—roughly 1 MDA per 20–40 fatty acids oxidized. MDA is also a byproduct of Thromboxane A₂ and Prostacyclin biosynthesis via the COX pathway (PGH₂ fragmentation), so not all MDA reflects oxidative damage—relevant to biomarker interpretation.

## Chemical Reactivity and Adduct Formation

At neutral pH MDA exists mainly as its enolate and is highly electrophilic. Its best-characterized DNA adduct is M₁dG (pyrimidopurinone deoxyguanosine), formed with the exocyclic amino group and N1 of deoxyguanosine. M₁dG is mutagenic (G→T transversions, frameshifts), repaired mainly by Nucleotide Excision Repair but not Base Excision Repair; elevated M₁dG occurs in colorectal cancer and Helicobacter pylori gastritis, linking MDA to carcinogenesis. MDA forms stable, fluorescent MDA-lysine cross-links on proteins (lysine/histidine), recognized by RAGE receptors, triggering inflammation. MDA modification o

nodes.label: Aspirin
nodes.description:
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, ASA) is a salicylate derivative and one of the most widely used medications globally. It irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 and -2 (COX-1/COX-2), blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxanes for the lifetime of the platelet (~7–10 days). This gives aspirin both anti-inflammatory/analgesic properties and a durable antiplatelet effect that underlies its use in cardiovascular prophylaxis.

## Mechanism of Action

Aspirin's acetyl group covalently modifies a serine residue (Ser529 in COX-1, Ser516 in COX-2) in the enzyme's active channel, permanently disabling prostaglandin G/H synthase activity. COX-derived prostaglandins (especially PGI2 from endothelium and TxA2 from platelets) normally balance vasodilation/anticoagulation against vasoconstriction/aggregation. By suppressing TxA2 synthesis in platelets—which cannot resynthesize COX—aspirin shifts hemostasis toward reduced clot formation at low (75–325 mg) doses.

## Interaction with COMT Genotype

Beyond COX, emerging pharmacogenetic evidence links aspirin response to COMT variation. The Val158Met polymorphism (rs4680) determines catecholamine and dopamine clearance efficiency and influences vascular tone and platelet reactivity. Observational and subgroup analyses suggest a stratified effect on Cardiovascular Disease risk:

nodes.description:
Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN) is a direct precursor to NAD+ and a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of NAD+ in cells, used to enhance mitochondrial energy production and support longevity pathways.

nodes.label: Preiss-Handler pathway
nodes.description:
The Preiss-Handler pathway is the de novo biosynthesis route to NAD+, the essential redox and signaling cofactor. It converts the amino acid Tryptophan (or dietary niacin/vitamin B3) into NAD+ through a sequence culminating in the ATP-dependent condensation of quinolinate with phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate to form nicotinic acid mononucleotide — the defining "Preiss-Handler reaction."

## Steps & Intermediates

Tryptophan is degraded via the kynurenine route to quinolinate (the committed precursor), whereas niacin enters from the opposite side as nicotinic acid. Quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase then produces nicotinic acid mononucleotide, which is converted to NMN and finally adenylylated to NAD+. This contrasts with the NAD+ Salvage Pathway, which recycles nicotinamide riboside/nicotinamide back to NAD+ via NAMPT.

## Regulation & Physiology

De novo synthesis is comparatively low-capacity and subordinate to salvage in most adult tissues, but it remains essential when salvage precursors are limiting. Because cellular NAD+ declines with Aging, understanding both de novo and salvage routes informs Longevity strategies using NAD+ precursors.

## Longevity Relevance

The pathway underpins why Vitamin B3 and tryptophan status influence NAD+ availability, linking nutrition to sirtuin and PARP activity and to the broader sirtuin–NAD+–autophagy longevity network.

> [!info] De Novo vs. Salvage

nodes.label: NMNAT
nodes.description:
NMNAT (Nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase) is a family of enzymes that catalyzes the final committed step in NAD+ biosynthesis: the conversion of nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) or nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) to NAD+ or NAAD (nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide), respectively. In mammals, three distinct isoforms — NMNAT1, NMNAT2, and NMNAT3 — localize to the nucleus, cytoplasm/Golgi apparatus, and mitochondria, respectively. Each isoform serves as the rate-limiting enzyme for NAD+ production within its respective subcellular compartment, making NMNAT a critical node in cellular energy metabolism and redox homeostasis. Beyond its catalytic role, NMNAT — particularly NMNAT2 — possesses a neuroprotective chaperone function that is independent of NAD+ synthesis, enabling it to stabilize misfolded proteins and prevent toxic aggregation implicated in neurodegenerative diseases.

## Structure & Domains

All three NMNAT isoforms share a conserved Rossmann-fold catalytic domain composed of an α/β/α sandwich architecture, characteristic of nucleotide-binding enzymes. The active site binds both the substrate (NMN or NaMN) and ATP, catalyzing the transfer of an AMP moiety to the mononucleotide to form the dinucleotide product. The catalytic mechanism follows a sequential Bi Bi ordered mechanism: ATP binds first, followed by NMN, and products are released in the order of pyrophosphate then NAD+.

nodes.label: PARP2
nodes.description:
PARP2 (poly[ADP-ribose] polymerase 2) is a member of the PARP enzyme family that, together with PARP1, accounts for the majority of DNA-damage-induced poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation (PARylation) in the nucleus.

## Structure & Mechanism of Action

- Contains a catalytic ADP-ribosyltransferase domain and a WGR/DNA-binding region that recognizes DNA strand breaks.
- Reaction: upon binding DNA damage, PARP2 consumes NAD+ to transfer ADP-ribose units onto target proteins (and itself), forming branched PAR chains that recruit DNA Repair machinery — particularly for Base Excision Repair and single-strand break repair.
- PARP2 is especially important at the later stages of the DNA-damage response and in maintaining genome and telomere stability.

## Physiological Role & NAD+/Sirtuin Crosstalk

> [!important] Competition with sirtuins
> Because both PARPs and sirtuins use NAD+ as substrate, chronic PARP activation depletes the cellular NAD⁺ pool and thereby restrains NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases. Elevated PARP2 activity specifically lowers SIRT1 activity both by substrate competition and by binding directly to the Sirt1 promoter to repress its transcription. This positions PARP2 at the intersection of Genomic Instability, NAD⁺ metabolism, and the metabolic/longevity functions of SIRT1 — a rationale for NAD⁺-boosting strategies (Nicotinamide Riboside, NMN) and PARP inhibitors in aging research.

## Documents

- Nicotinamide Riboside Review

nodes.label: SIRT4
nodes.description:
SIRT4 (Sirtuin 4) is a mitochondrial sirtuin classified in phylogenetic Class II, which includes sirtuins from bacteria, insects, nematodes, mould fungus, and protozoans — making SIRT4 and Class II sirtuins among the most ancient in evolutionary terms. Unlike SIRT1 and SIRT3, SIRT4's primary enzymatic activity is mono-ADP-ribosylation rather than deacetylation, though it also exhibits weak deacetylase activity.

## Enzymatic Activity

SIRT4 is a mono-ADP-ribosyl transferase using NAD⁺ as a donor (see NAD+). It generates OAADPr as a by-product. No robust deacetylase activity has been confirmed as a primary function, though weak deacetylase activity has been reported under specific conditions. This makes SIRT4 one of only two mammalian sirtuins (along with SIRT6) whose primary characterised activity is mono-ADP-ribosylation.

## Subcellular Localisation

Mitochondrial — SIRT4, along with SIRT3 and SIRT5, is one of the three mitochondrial sirtuins, localised to the mitochondrial matrix.

## Metabolic Functions

### Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GDH) Regulation

The primary characterised function of SIRT4 is regulation of GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase) in pancreatic β-cells:

- GDH regulates glutamate and glutamine metabolism, promotes ATP synthesis, and enhances insulin secretion.
- SIRT4 mono-ADP-ribosylates GDH, thereby inhibiting its activity and slowing the conversion of glutamate into α-ketoglutarate.
- Consequence: reduced amino-acid-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic

nodes.label: SIRT5
nodes.description:
SIRT5 (Sirtuin 5) is a mitochondrial sirtuin and the sole mammalian member of phylogenetic Class III sirtuins — a class distributed widely in all prokaryotes (both bacteria and archaea). This deep evolutionary conservation positions SIRT5 (along with SIRT4 of Class II) as one of the most ancient mammalian sirtuins.

## Enzymatic Activity

Unlike most other sirtuins, SIRT5 possesses very weak NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase activity. Its primary catalytic functions are lysine desuccinylation, demalonylation, and deglutarylation — the removal of negatively charged five-carbon succinyl, three-carbon malonyl, and five-carbon glutaryl groups from lysine residues. This broad deacylase activity allows SIRT5 to regulate mitochondrial metabolism at multiple nodes simultaneously. The reactions consume NAD+ and produce nicotinamide and the corresponding acyl-ADP-ribose by-products.

## Subcellular Localisation

Mitochondrial — SIRT5 is one of the three mitochondrial sirtuins, along with SIRT3 and SIRT4, localised to the mitochondrial matrix. SIRT5 has also been detected in the cytosol and nucleus under specific conditions, suggesting context-dependent subcellular trafficking.

## Evolutionary Classification

SIRT5 belongs to Class III, which:

- Contains sirtuins broadly distributed in all prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea)
- Represents one of the most ancient sirtuin lineages
- Along with Class II and Class U (undetermined), was among the earliest sirtuin classes to evolve

nodes.label: Gut Microbiome
nodes.description:
Overview: The Gut Microbiome comprises the trillions of microorganisms—bacteria, archaea, viruses, and fungi—residing in the Gastrointestinal Tract. Dominated by the phyla Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes, it functions as a metabolic and immune organ in its own right.

Physiological function: The microbiome ferments dietary fiber into Short-chain Fatty Acids (notably Butyrate), synthesizes vitamins, trains the Immune System, maintains barrier integrity, and modulates Metabolism and Inflammation. It communicates with the brain via the Gut-Brain Axis using neural, endocrine, and immune signals.

Relevance to aging and disease: With Aging, microbial diversity often declines and Dysbiosis emerges, correlating with inflammaging, metabolic dysfunction, and neurodegeneration. Dietary patterns, Fasting, and exercise shift composition toward beneficial taxa. Senotherapeutics such as fisetin have been reported to remodel the microbiome alongside healthspan benefits.

Research context: The microbiome is a target for interventions—probiotics, prebiotics, fermented foods, and fecal microbiota transplantation—aimed at extending healthspan and mitigating age-related disease.

- A systematic review positioning the gut microbiome at the core of age-associated immune and metabolic change.

nodes.label: Muscle Atrophy
nodes.description:
Muscle atrophy is the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, cross-sectional area, and strength. It arises whenever net muscle protein balance becomes negative—i.e., protein degradation outpaces protein synthesis. Atrophy is a hallmark of sarcopenia (age-related), cachexia, disuse (immobilization/bed rest), denervation, and numerous chronic diseases.

## Etiology & Pathophysiology

Atrophy reflects coordinated molecular reprogramming:

- Suppressed synthesis: Inhibition of the mTORC1 / PI3K–Akt axis reduces translational initiation and ribosome biogenesis.
- Activated degradation: The ubiquitin–proteasome system is upregulated via transcription factors of the FoxO family, inducing the E3 ligases Atrogin-1 (MAFbx) and MuRF1 (Muscle RING-finger 1).
- Autophagy/mitophagy: Excessive mitophagy and lysosomal flux can remove mitochondrial and contractile components.
- Inflammation & oxidative stress: TNF-α, NF-κB signaling, and oxidative stress amplify catabolism.

## Clinical Presentation & Biomarkers

Manifestations include reduced muscle volume, weakness, fatigability, and impaired mobility. Molecular biomarkers include elevated circulating Atrogin-1/MuRF1 expression, myofiber atrophy, and shifts toward fast-to-slow or pathological fiber typing. MRI/DEXA quantify lean mass loss.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Membrane Potential
nodes.description:
The Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (ΔΨm) is the electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane generated by the Mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain. It drives ATP synthesis and maintains mitochondrial integrity; its collapse (depolarization) is an early event in oxidative neuronal injury.

## Measurement in the methylene blue study

The methylene blue derivative study quantified ΔΨm in HT-22 cells by two methods [^1]:

- TMRE/NAO FRET: glutamate (20 mM, 12 h) depolarized mitochondria (↑ NAO fluorescence), an effect attenuated by Methylene blue, Toluidine Blue O, Phenothiazine, and 2-Chlorophenothiazine (EC50s 17.72, 1.54, 21.18, 45.09 nM). Chlorpromazine, Promethazine, and Neutral Red were far weaker.
- JC-1 dye: glutamate shifted JC-1 from polymer (red) to monomer (green); MB co-treatment preserved the polymer signal [^1].

A strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.9456) linked ΔΨm preservation with neuroprotection across the compound series [^1].

## Documents

- ΔΨm depolarization by glutamate is attenuated most potently by TB and MB; preservation of ΔΨm correlates strongly with viability.

- Toluidine Blue O — most potent ΔΨm preservation.

nodes.label: PGC-1α
nodes.description:
PGC-1α (encoded by PPARGC1A) is a transcriptional coactivator that serves as the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative metabolism, and antioxidant defense. It links external stimuli (exercise, cold, fasting) to the activation of mitochondrial and metabolic gene programs.

## Structure & Domains

- N-terminal activation domain — interacts with nuclear receptors (PPARγ, ERRalpha) and CREB; recruits P300/CBP and the Mediator complex
- Central regulatory region — harbors phosphorylation sites for AMPK and p38 MAPK, as well as acetylation sites targeted by SIRT1 and GCN5
- C-terminal domain — contains an RNA recognition motif (RRM) and serine/arginine-rich (RS) domain that couples transcription to pre-mRNA splicing

## Mechanism of Action

PGC-1α lacks intrinsic DNA-binding activity and exerts its coactivator functions through physical interaction with diverse transcription factors:

- SIRT1 deacetylation: SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α at multiple lysine residues (e.g., K778) in an NAD+-dependent manner, enhancing its transcriptional activity toward mitochondrial genes (PMID 15592568, 17086196). This couples the cellular NAD+/NADH ratio to oxidative capacity.
- AMPK phosphorylation: AMPK phosphorylates PGC-1α at Thr177 and Ser538, promoting its deacetylation by SIRT1 and increasing its stability. This reciprocal regulation establishes a feed-forward loop linking mitochondrial biogenesis to metabolic state.

nodes.label: Muscle Hypertrophy
nodes.description:
Muscle hypertrophy is the expansion of skeletal muscle size via increased myofibrillar protein accretion, principally triggered by resistance exercise and anabolic stimuli. It is the physiological counterpoint to Muscle Atrophy.

## Mechanism of Action & Physiology

Hypertrophy requires a positive net protein balance: mechanical tension and metabolic stress activate mTORC1 (via PI3K/Akt and leucine sensing), boosting translation, while suppressing degradation through the Ubiquitin-Proteasome System and FOXO–Atrogin-1/MuRF1 axis. Satellite cell proliferation adds myonuclei to support growth.

## Applications

Resistance training, adequate protein/Leucine, and Creatine supplementation are first-line. Urolithin A may augment hypertrophy by enhancing mitochondrial function, ATP supply, and recovery, supporting longer, more intense training.

## Connections

- mTORC1 → promotes → Muscle Hypertrophy
- FOXO / Atrogin-1 → opposes → Muscle Hypertrophy
- Urolithin A → supports → Muscle Hypertrophy

nodes.label: LKB1
nodes.description:
LKB1 (Liver Kinase B1), also known as STK11, is a master upstream serine/threonine kinase that regulates cellular energy metabolism, cell polarity, and tumour suppression. LKB1 phosphorylates and activates [14 AMPK-family kinases](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15448698), making it a central node in the cellular stress response network.

## Structure and Domains

LKB1 is a 433-amino-acid protein containing an N-terminal nuclear localisation signal (NLS), a central serine/threonine kinase domain, and a C-terminal regulatory domain. LKB1 functions as a heterotrimeric complex with two regulatory subunits:

- STRAD (STE20-related adaptor): A pseudokinase that binds LKB1 and promotes its translocation from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
- MO25 (Mouse protein 25): A scaffold protein that stabilises the LKB1-STRAD interaction and enhances LKB1 catalytic activity by ~100-fold.

Without STRAD and MO25 binding, LKB1 remains in the nucleus and exhibits minimal kinase activity. This tripartite complex is essential for LKB1 function.

## Regulation of AMPK and Energy Homeostasis

LKB1 is the primary upstream kinase that activates AMPK in response to energy stress:

1. Energy Stress Detection: Rising AMP:ATP or ADP:ATP ratios are sensed by AMPK, which undergoes conformational changes promoting LKB1-mediated phosphorylation.
2. Phosphorylation: LKB1 phosphorylates AMPK at Thr172 within the activation loop of the AMPK α-subunit, increasing AMPK activity by >100-fold.

nodes.label: TLR3
nodes.description:
TLR3 (Toll-like receptor 3) is an endosomal toll-like receptor expressed on immune and epithelial cells that recognizes double-stranded RNA (dsRNA)—including viral replication intermediates and the synthetic analog poly(I:C). Unlike most TLRs, TLR3 signals exclusively through the TRIF (TICAM1) adaptor rather than MyD88.

## Structure & Localization

TLR3 is a type I transmembrane glycoprotein with an extracellular leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domain for ligand sensing and a cytoplasmic Toll/IL-1 receptor (TIR) domain that recruits TRIF. It resides primarily in endosomes/lysosomes where it encounters dsRNA internalized or generated during infection.

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

1. dsRNA binding induces TLR3 dimerization and recruitment of TRIF via its TIR domain.
2. TRIF engages TRAF3 → activates TBK1/IKKε → phosphorylates IRF3 → type I interferon (IFN-β) production.
3. TRIF also activates RIPK1/TRAF6 → NF-κB and MAPK pathways → pro-inflammatory cytokine expression (TNF-α, IL-6).
4. The TLR3/TRIF axis can converge on the NF-κB/STAT1 axis driving inflammatory gene programs.

## Physiological Function

TLR3 is a frontline antiviral sensor initiating interferon and inflammatory responses. It also contributes to tissue responses to endogenous dsRNA-like signals during injury and sterile inflammation.

## Pathology & Clinical Relevance

- Excessive TLR3/TRIF signaling underlies viral encephalitis, autoimmune/inflammatory conditions, and exaggerated responses to tissue injury.

nodes.label: TRIF
nodes.description:

- Interferon branch: TRIF recruits TRAF3 → TBK1/IKKε phosphorylates IRF3 → dimerization and translocation to nucleus → type I interferon (IFN-β) transcription.
- Inflammatory branch: TRIF engages RIPK1 and TRAF6 → activation of NF-κB and MAPK pathways → TNF-α, IL-6, and other cytokines.
- STAT1 axis: TRIF-dependent pathways converge on the NF-κB/STAT1 axis, amplifying inflammatory gene expression.

TRIF mediates host defense against viruses (via dsRNA-sensing TLR3) and Gram-negative bacteria (via TLR4), balancing interferon induction with controlled inflammation.

nodes.label: Ubiquitin-Proteasome System
nodes.description:
The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is the primary pathway for selective protein degradation; it regulates TFEB levels via E3 ligases like STUB1 which target phosphorylated TFEB.
## Function
The UPS degrades ubiquitin-tagged proteins via the 26S proteasome. Ubiquitin is conjugated by E1-E2-E3 cascade and recycled by deubiquitinases (DUBs).
## Crosstalk with Autophagy
UPS and Autophagy are complementary degradation systems. When the proteasome is impaired (e.g., aging, proteotoxic stress), autophagy is upregulated as a compensatory mechanism.
The Ubiquitin-Proteasome System (UPS) is the primary mechanism for the regulated degradation of short-lived, damaged, or misfolded proteins within the cell.
## Mechanism
Proteins destined for degradation are tagged with a small protein called Ubiquitin. These ubiquitinated proteins are then recognized and broken down by a large protein complex called the proteasome.
## Impairment in Parkinson's Disease
UPS dysfunction is a hallmark of Parkinson's Disease and is closely linked to the formation of protein inclusions.
- Lewy Bodies: The presence of Ubiquitin and p62 in Lewy Bodies indicates that the cell has attempted, but failed, to degrade aggregated Alpha-synuclein via the UPS.
- Neuromelanin Interference: The progressive accumulation of Neuromelanin-filled autophagic structures can physically interfere with the UPS, leading to a general failure of cellular proteostasis.
- Selective Vulnerability: UPS impairment is specifically observed

nodes.label: Mitochondrial Dysfunction
nodes.description:
Mitochondrial Dysfunction refers to the impairment of mitochondrial processes, particularly the production of ATP and the regulation of cellular metabolism.
## In Parkinson's Disease
Mitochondrial dysfunction is a central feature of Parkinson's Disease and is thought to be both a cause and a consequence of other pathological processes.
- Energy Failure: Neurons in the Substantia Nigra have high energy demands, making them particularly sensitive to mitochondrial impairment.
- Oxidative Stress: Defective mitochondria are a major source of reactive oxygen species, leading to increased Oxidative Stress.
- Link to Neuromelanin: The accumulation of Neuromelanin-filled autophagic structures may interfere with the turnover of damaged mitochondria, a process known as Mitophagy.
- Toxin Sensitivity: Many neurotoxins associated with PD, such as MPTP, act by inhibiting the mitochondrial respiratory chain (specifically Complex I).

nodes.label: Senolytics
nodes.description:
Senolytics are a class of small molecules and peptides that selectively induce death in Senescent Cells by targeting SCAPs. The conceptual breakthrough (Kirkland, Tchkonia, Zhu and colleagues) was that senescent cells are not merely arrested but are actively kept alive by upregulated pro-survival pathways; transiently disabling those pathways tips them into Apoptosis while sparing healthy cells (Zhu et al., Nat Med 2015; PMID 25594185).

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

- SCAP disruption: Senolytics neutralize anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members and survival kinases, permitting BAX/BAK-driven MOMP and Caspase-3 execution.
- Heterogeneity of targets: Different senolytic classes exploit different dominant SCAPs, underlying cell-type selectivity.

## Key Senolytics

- Dasatinib + Quercetin (D+Q): First-in-class combination; dasatinib inhibits tyrosine kinases, quercetin inhibits BCL-2 family proteins and PI3K. Shown to clear senescent cells in vitro, in aged mice, and in human trials.
- Navitoclax (ABT-263): Potent BCL-2/BCL-XL inhibitor; highly effective but limited by thrombocytopenia from platelet BCL-XL dependence.
- ABT-737: Precursor BH3-mimetic that inhibits BCL-2/BCL-XL/BCL-W.
- Fisetin: Naturally occurring flavonoid with broad senolytic activity across tissues.
- Piperlongumine: Alkylating-agent-derived senolytic engaging oxidative-stress–related SCAPs.

nodes.label: Senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathways
nodes.description:
Senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathways (SCAPs) are a network of pro-survival mechanisms that allow Senescent Cells to persist and resist Apoptosis despite high levels of cellular stress, DNA Damage, and mitochondrial leak (e.g., Minority MOMP). Senescent cells are "primed to die" yet survive because SCAPs raise the apoptotic threshold—a vulnerability that Senolytics exploit by tipping the cell back toward death.

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

- BCL-2 family upregulation: Senescent cells elevate anti-apoptotic members—BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL-1, BCL-W—that sequester pro-apoptotic BAX/BAK and prevent MOMP (Zhu et al., Nat Med 2015; PMID 25594185).
- Survival kinase signaling: PI3K/Akt and related pro-growth cascades promote survival and metabolic fitness in the arrested state.
- p53 modulation: Senescence-associated p53 activity is rewired—often blunted for death execution while retained for arrest—so the cell stays arrested but not eliminated.
- Unfolded Protein Response (UPR): The UPR (PERK, ATF6, IRE1) and ER Stress buffering support proteostasis under chronic SASP burdens.
- Senescence-associated mitochondrial dysfunction (SAMD): Metabolic adaptations favoring survival over death.

## Role in Senescence

- SCAPs are the reason senescent cells accumulate rather than self-eliminate, underpinning Inflammaging and tissue dysfunction.

nodes.label: Neurotoxicity
nodes.description:
Neurotoxicity denotes the capacity of a chemical, drug, or endogenous metabolite to injure or kill neurons, disrupting central nervous system structure and function. Within this knowledge graph, neurotoxicity arises in two distinct contexts: (1) as a risk of SIRT2 overactivity, where excessive deacetylation impairs neuronal protein-homeostasis and microtubule defenses, and (2) as a hypothetical concern tied to adrenochrome-derived oxidative pressure in senotherapeutic strategies.

## Mechanism / Structure

> [!info] SIRT2 overactivity and neuronal damage
> Direct SIRT2 activation is generally avoided therapeutically because overactivity is linked to neurotoxicity in neurodegenerative contexts. Excessive SIRT2-dependent deacetylation may compromise microtubule stability and protein-homeostasis (proteostasis) networks that neurons depend on heavily. Consequently, SIRT2 inhibitors — rather than activators — are pursued for Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease, contrasting with the activation-seeking strategy used for most other sirtuins such as SIRT1 or SIRT3.

This distinguishes SIRT2 from its siblings: whereas SIRT1/SIRT3 activation is broadly sought for metabolic and cardioprotective benefit, SIRT2 sits on the opposite side of the risk–benefit curve because of its neuronal liabilities.

A separate, more speculative thread connects neurotoxicity to adrenochrome. A mechanistic hypothesis proposes adrenochrome or its derivatives as senotherap

Dopamine is a major Neurotransmitters in the brain that plays a critical role in reward, motivation, motor control, and Executive Function.
## Oxidation and Pigmentation
Like other Catecholamines, Dopamine can undergo Oxidation (spontaneous or enzymatic) to form reactive intermediates:

- Parkinson's Disease: Characterized by a lack of dopamine in certain brain regions.

nodes.label: Fibroblasts
nodes.description:
Fibroblasts are the principal resident cells of connective tissue. They synthesize and maintain the Extracellular Matrix (ECM) and Collagen fibers that form the structural stroma supporting epithelia, blood vessels, and organs. They are mesenchymally derived, spindle-shaped, and motile, and they play a central role in tissue homeostasis, wound repair, and fibrosis.

## Structure and Identity

Fibroblasts are characterized by an elongated, fibroblast-like morphology, a prominent rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi (reflecting active protein secretion), and expression of markers such as vimentin, fibroblast-specific protein 1 (FSP1/S100A4), platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha/beta (PDGFRα/β), and TE7. They are distinct from the related but contractile myofibroblasts (α-SMA+), which appear during wound healing and fibrosis. Fibroblasts are heterogeneous and tissue-specific: dermal, pulmonary, cardiac, and tendon fibroblasts differ in transcriptional profile and function.

## Physiological Function

The core function of fibroblasts is ECM production—secreting structural proteins (collagen types I, III, and V), glycoproteins (fibronectin, laminin), and proteoglycans—together with matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that remodel the scaffold. They respond to injury by proliferating and migrating into the wound bed, depositing granulation tissue, and coordinating with immune cells. In homeostasis they continually turnover matrix to preserve tissue mechanical integrity.

nodes.label: Catechol
nodes.description:
Catechol (pyrocatechol, 1,2-dihydroxybenzene, C₆H₄(OH)₂) is an organic compound consisting of a benzene ring bearing two adjacent hydroxyl groups (ortho-diphenol). It is the parent structural scaffold of the catecholamine family, which includes Dopamine, Norepinephrine, and Epinephrine. Catechol is a white crystalline solid that readily oxidizes to form ortho-quinones, a process mechanistically analogous to the oxidation of Epinephrine to Adrenochrome.

## Chemical Properties

Catechol exhibits two sequential acid dissociations: pKₐ₁ ≈ 9.5 (first hydroxyl) and pKₐ₂ ≈ 12.8 (second hydroxyl). It is soluble in water, ethanol, and diethyl ether. A classic qualitative test is the formation of an intense green color upon reaction with FeCl₃, characteristic of phenols. Catechol forms stable complexes with many metal ions, including Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, and Al³⁺, a property relevant to its biological metal-chelation activity.

Autoxidation & Redox Cycling: In neutral to alkaline solution, catechol undergoes autoxidation via sequential one-electron transfers: catechol → o-semiquinone radical → o-benzoquinone. This reaction generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide (O₂⁻), hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), and hydroxyl radical (•OH), establishing a redox-cycling loop that can deplete cellular antioxidants like Glutathione. The instability of catechol under alkaline conditions leads to rapid polymerization into brown melanin-like pigments — a process closely related to the browning of Ep

nodes.label: Quinone
nodes.description:
Quinones are a class of organic compounds derived from aromatic compounds (such as benzene or naphthalene) by conversion of an even number of -CH= groups into -C(=O)- groups, resulting in a fully conjugated cyclic dione structure.

## Role in Aminochromes
The formation of a quinone moiety is the first step in the Oxidation of Catecholamines to Aminochromes.
- Catechol to o-Quinone: The two hydroxyl groups on the benzene ring of a catecholamine (like Dopamine or Epinephrine) are oxidized to carbonyl groups, forming an unstable ortho-quinone (o-quinone).
- Cyclization: This o-quinone intermediate then undergoes internal cyclization to form the Indoline ring system found in Adrenochrome and Dopaminochrome.

## Biochemical Properties
Quinones are highly reactive and are potent electrophiles. They can react with cellular nucleophiles (like glutathione or proteins) or participate in Redox Cycling, generating Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS).
