nodes.label: LIPL-3
nodes.description: LIPL-3 is a lysosomal lipase in C. elegans that, like LIPL-1, co-localizes with the lysosomal marker PGP-2 and contributes to intralysosomal lipid hydrolysis. It is transcriptionally induced by HLH-30 under fasting conditions, enabling the breakdown of lipid droplets delivered via lipophagy. Together with other lipl family members, LIPL-3 is required for efficient energy mobilization during starvation. Its lysosomal localization anchors it within the autophagy-lysosomal degradative system.

nodes.label: MAX
nodes.description: The mammalian transcription factor MAX, a partner of MYC, is the functional homolog of C. elegans MXL-3, as expression of mouse MAX in worms rescued the mxl-3 mutant phenotype. This conservation indicates that the MYC/MAX network's repression of lysosomal and metabolic genes is an ancient feature retained from nematodes to mammals. The rescue experiment directly demonstrates mechanistic equivalence between the worm repressor and its mammalian counterpart. It strengthens the translational relevance of MXL-3 studies to human lipid and lysosomal regulation.

nodes.label: Lipophagy
nodes.description: Lipophagy—the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets—is conserved across metazoans, as shown by the fact that inactivation of the autophagy genes lgg-1 and lgg-2 in C. elegans leads to increased fat accumulation. By delivering lipid droplets to lysosomes for lipase-mediated hydrolysis, lipophagy mobilizes stored energy during fasting. The conservation from worms to mammals indicates an ancient and essential role for autophagy in lipid homeostasis. Defective lipophagy contributes to hepatic steatosis and metabolic disease in higher organisms.

nodes.label: Metazoans
nodes.description: Lipophagy—the selective autophagic degradation of lipid droplets—is conserved across metazoans, as shown by the fact that inactivation of the autophagy genes lgg-1 and lgg-2 in C. elegans leads to increased fat accumulation. By delivering lipid droplets to lysosomes for lipase-mediated hydrolysis, lipophagy mobilizes stored energy during fasting. The conservation from worms to mammals indicates an ancient and essential role for autophagy in lipid homeostasis. Defective lipophagy contributes to hepatic steatosis and metabolic disease in higher organisms.

nodes.label: DAF-2
nodes.description: DAF-2, the C. elegans insulin/IGF-1 receptor ortholog, partially regulates MXL-3 expression such that impaired insulin signaling leads to modest repression of mxl-3 transcription. This places MXL-3 downstream of the insulin-signaling axis that broadly controls metabolism and longevity in worms. The partial effect indicates that additional nutrient and developmental inputs also govern mxl-3, consistent with its role as a multifactorial repressor. The linkage reinforces the canonical insulin→autophagy/lipid regulatory cascade.

nodes.label: MXL-3 expression

The partial effect indicates that additional nutrient and developmental inputs also govern mxl-3, consistent with its role as a multifactorial repressor. nodes.label: CeTOR
nodes.description: CeTOR, the C. elegans ortholog of mTOR, controls HLH-30 at the transcriptional level; inactivation of CeTOR induces hlh-30 expression, increasing the abundance of the master degradative transcription factor. This upstream control parallels mammalian mTORC1's post-translational repression of TFEB, adding a transcriptional layer in worms. By inducing HLH-30, CeTOR inhibition engages the full lysosomal-autophagic and lipolytic program. The relationship confirms mTOR as an evolutionarily conserved suppressor of the TFEB/HLH-30 axis.

nodes.label: HLH-30 transcription
nodes.description: CeTOR, the C. elegans ortholog of mTOR, controls HLH-30 at the transcriptional level; inactivation of CeTOR induces hlh-30 expression, increasing the abundance of the master degradative transcription factor. This upstream control parallels mammalian mTORC1's post-translational repression of TFEB, adding a transcriptional layer in worms. By inducing HLH-30, CeTOR inhibition engages the full lysosomal-autophagic and lipolytic program. The relationship confirms mTOR as an evolutionarily conserved suppressor of the TFEB/HLH-30 axis.

nodes.label: Starvation survival
nodes.description: HLH-30 is required for survival during prolonged starvation; hlh-30 mutant animals die prematurely under nutrient-deprived conditions due to their inability to mount sufficient autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lipid mobilization. By activating the clearance and energy-mobilization programs, HLH-30 enables worms to withstand food absence. This essential role mirrors the dependence of mammalian cells on TFEB for stress resilience. The phenotype establishes HLH-30 as a critical effector of adaptive starvation responses.

nodes.label: Peroxisome Biogenesis Network
nodes.description: The peroxisome biogenesis network receives material from autophagy when damaged peroxisomes are engulfed and fragmented, generating precursors that can be reassembled into functional peroxisomes. This autophagic-lysosomal processing of peroxisomal components allows recycling of membrane and matrix constituents to support new organelle formation. The relationship couples selective peroxisome degradation (pexophagy) to organelle turnover and renewal. It highlights autophagy's role not only in disposal but also in enabling peroxisome homeostasis.

nodes.label: PERO1
nodes.description: PERO1 functions as a sensor of oleic acid accumulation on damaged peroxisomes, triggering autophagic removal of these defective organelles. By detecting lipid imbalance indicative of peroxisomal dysfunction, PERO1 initiates quality-control degradation that prevents the propagation of impaired organelles. This lipid-sensing mechanism links metabolic state to organelle surveillance. The pathway exemplifies how selective autophagy integrates metabolic cues to maintain peroxisome integrity.

nodes.label: Oleic acid accumulation
nodes.description: PERO1 functions as a sensor of oleic acid accumulation on damaged peroxisomes, triggering autophagic removal of these defective organelles. By detecting lipid imbalance indicative of peroxisomal dysfunction, PERO1 initiates quality-control degradation that prevents the propagation of impaired organelles. This lipid-sensing mechanism links metabolic state to organelle surveillance. The pathway exemplifies how selective autophagy integrates metabolic cues to maintain peroxisome integrity.

nodes.label: Selective Autophagy
nodes.description: Selective autophagy targets damaged peroxisomes for degradation through a process termed pexophagy, in which ubiquitin tagging of peroxisomal proteins and recruitment of ESCRT (endosomal sorting complex required for transport) machinery mark the organelle for autophagic engulfment. This cargo-specific pathway contrasts with bulk autophagy by requiring receptor proteins that bridge the peroxisome to the autophagosomal membrane. Pexophagy protects cells from the oxidative and metabolic damage caused by defective peroxisomes. Its failure leads to accumulation of aberrant organelles and disease.

nodes.label: Damaged peroxisomes
nodes.description: Selective autophagy targets damaged peroxisomes for degradation through a process termed pexophagy, in which ubiquitin tagging of peroxisomal proteins and recruitment of ESCRT (endosomal sorting complex required for transport) machinery mark the organelle for autophagic engulfment. This cargo-specific pathway contrasts with bulk autophagy by requiring receptor proteins that bridge the peroxisome to the autophagosomal membrane. Pexophagy protects cells from the oxidative and metabolic damage caused by defective peroxisomes. Its failure leads to accumulation of aberrant organelles and disease.

nodes.label: PEX1
nodes.description: PEX1 is an ATPase essential for peroxisome membrane assembly and matrix protein import, operating as part of the peroxisomal AAA (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities) machinery. Loss of PEX1 causes a complete lack of functional peroxisomes, as import and biogenesis cannot proceed. This essential role makes PEX1 mutations among the most common causes of peroxisome biogenesis disorders. The gene thus sits at the foundation of peroxisome formation and metabolic competence.

nodes.label: Peroxisome membrane assembly
nodes.description: PEX1 is an ATPase essential for peroxisome membrane assembly and matrix protein import, operating as part of the peroxisomal AAA (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities) machinery. Loss of PEX1 causes a complete lack of functional peroxisomes, as import and biogenesis cannot proceed. This essential role makes PEX1 mutations among the most common causes of peroxisome biogenesis disorders. The gene thus sits at the foundation of peroxisome formation and metabolic competence.

nodes.label: ABCD1
nodes.description: Mutations in ABCD1, encoding a peroxisomal ATP-binding cassette transporter for very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD). Impaired ABCD1 disrupts VLCFA import into peroxisomes for beta-oxidation, leading to toxic accumulation of VLCFAs in adrenal cortex and central nervous system white matter. The resulting demyelination and adrenal insufficiency define the clinical syndrome. The disorder illustrates how peroxisomal transport defects produce severe neurodegeneration and underscores the importance of peroxisomal lipid homeostasis.

nodes.label: Adrenoleukodystrophy
nodes.description:
Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) is a severe genetic disorder often caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene, which encodes a transporter responsible for moving very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) into the Peroxisome for degradation. Defective VLCFA transport impairs peroxisomal lipid turnover and Beta-Oxidation, leading to the toxic accumulation of VLCFAs. This accumulation induces severe oxidative stress and inflammation, primarily damaging the myelin sheath in the brain and affecting the adrenal glands. It represents a significant form of peroxisomal dysfunction that highlights the critical role of these organelles in lipid homeostasis.

## Pathophysiology

ALD is caused by ABCD1 mutations, leading to accumulation of VLCFAs and peroxisomal dysfunction. Impaired Autophagy contributes to neuroinflammation and demyelination.

nodes.label: Zellweger syndrome
nodes.description: Zellweger syndrome, the most severe form of the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, is caused by mutations in PEX genes required for peroxisome assembly and matrix protein import. Affected individuals lack functional peroxisomes, leading to accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, bile acid intermediates, and pipecolic acid, with profound neurologic, hepatic, and skeletal abnormalities. The spectrum's severity correlates with the degree of residual peroxisomal function. These disorders highlight the non-redundant essentiality of peroxisomes in human development.

nodes.label: PEX gene mutations

Affected individuals lack functional peroxisomes, leading to accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, bile acid intermediates, and pipecolic acid, with profound neurologic, hepatic, and skeletal abnormalities. The spectrum's severity correlates with the degree of residual peroxisomal function. These disorders highlight the non-redundant essentiality of peroxisomes in human development.

nodes.label: Lysosomal biogenesis
nodes.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
nodes.description: TFEB is a master transcriptional regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, and its overexpression drives coordinated activation of numerous lysosomal genes encoding membrane proteins, hydrolases, and v-ATPase subunits. This global upregulation increases both the number and functional capacity of lysosomes, expanding degradative reserve. As the central node of the CLEAR network, TFEB integrates diverse stress signals into a unified lysosomal expansion program. Its master-regulator status makes it a prime target for therapies aimed at enhancing cellular clearance.

nodes.label: TFE3 at S321
nodes.description: mTORC1 phosphorylates TFE3 at serine 321, an analog of the TFEB S211 site, thereby promoting cytosolic retention and inhibiting TFE3's transcriptional activity under nutrient-replete conditions. This parallel modification ensures that both MiT/TFE family master regulators are coordinately repressed by mTORC1. Upon starvation or mTORC1 inhibition, dephosphorylation permits TFE3 nuclear entry and activation of lysosomal genes. The conserved regulatory logic highlights the unified control of the degradative program.

nodes.label: Lipid catabolism
nodes.description: TFEB regulates lipid catabolism by upregulating genes involved in fatty acid import, beta-oxidation, lysosomal acid lipase (LAL)-mediated lipophagy, and the transcriptional coactivators PGC-1α and PPAR-α. Through these targets, TFEB coordinates the mobilization and oxidation of stored lipids during fasting and stress. This lipid-catabolic program complements TFEB's role in protein and organelle turnover, rendering it a comprehensive metabolic regulator. Enhanced TFEB activity improves lipid handling and protects against hepatic steatosis.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial stress
nodes.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
nodes.description: TFEB is activated in response to mitochondrial stress, a process requiring mitophagy machinery including PINK1, Parkin, Atg9A, and Atg5 to signal and enable TFEB nuclear translocation. As damaged mitochondria are selected for autophagic removal, TFEB coordinates a compensatory lysosomal and autophagic response that restores organelle quality. This coupling ensures that mitochondrial turnover is matched by degradative capacity. The axis links mitochondrial quality control to the broader autophagy-lysosomal network and to metabolic homeostasis.

nodes.label: Immune response
nodes.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
nodes.description: TFEB regulates innate and adaptive immune responses, becoming activated during dendritic cell maturation to enhance antigen processing and presentation via expanded lysosomal and MHC-related machinery. By boosting degradative capacity, TFEB improves the efficiency of antigen degradation and epitope loading, strengthening T cell priming. TFEB activity also influences macrophage polarization and immune cell metabolism. These roles position the autophagy-lysosomal master regulator as an important modulator of immunity.

nodes.label: PGC1-alpha
nodes.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
nodes.description: TFEB and the mitochondrial biogenesis coactivator PGC-1α form a positive feedback loop: PGC-1α modulates mitophagy by regulating TFEB expression, while TFEB induces PGC-1α transcription, reinforcing mitochondrial turnover and biogenesis. This reciprocal regulation couples lysosomal-autophagic clearance with mitochondrial network expansion under stress. The loop ensures coordinated enhancement of both degradative and biosynthetic mitochondrial programs. Its disruption impairs metabolic adaptation and is relevant to aging and myopathy.

nodes.label: MALAT1 in renal carcinoma
nodes.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
nodes.description: In a subset of translocation renal cell carcinomas (t(6;11) RCC), the TFEB gene is fused with the long non-coding RNA locus MALAT1, producing a MALAT1-TFEB fusion that drives overexpression of intact TFEB. The fusion places TFEB under the strong promoter activity of MALAT1, leading to constitutive activation of the lysosomal-autophagic and proliferative programs. This genetic rearrangement defines a distinct clinicopathologic entity of RCC with characteristic biphasic histology. The finding established TFEB as an oncogene when deregulated by chromosomal translocation.

nodes.label: Xp11 translocation RCC
nodes.description: TFE3 is recurrently involved in Xp11.2 translocation renal cell carcinomas, in which it fuses with partner genes such as ASPSCR1, PRCC, or SFPQ, creating chimeric transcription factors that drive tumorigenesis. These gene fusions define a distinct subset of RCC, often arising in children and young adults, with characteristic clear-cell or papillary features. The fusion proteins typically retain the TFE3 DNA-binding domain and are constitutively active, deregulating MiT/TFE target genes. Detection of TFE3 rearrangement is important for correct diagnosis and classification of these tumors.

nodes.label: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
nodes.source_file: _document_ - From the regulatory mechanism of TFEB to its therapeutic implications - Cell Death Discovery.md
nodes.description: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA), TFEB remains constitutively nuclear-localized and active independent of nutrient status, supporting the tumor's high demand for lysosomal degradation and metabolic flexibility. This aberrant activation promotes expression of glutaminase and other catabolic genes that fuel PDA growth under the harsh tumor microenvironment. The nutrient-independent nuclear TFEB state distinguishes PDA from normal epithelial regulation and contributes to therapy resistance. Targeting TFEB or its effectors is being explored as a therapeutic strategy in this lethal cancer.

nodes.label: mTORC1 activation
nodes.description: The lysosome serves as the physical platform for mTORC1 activation, hosting the recruitment of mTORC1 via Rag GTPases and Ragulator and its encounter with the activator Rheb at the lysosomal surface. Amino-acid sensing, growth-factor inputs, and calcium signals all converge at this organelle to determine mTORC1 activity. By colocalizing mTORC1 with its upstream regulators, the lysosome functionally couples nutrient detection to the control of autophagy and anabolism. This spatial organization is essential for the rapid, reversible regulation of the pathway.

nodes.label: Longevity in C. elegans
nodes.description: HLH-30 regulates longevity in C. elegans, as its overexpression extends lifespan while loss of hlh-30 shortens it and suppresses the longevity of other mutants. By inducing autophagy, lysosomal biogenesis, and lipid mobilization, HLH-30 preserves proteostasis and metabolic homeostasis that decline with age. Its activity integrates insulin, mTOR, and dietary signals into a pro-longevity transcriptional program. The worm findings provide a conserved model for how TFEB orthologs promote healthspan in higher organisms.

nodes.label: Adaptive autophagy
nodes.description: Moderate caloric restriction induces adaptive autophagy—a beneficial, hormetic form of the pathway that enhances cellular clearance and resilience without causing damage. This adaptive response, driven by AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition, contributes substantially to the lifespan and healthspan extension observed with CR. Unlike pathological autophagy, adaptive autophagy is precisely regulated and supports rather than threatens cell survival. It represents the mechanistic core of CR's pro-longevity effects.

nodes.label: Excessive autophagy
nodes.description: Prolonged or severe caloric restriction can drive excessive autophagy that crosses into autophagic cell death, particularly when degradative flux outpaces biosynthetic capacity. This maladaptive extreme underscores the biphasic, hormetic nature of autophagy, where too little or too much is detrimental. The balance between adaptive and excessive autophagy determines whether CR is protective or harmful. Understanding this threshold is important for safely translating CR-mimetic strategies.

nodes.label: ATG4B
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The Beneficial and Adverse Effects of Autophagic Response to Caloric Restriction and Fasting.md
nodes.description: SIRT2, a cytosolic NAD+-dependent deacetylase, deacetylates ATG4B in response to starvation, modulating the activity of this cysteine protease that processes and delipidates the autophagosome marker LC3/GABARAP. Deacetylation of ATG4B influences the dynamics of LC3 conjugation and autophagosome maturation, fine-tuning autophagic flux. Because SIRT2 activity rises when NAD+ is elevated during CR and exercise, this modification links energy status to autophagosome biogenesis. The SIRT2-ATG4B axis adds an acetylation layer to core autophagy machinery regulation.

nodes.label: Insulin signaling
nodes.description: Insulin signaling inhibits autophagy by activating the PI3K-Akt axis, which in turn activates mTORC1 and promotes phosphorylation of ULK1 and TFEB that suppress autophagic initiation and lysosomal gene expression. Through this cascade, the fed-state hormone maintains an anabolic, autophagy-off condition in peripheral tissues. The relief of insulin signaling during fasting or caloric restriction is therefore prerequisite for autophagic induction. This relationship is a primary reason why nutrient excess and insulin resistance are associated with impaired autophagy and metabolic disease.

nodes.label: Chemotherapy sensitivity
nodes.description: Caloric restriction increases the sensitivity of tumor cells to chemotherapy by creating a differential stress resistance in which normal cells enter a protective, autophagy-dependent quiescent state while cancer cells remain vulnerable. CR additionally stimulates CD8+ T cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity and enhances apoptotic priming of malignant cells. The improved therapeutic index allows lower effective doses and reduced toxicity. These effects position CR and its mimetics as adjuncts to conventional cancer therapy.

nodes.label: FOXO1
nodes.description: Akt phosphorylates and inhibits the FOXO1/FOXO3 transcription factors, which normally promote autophagy and stress-resistance gene expression, thereby indirectly suppressing autophagy downstream of insulin/PI3K signaling. The reciprocal interaction reflects the broader antagonism between growth-factor-driven anabolism (via Akt-mTOR) and the autophagy-promoting FOXO program. When Akt is inactive during fasting, FOXO factors are de-repressed and contribute to autophagic and longevity pathways. This axis embeds autophagy control within the insulin-signaling network that also regulates mTORC1.

The reciprocal interaction reflects the broader antagonism between growth-factor-driven anabolism (via Akt-mTOR) and the autophagy-promoting FOXO program. When Akt is inactive during fasting, FOXO factors are de-repressed and contribute to autophagic and longevity pathways. This axis embeds autophagy control within the insulin-signaling network that also regulates mTORC1.

nodes.label: Ketogenic Diet
nodes.description: Ketogenic diets, characterized by high fat and very low carbohydrate intake, activate autophagy by lowering insulin and glucose while elevating ketone bodies and AMPK activity. The metabolic shift toward fatty-acid oxidation and mild energy stress mimics aspects of caloric restriction, engaging the autophagic machinery. This activation contributes to the reported healing and neuroprotective effects of ketogenic regimens in epilepsy, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disease. The diet thus provides a non-fasting nutritional strategy to recruit autophagic clearance.

nodes.label: Cancer treatment
nodes.description: During cancer treatment, autophagy plays a dual role that depends on context: it can protect tumor cells from chemotherapy- and radiation-induced damage, limiting therapeutic efficacy, yet it can also promote therapy-induced cell death when excessive or when it facilitates terminal differentiation and antigen presentation. In normal tissues, treatment-induced autophagy is generally cytoprotective and reduces toxicity, widening the therapeutic window. The opposing outcomes necessitate careful stratification of when to inhibit versus enhance autophagy in the clinic. This duality mirrors autophagy's broader role in cancer initiation versus progression.

nodes.label: S130 enhances CR effect
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The Beneficial and Adverse Effects of Autophagic Response to Caloric Restriction and Fasting.md
nodes.description: The small-molecule ATG4B inhibitor S130 blocks the cysteine protease required for LC3 processing and autophagosome maturation; when combined with caloric restriction, this inhibition shifts the balance toward apoptotic death in colorectal cancer cells. By preventing autophagic protection of tumor cells while CR imposes metabolic stress, S130 sensitizes malignancy to cell death. The synergy illustrates a therapeutic strategy of pairing CR or CR-mimetics with targeted autophagy inhibition in cancer. The approach exploits the reliance of some tumors on basal autophagy for survival.

nodes.label: P300
nodes.source_file: _document_ - The Beneficial and Adverse Effects of Autophagic Response to Caloric Restriction and Fasting.md
nodes.description: The acetyltransferase p300 acetylates ATG4B, an modification that inhibits its proteolytic activity required for LC3 lipidation and autophagosome formation, thereby restraining autophagy under normal conditions. This acetylation-dependent repression adds a transcriptional coactivator-derived control layer to core autophagy machinery beyond the well-studied phosphorylation circuits. Relief of p300-mediated acetylation during stress can de-repress ATG4B and facilitate autophagic flux. The finding situates autophagy regulation within the broader acetylome governed by p300/CBP.

nodes.source_file: _document_ - The Beneficial and Adverse Effects of Autophagic Response to Caloric Restriction and Fasting.md

nodes.label: Hallmarks of Cancer
nodes.description:
The Hallmarks of Cancer are the core biological capabilities that all cancers acquire during their multistep development, originally articulated by Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg (2000) and expanded (2011) into a unifying framework for tumor biology. The concept distills the complexity of malignancy into a set of shared enabling characteristics.

## The Ten Hallmarks

1. Sustaining Proliferative Signaling — autonomous growth-factor production and receptor activation (e.g., EGFR, RAS).
2. Evading Growth Suppressors — inactivation of Tumor Suppressor Genes such as RB1 and p53.
3. Resisting Cell Death — disabling Apoptosis via BCL-2 family or Caspase-8 inhibition.
4. Enabling Replicative Immortality — telomerase reactivation.
5. Inducing Angiogenesis — neovessel formation through VEGF and Angiogenesis.
6. Activating Invasion and Metastasis — EMT and dissemination.
7. Deregulating Cellular Energetics — Metabolic Reprogramming and the Warburg Effect.
8. Evading Immune Destruction — immune checkpoint and suppression of surveillance.
9. Genome Instability and Mutation — mutator phenotypes enabling diversification.
10. Tumor-Promoting Inflammation — Inflammation via the Tumor Microenvironment.

## Enabling Characteristics & Emerging Hallmarks

Two "enabling" traits — genome instability and tumor-promoting inflammation — fuel the acquisition of the core hallmarks. Emerging additions include unlocking phenotypic plasticity, non-mutational epigenetic reprogramming, Polymicrobial ec

nodes.label: Metabolic Reprogramming
nodes.description:
Metabolic Reprogramming refers to the ability of Cancer cells to alter their metabolism to support increased proliferation, survival, and adaptation to the tumour microenvironment. It is considered one of the Hallmarks of Cancer.

## Key Features
- Aerobic Glycolysis: Also known as the Warburg Effect, where cells prefer Glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen.
- Enhanced Glutaminolysis: Increased dependence on Glutamine for carbon and nitrogen.
- Lipid Metabolism: Alterations in fatty acid synthesis and oxidation.
- Pentose Phosphate Pathway: Increased flux to provide ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis and NADPH for antioxidant defense.

## Therapeutic Targeting
Metabolic reprogramming creates vulnerabilities that can be targeted:
- Inhibiting glucose transporters like GLUT1.
- Targeting glycolytic enzymes like Hexokinase 2 and Pyruvate Kinase M2.
- Compounds like Fenbendazole are being studied for their ability to interfere with these metabolic shifts.

## Connections

- Key Molecules: Glucose, Glutamine, Lactate, ATP, NADPH
- Regulators: p53, MYC, HIF-1α, mTOR

nodes.label: ERK
nodes.description:
ERK (extracellular signal-regulated kinase) refers to the effector kinases of the RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK limb of the MAPK Signaling cascade — principally ERK1/2 (p44/p42) plus ERK5. ERK generally promotes cell survival and proliferation by phosphorylating and inactivating pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bim and stabilizing anti-apoptotic proteins such as Mcl-1, making it a central node in oncogenic growth and apoptotic resistance.

## Structure & Activation

ERK1/2 are serine/threonine kinases activated by dual phosphorylation on conserved Thr and Tyr residues by the upstream kinase MEK1/2. MEK itself is activated by RAF kinases downstream of RAS GTPases, which integrate growth-factor receptor signals (e.g., EGFR). Once activated, ERK translocates to the nucleus and cytoplasm to phosphorylate >200 substrates — transcription factors (ELK1, c-Fos, MYC), ribosomal S6 kinase, and apoptotic regulators.

## Mechanism of Action

A key anti-apoptotic mechanism is ERK-mediated phosphorylation of the BH3-only protein Bim. Phosphorylated Bim is recognized by the E3 ligase c-CBL and targeted for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, removing a critical trigger of mitochondrial apoptosis. ERK also phosphorylates and stabilizes Mcl-1, an anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family member, and can restrain Caspase-2 and BAD activity. Through these actions, sustained ERK signaling keeps the intrinsic death pathway disengaged while driving cyclin D expression and proliferation.

nodes.label: Wnt
nodes.description:
Wnt signaling comprises a family of evolutionary conserved pathways initiated by secreted Wnt glycoproteins binding Frizzled/LRP receptors. The canonical Wnt/β-catenin arm controls gene transcription via β-catenin/TCF complexes and is pivotal in embryonic patterning, stem-cell maintenance, and tissue regeneration. Its dysregulation is among the most frequent events in human Cancer.

## Pathway Mechanisms

In the OFF state, a destruction complex (APC, Axin, GSK-3β, CK1) phosphorylates β-catenin, marking it for Ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Wnt binding to Frizzled and LRP5/6 inhibits this complex; stabilized β-catenin accumulates, translocates to the nucleus, and with TCF/LEF factors drives targets such as MYC, CCND1, AXIN2, and LGR5. Non-canonical Wnt pathways (planar cell polarity, Wnt/Ca²⁺) regulate polarity and calcium flux independently of β-catenin.

## Role in Cancer

Canonical Wnt activation occurs via inactivating mutations in APC or β-catenin (CTNNB1) — the hallmark of Colorectal Cancer — and via upstream receptor/ligand overexpression in Breast Cancer, hepatocellular, and other tumors. Constitutive Wnt signaling sustains cancer stem cells, proliferation, and EMT, and confers therapy resistance. The pathway thus satisfies multiple Hallmarks of Cancer.

nodes.label: JAK2
nodes.description:
Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase of the JAK family that couples type I/II cytokine receptors to the JAK/STAT cascade. Upon ligand binding, JAK2 trans-phosphorylates its receptor and downstream STAT transcription factors (notably STAT3 and STAT5), orchestrating gene programs for proliferation, survival, differentiation, and Inflammation. Dysregulated JAK2 activity is a driver in hematologic malignancies and supports numerous solid tumors.

## Structure & Activation

JAK2 contains seven JAK-homology (JH) domains: the C-terminal JH1 is the kinase domain, JH2 is a pseudokinase domain that autoregulates JH1, and JH3–JH7 mediate receptor association. In the resting state the pseudokinase domain restrains the kinase. Ligand engagement (e.g., by erythropoietin, growth hormone, or IL-6 family cytokines) induces receptor dimerization, juxtaposing JAK2 molecules to enable trans-activation phosphorylation of activation-loop tyrosines in JH1.

## Mechanism of Action

Activated JAK2 phosphorylates STAT proteins on conserved tyrosine residues; phosphorylated STATs dimerize via SH2 domains and translocate to the nucleus to induce transcription of anti-apoptotic (BCL-XL, Mcl-1) and proliferative (cyclin D) genes. JAK2 also cross-talks with PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK cascades, reinforcing survival signals and Chemotherapy resistance. Aberrant activation—through mutation, translocation, or autocrine cytokine loops—locks cells into a proliferative state.

nodes.label: YAP1
nodes.description:
YAP1 (Yes-associated protein 1) is a potent transcriptional co-activator and the chief downstream effector of the Hippo Signaling Pathway, which governs organ size, tissue homeostasis, and regeneration. When Hippo signaling is off, YAP1 escapes phosphorylation, translocates to the nucleus, and with TEAD factors drives expression of genes promoting proliferation, survival, EMT, and Metastasis — endowing YAP1 with clear oncogenic properties.

## Structure and Regulation

YAP1 contains a WW domain that binds PPxY motifs (e.g., in TEADs) and a transcriptional activation domain. The Hippo kinase cascade (MST1/2 → LATS1/2) phosphorylates YAP1 at Ser127, inducing 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic retention; further phosphorylation (Ser381) primes Ubiquitination and degradation. Mechanical cues (cell density, stiffness, junctional tension) and GPCR/PI3K signals modulate this gate, so YAP1 integrates both biochemical and biomechanical inputs.

## Oncogenic Role in Cancer

YAP1 is overexpressed or hyperactive in Gastric Cancer, Lung Cancer, liver, ovarian, and many other malignancies, where it fuels tumor growth, stemness, and therapy resistance. Nuclear YAP1 correlates with poor prognosis and aggressive EMT. Because YAP1 lacks a classic druggable pocket, targeting focuses on upstream regulators and downstream partners.

nodes.label: EGFR
nodes.description:
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase that regulates cell proliferation, survival, and differentiation. It is frequently overexpressed or mutated in numerous cancers.

## Role in Cancer

- Overexpression: Found in triple-negative breast cancer, non-small-cell lung cancer, glioblastoma, and Colorectal Cancer
- Signaling: Activates PI3K/Akt and MAPK pathways

## Therapeutic Targeting

EGFR is a major drug target. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (erlotinib, gefitinib) and monoclonal antibodies (cetuximab) are used clinically.

nodes.label: HER2
nodes.description:
Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2; also known as ErbB-2 or CD340) is a protein encoded by the ERBB2 gene. It is a member of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR/ErbB) family.

## Role in Cancer
- Amplification: Overexpression or amplification of this oncogene plays an important role in the development and progression of certain aggressive types of Breast Cancer.
- HER2-enriched: A specific subtype of breast cancer defined by HER2 overexpression.

## Therapeutics
- Targeted Therapies: HER2 is the target of several drugs, including the monoclonal antibody trastuzumab.

nodes.label: BRCA
nodes.description:
BRCA (BReast CAncer gene) denotes two tumor suppressor genes, BRCA1 and BRCA2, whose protein products are essential for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination (HR). Germline pathogenic variants markedly increase lifetime risk of Breast Cancer, ovarian cancer, prostate, pancreatic, and other malignancies, and define tumors exquisitely sensitive to specific therapies.

## Protein Function & DNA Repair

- BRCA1: Forms the BRCA1-A complex and, with PALB2, recruits BRCA2; it also participates in checkpoint control, ubiquitylation (via BARD1), and transcription regulation.
- BRCA2: Directly loads RAD51 onto single-stranded DNA to drive strand invasion during HR.
Loss of either gene cripples HR, forcing error-prone repair and genomic instability — a hallmark of Cancer.

## Hallmarks of BRCAness

HR deficiency (HRD) yields characteristic genomic scars (loss of heterozygosity, telomeric allelic imbalance, large-scale transitions). "BRCAness" describes sporadic tumors phenocopying BRCA mutation via other HR defects (e.g., ATM, PALB2 loss), sharing therapeutic vulnerabilities.

## Cancer Risk & Inheritance

- Penetrance: BRCA1 mutations confer ~55–70% lifetime breast and 40–60% ovarian cancer risk; BRCA2 similarly elevates breast, ovarian, and male breast/prostate risk.
- Inheritance: Autosomal dominant; genetic counseling and testing guide surveillance and prophylactic surgery.

## Therapeutic Relevance

- PARP inhibitors: Exploit synthetic lethality — inhib

nodes.label: Ki-67
nodes.description: Ki-67 is expressed in all active phases of the cell cycle and absent in quiescent cells, making it a robust immunohistochemical readout of proliferation. A high Ki-67 labeling index correlates with aggressive biology and, in some tumors, informs adjuvant therapy decisions. The relationship is directional as a biomarker: proliferation evidences the tumor's growth fraction rather than causing it. It is particularly integrated into grading of breast and neuroendocrine neoplasms.

nodes.label: docetaxel
nodes.description:
Docetaxel (brand name Taxotere, among others) is a semisynthetic taxane Chemotherapy agent derived from the European yew (Taxus baccata). It treats numerous cancers, including Breast Cancer, non-small-cell lung cancer, prostate cancer, gastric cancer, and head-and-neck cancer. Docetaxel stabilizes microtubules, blocking mitotic progression and triggering Apoptosis; it also shows strong synergy with natural compounds such as melittin in aggressive subtypes like triple-negative breast cancer.

## Chemistry & Pharmacokinetics

Docetaxel is a docetaxel ester of 10-deacetyl-baccatin III, more watersoluble and potent than the parent paclitaxel. It is formulated with polysorbate 80 and administered intravenously; it distributes widely, is metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 in the liver, and is excreted partly fecally. Dose is limited by neutropenia, fluid retention, and neuropathy. Premedication with corticosteroids reduces hypersensitivity and edema.

## Mechanism of Action

Docetaxel binds β-tubulin in microtubules, promoting and locking polymer assembly while preventing depolymerization. Cells entering mitosis with stabilized spindles cannot progress past metaphase, activating the spindle-assembly checkpoint and inducing prolonged mitotic arrest that collapses into mitotic catastrophe and caspase-dependent Apoptosis. Docetaxel also affects interphase microtubules, disrupting motility and intracellular trafficking, and can inhibit Angiogenesis and promote dendritic-cell maturation, c

nodes.label: trastuzumab
nodes.description:
Trastuzumab (brand name Herceptin, among others) is a recombinant humanized monoclonal IgG1 Antibody that binds subdomain IV of the extracellular region of the HER2 (ERBB2) receptor. It is a foundational targeted therapy for HER2-positive Breast Cancer and Gastric Cancer, and a prototype of precision oncology.

## Mechanism of Action

Trastuzumab inhibits HER2 signaling through several coordinated mechanisms. By binding HER2, it sterically hinders ligand-independent dimerization with other ERBB family members (EGFR, HER3), suppressing downstream PI3K/AKT and MAPK proliferative signaling. It accelerates HER2 receptor internalization and degradation, and it inhibits Angiogenesis indirectly by reducing VEGF production. Critically, its IgG1 Fc region engages Fcγ receptors on immune effector cells to mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) against HER2-overexpressing tumor cells.

## Resistance and Biomarkers

Response requires HER2 amplification/overexpression, assessed by IHC and FISH. Resistance arises via PIK3CA mutations, PTEN loss, HER2 extracellular-domain cleavage (p95HER2), and activation of compensatory pathways such as SRC kinase/FAK. Newer agents (pertuzumab, trastuzumab emtansine [T-DM1], trastuzumab deruxtecan) address some resistance mechanisms.

## Role Beyond Direct Therapy

Trastuzumab is also exploited as a targeting vector for selective drug delivery. Immunoliposomes bearing trastuzumab can ferry membranolytic peptides such as melittin specifica

nodes.label: Ivermectin
nodes.description:
Ivermectin is a macrolide antiparasitic drug with a 16-membered ring that is widely used for the treatment of many parasitic diseases such as river blindness, elephantiasis and Scabies. It was derived from Avermectin. Satoshi ōmura and William C. Campbell won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for its discovery.

## Anticancer Potential
Ivermectin has been reported to inhibit the proliferation of several tumor cells by regulating multiple signaling pathways. It exerts powerful antitumor effects, including the inhibition of proliferation, Metastasis, and angiogenic activity.

### Mechanisms of Action
- Inhibition of Signaling Pathways: Regulates Wnt/β-catenin, Akt/mTOR, and MAPK pathways.
- Molecular Targets: Primarily acts as a PAK1 inhibitor. Also inhibits YAP1, HSP27, and KPNB1.
- Programmed Cell Death: Induces Apoptosis, Autophagy, and Pyroptosis.
- Tumor Microenvironment: Regulates the tumor microenvironment and mediates immunogenic cell death (e.g., through HMGB1 release).
- Cancer Stem Cells: Inhibits Cancer Stem Cells (CSCs) by regulating the PAK1-STAT3 axis.
- Multidrug Resistance: Reverses Multidrug Resistance (MDR) by inhibiting P-gp and other MDR-associated proteins.

### Synergistic Effects
Ivermectin shows synergistic effects when used in combination with other chemotherapy drugs such as Cisplatin, docetaxel, paclitaxel, Daunorubicin, cytarabine, erlotinib, Dasatinib, and dabrafenib.

nodes.label: Fenbendazole
nodes.description:
Fenbendazole is a broad-spectrum Benzimidazole anthelmintic agent used to treat gastrointestinal parasites in animals, including giardia, roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, and certain tapeworms. It is being investigated as a candidate for Drug Repositioning in Cancer therapy due to its ability to interfere with Microtubule polymerization and modulate cellular energy metabolism.

## Overview

Fenbendazole (methyl N-(6-phenylsulfanyl-1H-benzimidazol-2-yl)carbamate) is not FDA/EMA-approved for human use; its human pharmacokinetics are inferred from animal studies and from its major metabolite Oxfendazole, which has completed a phase I trial. Its low cost, oral availability, and unique anti-proliferative activities make it the preferred benzimidazole for cancer repurposing over Albendazole and Mebendazole (which is used human antiparasitically).

## Mechanism of Action in Cancer

Fenbendazole exerts multiple, partially overlapping anticancer effects:

- Microtubule destabilization: Acts as a moderate microtubule destabilizing agent, similar in class to Vincristine but with lower toxicity, inducing G2/M arrest (4, 10, 35).
- Glycolysis / glucose starvation: Suppresses Glycolysis by down-regulating Glucose uptake (via GLUT1) and inhibiting Hexokinase 2; reduces lactate and reverses drug resistance (4, 7, 13-17).
- p53 activation: Increases p53 activity by down-regulating MDM2 and MdmX, driving mitochondrial p53-p21 signaling that suppresses GLUT expression (4, 35).

nodes.label: melittin
nodes.description:
Melittin is a positively charged, amphipathic 26-amino-acid peptide that constitutes approximately half of Honeybee venom by dry weight. It is known for its ability to associate with phospholipids in the cell membrane, forming pores and inducing cell death.

## anticancer Activity
Melittin has shown selective cytotoxic effects against several cancer types, particularly:
- triple-negative breast cancer
- HER2-enriched breast cancer
- Melanoma
- non-small-cell lung cancer
- glioblastoma

## Mechanism of Action
- Membrane Disruption: Forms ~4.4 nm-diameter transmembrane toroidal pores.
- Signaling Inhibition: Suppresses the phosphorylation and activation of receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR and HER2.
- Synergy: Enhances the effect of chemotherapeutic agents like docetaxel and Cisplatin.

## Documents

List of documents that mention this entity

- Honeybee venom and melittin suppress growth factor receptor activation in HER2-enriched and triple-negative breast cancer - npj Precision Oncology
- Here, we demonstrate that honeybee venom and its major component melittin potently induce cell death, particularly in the aggressive triple-negative breast cancer and HER2-enriched breast cancer subtypes.

## Connections
- Honeybee: The source of melittin.
- EGFR: A target of melittin signaling inhibition.

nodes.label: Nutlins
nodes.description:
Nutlins are a family of small-molecule cis-imidazoline analogs that act as potent, selective inhibitors of the MDM2–p53 interaction. By displacing p53 from its principal negative regulator, nutlins reactivate the p53 tumor-suppressor network in cancers retaining wild-type p53, triggering cell-cycle arrest, Senescence, or Apoptosis.

## Structure and Pharmacology

The prototype, Nutlin-3, is a chiral cis-imidazoline that fits the hydrophobic p53-binding pocket of MDM2, competing with the p53 transactivation domain. Nutlins are highly selective for MDM2 over related E3 ligases (e.g., MDMX to a lesser extent) and do not directly damage DNA, distinguishing them from conventional Chemotherapy.

## Mechanism of Action

MDM2 normally ubiquitinates p53, targeting it for proteasomal degradation and keeping basal p53 low. Nutlins occupy the MDM2 pocket, preventing p53 binding and degradation. Stabilized p53 accumulates, translocates to the nucleus, and induces transcription of p21 (arrest), pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins (PUMA, NOXA, Bim), and senescent program mediators. The cellular outcome depends on context: sustained p53 yields apoptosis in many tumor cells, whereas milder activation enforces senescence or reversible arrest in normal tissue.

## Physiological and Pathological Relevance

The p53 pathway is inactivated in most cancers, frequently by MDM2 amplification rather than p53 mutation. Nutlins specifically exploit MDM2-dependent inactivation, sparing tumors with p53 mutatio

nodes.label: BH3 mimetics
nodes.description:
BH3 mimetics are small-molecule inhibitors designed to occupy the hydrophobic BH3-binding groove of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins, displacing the pro-apoptotic effectors Bax and Bak and thereby unleashing the Intrinsic Pathway of Apoptosis. They translate the structural logic of BH3-only proteins (e.g., Bim, Puma) into druggable compounds.

## Major Agents & Selectivity

- ABT-737: First-generation pan-inhibitor of Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, and Bcl-w (weak vs Mcl-1).
- ABT-263 (navitoclax): Oral analog; thrombocytopenia limits dosing due to Bcl-xL inhibition on platelets.
- ABT-199 (venetoclax): Bcl-2-selective; approved for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and other hematological malignancies.
- Mcl-1–selective: S63845, AZD5991 — critical where Mcl-1 drives resistance.
- A1/Bfl-1–selective: A-1331852 — addresses resistance to other mimetics.

## Mechanism of Action

By binding the groove, BH3 mimetics neutralize the "apoptosis brake." When the pro-survival capacity is exceeded, Bak/Bax oligomerize, mitochondria release Cytochrome c, and the Apoptosome activates Caspase-9 → Caspase-3. Efficacy depends on "primed" tumor cells with high BH3-only pressure and low Mcl-1.

## Resistance & Combination Strategy

- Mcl-1/A1 up-regulation permits escape; combining Bcl-2 with Mcl-1 inhibitors overcomes redundancy.
- BCL-2 mutations and altered dependence confer intrinsic resistance.
- Synergy with Chemotherapy, BTK inhibitors, and Venetoclax-based regimens is well established.

nodes.label: BET inhibitors
nodes.description:
BET (Bromodomain and Extra-Terminal) inhibitors are a class of epigenetic drugs that target the bromodomains of BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT. These proteins recognize acetylated lysine residues on histone tails and regulate transcription of oncogenes (e.g., MYC, BCL2), inflammatory genes, and Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype factors.

## Mechanism

- BET proteins (especially BRD4) bind acetylated histones at super-enhancer regions.
- BET inhibitors (e.g., JQ1, OTX015/Birabresib, ABBV-075/Mivebresib) displace BET proteins from chromatin.
- This selectively downregulates MYC and its transcriptional program.
- Also suppresses NF-κB-dependent transcription of inflammatory cytokines.

## Role in Senescence

BET inhibitors can suppress the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype by displacing BRD4 from the promoters of SASP genes including IL-6, IL-8, and MMP family members. This has been proposed as a Senomorphic strategy to block the harmful effects of SASP without eliminating senescent cells.

## Role in Cancer

- Downregulate MYC in MYC-driven cancers (e.g., leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma).
- Show synergy with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in preclinical models.
- OTX015 and ABBV-075 have been evaluated in Phase I/II clinical trials for hematologic and solid malignancies.

---

nodes.label: Multidrug Resistance
nodes.description:
Multidrug Resistance (MDR) is the phenomenon where tumor cells become resistant to a wide variety of structurally and functionally unrelated chemotherapy drugs. It is a major cause of treatment failure, relapse, and death in cancer patients.

## Mechanisms
- Efflux Pumps: Overexpression of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters, such as P-gp (P-glycoprotein), which pump drugs out of the cell.
- Signaling Pathways: Activation of pathways like EGFR, ERK, Akt, and NF-κB can upregulate the expression of MDR-associated proteins.

## Reversal of MDR
Developing agents that can reverse MDR is a critical area of oncology research.
- Ivermectin: Has been shown to reverse drug resistance in various cancers (e.g., vincristine-resistant colorectal cancer, doxorubicin-resistant breast cancer). It works by inhibiting P-gp and downregulating its expression via the EGFR/ERK/Akt/NF-κB signaling pathway.

## Documents

List of documents that mention this entity

- Apoptosis in cancer from pathogenesis to treatment
- Overexpression of Bcl-xL has also been reported to confer a Multidrug Resistance phenotype in tumour cells and prevent them from undergoing apoptosis \[\].

- Ivermectin, a potential anticancer drug derived from an antiparasitic drug
- Interestingly, ivermectin can also inhibit Cancer Stem Cells and reverse Multidrug Resistance and exerts the optimal effect when used in combination with other chemotherapy drugs. !graphic file with name ga1_lrg.

nodes.label: Integrins
nodes.description:
Integrins are a family of evolutionarily conserved, non-covalently associated α/β heterodimeric transmembrane receptors that physically and biochemically couple the extracellular matrix (ECM) to the intracellular actin cytoskeleton. They are central to cell adhesion, migration, proliferation, and survival, and they are pivotal in Cancer progression, where they govern Angiogenesis, invasive migration, and Metastasis.

## Structure & Diversity

The human integrin family comprises 18 α and 8 β subunits that pair to form 24 distinct receptors, each with defined ligand specificity. The extracellular headpiece (composed of the α I-domain or β propeller and the β I-like domain) contains the ligand-binding site; ligand affinity is regulated allosterically through "bent" (low-affinity) versus "extended" (high-affinity) conformations. The short cytoplasmic tails lack enzymatic activity but recruit large adaptor complexes (talin, kindlin, α-actinin).

## Mechanism of Action

Integrins transduce signals in both directions. Outside-in signaling occurs when ECM ligands (e.g., fibronectin, collagen, laminin) engage the receptor, triggering clustering and assembly of focal adhesions that activate FAK, SRC, PI3K/AKT, and MAPK pathways to drive survival and proliferation. Inside-out signaling originates from intracellular cues (e.g., growth factor receptors, Ras) that alter talin/kindlin binding to switch integrins to high affinity. On endothelial and tumor cells, integrins such as αvβ3 and α5

nodes.label: Intrinsic Pathway
nodes.description: Apoptosis has the pathway Intrinsic Pathway. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. The intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway is initiated by intracellular damage and is gated at the outer mitochondrial membrane by the Bcl-2 family. The relationship is directional, with Apoptosis acting as the operative agent upon Intrinsic Pathway rather than the reverse. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

nodes.label: Extrinsic Pathway
nodes.description: Apoptosis has the pathway Extrinsic Pathway. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. The extrinsic (death-receptor) apoptotic pathway is triggered by extracellular ligands engaging cell-surface death receptors and proceeds through the DISC. The relationship is directional, with Apoptosis acting as the operative agent upon Extrinsic Pathway rather than the reverse. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

nodes.label: Endoplasmic Reticulum Pathway
nodes.description: Apoptosis has the pathway Endoplasmic Reticulum Pathway. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. The endoplasmic-reticulum stress pathway of apoptosis is initiated by unfolded-protein accumulation and engages CHOP and caspase-12. The relationship is directional, with Apoptosis acting as the operative agent upon Endoplasmic Reticulum Pathway rather than the reverse. Together these facts situate the relationship within the broader architecture of cancer biology, clarifying how the two entities connect as part of the hallmark or taxonomic framework.

nodes.label: Common Pathway
nodes.description: Apoptosis converges at Common Pathway. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. The common execution phase of apoptosis is the point at which all initiation routes converge on effector caspases that proteolyze the cellular proteome. The relationship is directional, with Apoptosis acting as the operative agent upon Common Pathway rather than the reverse. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

nodes.label: Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins
nodes.description: Apoptosis is inhibited by Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins (IAPs) are endogenous caspase-suppressor proteins that block cell death and are frequently co-opted by tumors. The directionality runs from Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins toward Apoptosis, so Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins is the active agent and Apoptosis the recipient of the effect. This restraint is biologically significant because it modulates the threshold at which the affected process engages, and when co-opted by tumors it fosters survival and treatment resistance that must be overcome therapeutically.

nodes.label: TRAIL
nodes.description: Apoptosis is induced by TRAIL. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. TRAIL (TNFSF10) is a death ligand that engages DR4 and DR5 to initiate extrinsic apoptosis with relative selectivity for malignant cells. The directionality runs from TRAIL toward Apoptosis, so TRAIL is the active agent and Apoptosis the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

nodes.label: Gossypol
nodes.description: Apoptosis is induced by Gossypol. Apoptosis is a genetically programmed, caspase-dependent form of cell death that dismantles cells without provoking inflammation. Gossypol is a natural BH3-mimetic derived from cottonseed that, unusually, also engages Mcl-1. The directionality runs from Gossypol toward Apoptosis, so Gossypol is the active agent and Apoptosis the recipient of the effect. This directional link makes the interaction a meaningful node in tumor biology, with implications for understanding disease progression and for identifying therapeutic or biomarker opportunities.

nodes.label: Bcl-2 family
nodes.description:
The Bcl-2 family of proteins consists of both pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic members that regulate the Intrinsic Pathway of Apoptosis. They are characterized by the presence of Bcl-2 homology (BH) domains.

## Classification
The family is divided into three functional groups:
1.  Anti-apoptotic proteins: Protect cells from apoptosis. Examples: Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1, Bcl-w, A1-Bfl-1.
2.  Pro-apoptotic effector proteins: Form pores in the mitochondrial membrane. Examples: Bax, Bak, Bok/Mtd.
3.  Pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins: Initiators of apoptosis that sense cellular stress. Examples: Bid, Bim, Puma, Noxa, Bad, Bmf, Hrk, Bik.

## Role in Cancer
Dysregulation of the balance between these groups is a hallmark of cancer, leading to evasion of cell death and resistance to therapy.

## Documents

- Apoptosis in cancer from pathogenesis to treatment
- This pathway is closely regulated by a group of proteins belonging to the Bcl-2 family, named after the BCL2 gene originally observed at the chromosomal breakpoint of the translocation of chromosome 18 to 14 in follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma \[\].

- Caspase
- Bcl-2 family: Regulates caspase activation through mitochondrial integrity. Phosphorylation: A major post-translational modification controlling caspase activity.

- Evading apoptosis in cancer

nodes.label: MOMP
nodes.description:
Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) is the decisive, largely irreversible event of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of Apoptosis. At MOMP, the outer mitochondrial membrane loses its barrier integrity, allowing the efflux of intermembrane-space proteins — most notably Cytochrome c and Smac DIABLO — that license the proteolytic caspase cascade and commit the cell to death.

## Mechanism of MOMP

MOMP is controlled by the Bcl-2 family of proteins. Pro-survival members (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1) preserve membrane integrity, whereas "effector" proteins Bax and Bak undergo activation and oligomerization to form pores in the outer membrane. Their activation is opposed by "sentinels" Bim and Bid (and unleashed from PUMA/NOXA), which neutralize the pro-survival block. Once Bax/Bak pores form, MOMP proceeds as a regulated, sometimes partial, permeabilization that can occur at the level of individual mitochondria.

## Physiological and Pathological Roles

Physiologically, MOMP eliminates damaged, infected, or superfluous cells during development and tissue turnover. Pathologically, failure of MOMP underpins the survival of Cancer cells and their resistance to Chemotherapy and radiotherapy, since many cytotoxic agents act upstream by triggering mitochondrial apoptosis. Conversely, excessive or mistimed MOMP drives degenerative and ischemic injury.

## Determinants and Regulation

The threshold for MOMP integrates diverse stresses: DNA damage (via p53), Oxidative Stress,

nodes.label: Apoptosome
nodes.description:
The Apoptosome is a ~700–1,400 kDa, wheel-like heptameric complex that assembles in the cytosol during the Intrinsic Pathway of Apoptosis to activate the initiator Caspase-9. It is the central execution platform linking mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization to the caspase cascade.

## Composition & Assembly

The apoptosome is built from seven copies each of:
1. Apaf-1 (apoptotic protease-activating factor 1) — the scaffold, containing CARD, nucleotide-binding (NB-ARC), and WD40 domains.
2. Cytochrome c — released from mitochondria; binds the Apaf-1 WD40 domain, triggering dATP/ATP-dependent oligomerization.
3. dATP/ATP — induces the conformational change enabling heptamerization.
4. pro-Caspase-9 — recruited via CARD–CARD interaction to the central hub.

Cytochrome c binding causes Apaf-1 to swap from an autoinhibited monomer to an active oligomer, forming the characteristic seven-spoked wheel.

## Mechanism of Action

Recruitment concentrates pro-caspase-9 at the apoptosome, enabling induced proximity and autocleavage that generate active caspase-9. Active caspase-9 then proteolytically activates executioner Caspase-3 and Caspase-7, which dismantle the cell through chromatin condensation, DNA fragmentation, and membrane blebbing. The apoptosome thus converts a mitochondrial "damage signal" into an irreversible proteolytic program.

## Regulation

- Inhibitors: XIAP and other IAPs can suppress caspase-9; SMAC/DIABLO released from mitochondria relieves this inhibition.

nodes.label: Caspase-9
nodes.description:
Caspase-9 is the initiator caspase of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway. It is activated within the apoptosome complex, formed when cytochrome C released from mitochondria binds Apaf-1 and recruits procaspase-9. Active Caspase-9 then cleaves and activates executioner caspases (Caspase-3, Caspase-7), committing the cell to apoptosis.

## Structure & Activation
Procaspase-9 contains a prodomain (CARD domain) and a catalytic domain. Upon MOMP, Cytochrome C binds Apaf-1 in the cytosol, inducing Apaf-1 oligomerization into the heptameric apoptosome. Procaspase-9 is recruited via CARD–CARD interactions, where proximity-induced dimerization activates it without proteolytic cleavage (though cleavage by Caspase-8 or Caspase-3 enhances activity).

## Mechanism of Action & Pathways
Active Caspase-9 cleaves Caspase-3 and Caspase-7 at specific Asp residues, initiating the execution phase of apoptosis. Caspase-9 activity is regulated by:
- Inhibition: XIAP directly binds and inhibits Caspase-9, preventing its activation. Phosphorylation of Caspase-9 at Ser196 by Akt also suppresses its activity.
- Activation: Release of XIAP (via Smac DIABLO or TBK1-mediated degradation) liberates Caspase-9.

> [!info] Akt-Mediated Phosphorylation of Caspase-9
> Akt phosphorylates Caspase-9 at Ser196 (human), suppressing its activity. This represents a key node linking growth factor signaling to apoptotic threshold control in cancer cells.

nodes.label: DISC
nodes.description:
The Death-Inducing Signaling Complex (DISC) is a multi-protein assembly that forms during the initiation of the Extrinsic Pathway of Apoptosis.

## Assembly
The DISC forms on the intracellular tails of death receptors (e.g., Fas, DR4, DR5, TNFR1) following ligand binding.
1.  Receptor Trimerization: Ligand binding causes receptors to cluster.
2.  Adaptor Recruitment: The adaptor protein FADD (and sometimes TRADD) is recruited to the receptor's death domain.
3.  Caspase Recruitment: FADD then recruits pro-Caspase-8 (or Caspase-10) molecules through death effector domain interactions.

## Function
The primary function of the DISC is to facilitate the proximity-induced auto-activation of Caspase-8. Once activated, caspase-8 is released into the cytoplasm to activate executioner caspases like Caspase-3.

## Documents

List of documents that mention this entity

- Apoptosis in cancer from pathogenesis to treatment
- Binding of the death ligand to the death receptor results in the formation of a binding site for an adaptor protein and the whole ligand-receptor-adaptor protein complex is known as the DISC \[\].

- Evading apoptosis in cancer
- In the Extrinsic Pathway, initiator Caspase-8 and Caspase-10 are activated through the formation of a death-inducing signal complex (DISC) in response to engagement of extracellular ligands (e.g. Fas or TNF ) by cell surface receptors (Figure 1).

nodes.label: Caspase-8
nodes.description:
Caspase-8 is an initiator caspase of the extrinsic apoptotic pathway, activated upon oligomerization at death-inducing signaling complexes (DISCs) formed by death receptors such as Fas and TRAIL receptors. It initiates the caspase cascade leading to activation of executioner caspases and apoptotic cell death.

## Structure & Activation
Caspase-8 contains two N-terminal death effector domains (DEDs) that mediate recruitment to DISCs, and a C-terminal catalytic domain with a large (p18) and small (p10) subunit. Upon death receptor ligation by FasL or TRAIL, procaspase-8 is recruited to the DISC, where proximity-induced auto-proteolytic cleavage activates it. Active Caspase-8 then directly activates executioner caspases (Caspase-3, Caspase-7) or cleaves the BH3-only protein Bid to engage the mitochondrial pathway.

## Mechanism of Action & Pathways

- Extrinsic Apoptosis: Caspase-8 is the primary initiator caspase downstream of death receptors (Fas, TRAIL-R1/R2, TNFR1). It directly activates Caspase-3 and Caspase-7 in type I cells.
- Mitochondrial Amplification: In type II cells, Caspase-8 cleaves Bid to truncated Bid (tBid), which activates BAX and BAK to trigger MOMP, amplifying the death signal.
- Non-Canonical Scaffolding: Phosphorylated Caspase-8 acquires scaffolding functions independent of its protease activity.

> [!important] Tyrosine Phosphorylation Switch
> In many cancers (colon, glioblastoma), Src family kinases phosphorylate Caspase-8 at Tyr380 (or Tyr397/Tyr465 de

nodes.label: SRC kinase
nodes.description:
SRC kinase (or Src, product of the SRC proto-oncogene) is a non-receptor cytoplasmic Tyrosine Kinase and the founding member of the SRC family of kinases (SFKs: Src, Yes, Fyn, Lyn, Lck, Blk, Hck, Fgr, Frk). Originally identified as the cellular homolog of the v-Src oncogene carried by Rous sarcoma virus, c-Src is a prototype Oncogene that integrates signals from receptor tyrosine kinases, integrins, and G-protein-coupled receptors to drive cell proliferation, survival, motility, and Angiogenesis.

## Structure and Regulation

Src is organized into an N-terminal myristoylation/palmitoylation motif (for membrane association), an SH3 domain, an SH2 domain, a catalytic kinase domain, and a short C-terminal tail containing Tyr527. In the inactive state, the phosphorylated tail (Tyr527, by Csk kinase) binds intramolecularly to the SH2 domain, and the SH3 domain engages the kinase domain, locking Src in a closed conformation. Dephosphorylation of Tyr527 (by phosphatases such as PTP1B or SHP-1) or phosphorylation of activation-loop Tyr416 releases the clamp and activates the kinase. This conformational switch is a classic example of intramolecular autoinhibition.

## Mechanism of Action and Signaling

Active Src phosphorylates a broad set of substrates on tyrosine residues, including focal adhesion kinase (FAK), p130Cas, Caspase-8, STAT transcription factors, and receptor tyrosine kinases such as HER2 and EGFR. Notably, Src phosphorylates Caspase-8 at Tyr380, which blocks caspase-8 m

nodes.label: SHP1
nodes.description:
SHP1 (PTPN6, SH2 domain-containing phosphatase 1) is a non-receptor tyrosine phosphatase that plays critical roles in immune signaling and apoptotic regulation. SHP1 dephosphorylates Caspase-8 at Tyr380, removing the inhibitory phosphate placed by Src family kinases and restoring the cell's sensitivity to death ligands (TRAIL, FasL).

## Structure & Activation
SHP1 contains two N-terminal SH2 domains that mediate recruitment to phosphotyrosine-containing motifs on receptors and signaling proteins, a catalytic phosphatase domain, and a C-terminal tail. SHP1 is autoinhibited by intramolecular interaction of the N-SH2 domain with the catalytic domain; binding of phosphotyrosine ligands to the SH2 domains relieves this autoinhibition.

## Mechanism of Action & Pathways

- Caspase-8 Dephosphorylation: SHP1 removes inhibitory phosphate groups from Caspase-8 at Tyr380 (and related Tyr397/Tyr465), restoring Caspase-8's ability to undergo proteolytic cleavage and maturation. This re-engages the extrinsic apoptotic pathway.

> [!important] Epigenetic Silencing of SHP1 in Cancer
> Many tumors epigenetically silence _PTPN6_ (SHP1) via promoter hypermethylation. This maintains Caspase-8 in its pro-migratory, anti-apoptotic phosphorylated state, enabling tumor cells to resist death ligand-induced apoptosis while promoting metastasis through the scaffolding functions of phosphorylated Caspase-8.

nodes.label: Bak
nodes.description:
BAK (Bcl-2 homologous antagonist/killer) is a pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family effector that resides constitutively embedded in the outer mitochondrial membrane of healthy cells. Unlike the mostly cytosolic BAX, BAK is activated in situ by BH3-only proteins (e.g., Bid), whereupon it oligomerizes to form the pores that drive Apoptosis.

## Structure & Activation
BAK contains BH1–BH3 domains and is held in check by anti-apoptotic partners such as Bcl-2 and Mcl-1. Displacement by activators (Bim, Bid, Puma, Noxa) liberates BAK to assemble large β-barrel pores. BAK and BAX are functionally redundant at the membrane yet operate from distinct cellular compartments.

## Mechanism of Action & MOMP
Activated BAK hetero-oligomerizes with BAX and additional BAK subunits, permeabilizing the outer membrane and releasing Cytochrome c and Smac DIABLO. This initiates the Caspases cascade and the execution phase of death. The resulting leakage also amplifies Reactive Oxygen Species and can trigger Mitophagy via Parkin.

## Phosphorylation-Dependent Licensing

> [!important] PTPN5-Mediated Dephosphorylation Licenses BAK
> BAK is maintained in an inactive state on the mitochondria through inhibitory phosphorylation at Tyr108. For BAK to be activated, it must be dephosphorylated at this site. This "licensing" is mediated by the PTPN5 (STEP), along with PTPN2 and PTPN23. nodes.label: Mcl-1
nodes.description:
Mcl-1 (Myeloid cell leukemia 1) is a potent anti-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family. It plays a critical role in the regulation of apoptosis and is a major factor in cancer cell survival and drug resistance.

## Role in Cancer
- Overexpression: Mcl-1 is one of the most frequently amplified genes in human cancers, including leukemia, Lymphoma, and various solid tumors.
- Resistance to BH3 Mimetics: Resistance to BH3 mimetics like ABT-737 and ABT-263 is often mediated by the upregulation of Mcl-1, which these drugs do not effectively inhibit.
- Rapid Turnover: Unlike Bcl-2 or Bcl-xL, Mcl-1 has a very short half-life and is rapidly degraded in response to various cellular stresses.

## Regulation
Mcl-1 stability is tightly controlled by post-translational modifications:
- Phosphorylation:
- GSK3: Phosphorylates Mcl-1 at Ser159 and Ser155, creating a phosphodegron that is recognized by the E3 ligase Beta-TrCP, leading to its degradation.
- JNK / ERK: Phosphorylate Mcl-1 at Thr163, which can stabilize the protein in certain contexts but also promotes GSK3-mediated phosphorylation.
- CDK1/CYCLIN B1: Phosphorylates Mcl-1 at Thr92 during mitosis, initiating its CDC20-dependent destruction.
- JNK, p38 MAPK, CK2: Can also phosphorylate Mcl-1 at various sites to modulate its stability.
- Ubiquitination:
- E3 Ligases: Mcl-1 is ubiquitinated for degradation by HUWE1 (MULE/ARF-BP1), Beta-TrCP, FBW7, and Trim17.

nodes.label: Smac DIABLO
nodes.description:
Smac/DIABLO (second mitochondria-derived activator of caspases) is a pro-apoptotic mitochondrial protein that promotes Caspase activation by neutralizing Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins (IAPs). Its function parallels that of Omi-HtrA2.

## Mechanism

Smac is synthesized as a precursor with an N-terminal Mitochondrial Targeting Sequence that is cleaved upon import into the Mitochondrial Intermembrane Space. Upon apoptotic stimulation (UV Radiation, Chemotherapy drugs, Fas Ligand), Smac is released into the Cytosol alongside Cytochrome c. Its exposed N-terminal Ala-Val-Pro-Ile (AVPI) IAP-Binding Motif (IBM) binds the BIR3 domain of XIAP, cIAP1, and cIAP2, displacing Caspase-9 and Caspase-3/Caspase-7 from IAP inhibition.

## Clinical Relevance

Smac mimetics (e.g., LCL161, Birinapant, Debio 1143) are Small Molecule IAP Antagonists in clinical trials for Cancer. They synergize with TNFα, TRAIL, and Chemotherapy to induce apoptosis in cancer cells. Loss of Smac expression contributes to Chemoresistance across multiple cancer types.

nodes.label: Bim
nodes.description:
Bim (Bcl-2-like protein 11) is a potent pro-apoptotic BH3-only member of the Bcl-2 family. It is a major initiator of the Intrinsic Pathway of apoptosis.

## Mechanism
Bim acts as a "direct activator" of the apoptotic effectors Bax and Bak. It can also bind and neutralize all anti-apoptotic members of the Bcl-2 family (e.g., Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1), thereby lowering the threshold for apoptosis.

## Regulation
Bim activity and stability are tightly regulated by several signaling pathways:
- ERK: Phosphorylates Bim at Ser69, promoting its degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. This phosphorylation also prevents the interaction between Bim and Bax.
- RSK: Phosphorylates Bim at S93/S94/S98, which is required for Beta-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination.
- JNK / p38 MAPK: Phosphorylate Bim to promote its pro-apoptotic activity by enhancing binding to anti-apoptotic members.
- PKA: Stabilizes Bim protein.
- E3 Ligases: Bim is targeted for degradation by SCF Complex (Beta-TrCP), c-CBL, TRIM2, and the Elongin B/C-Cullin 2-CIS complex.

## Role in Cancer
Reduced expression or loss of Bim is associated with tumor progression and resistance to therapy, particularly in lymphoid malignancies.

## Documents

nodes.label: Bid
nodes.description:
Bid (BH3 interacting-domain death agonist) is a pro-apoptotic BH3-only member of the Bcl-2 family of proteins. It serves as a critical link between the extrinsic (death receptor) and intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathways.

## Structure and Activation

Bid is a 22 kDa protein that exists in an inactive cytosolic conformation. Upon cleavage by caspase-8 (downstream of death receptor engagement), the N-terminal fragment (tBid, truncated Bid) translocates to the mitochondria, where it activates Bax and Bak to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP).

> [!important] Bid as an Apoptosis Amplifier
> tBid (truncated Bid) is a potent activator of Bax, directly triggering Bax conformational change and oligomerization at the mitochondrial outer membrane. This mechanism amplifies apoptotic signals from death receptors by engaging the mitochondrial apoptotic machinery.

## Regulation

Bid activity is regulated by:
- Caspase-8 cleavage: The primary activating event, converting full-length Bid to tBid
- Humanin: Directly binds and nullifies tBid activity, blocking its ability to activate Bax and Bak
- Phosphorylation: JNK-mediated phosphorylation at Ser61 and Ser78 enhances Bid pro-apoptotic activity
- Deamidation: Asparagine deamidation at positions 60 and 85 activates Bid independently of caspase cleavage

## Biological Significance

Bid is essential for:
- Amplification of death receptor-mediated apoptosis
- Developmental tissue remodeling

nodes.label: Apaf-1
nodes.description:
Apaf-1 (Apoptotic protease-activating factor 1) is a key cytoplasmic protein involved in the Intrinsic Pathway of apoptosis.

## Function
Apaf-1 acts as the scaffold for the assembly of the Apoptosome. Upon binding to Cytochrome c (released from the mitochondria) and dATP/ATP, Apaf-1 undergoes a conformational change that allows it to oligomerize into a heptameric wheel-like structure.

## Regulation
Apaf-1 activity and oligomerization are regulated by several factors:
- RSK: Phosphorylates Apaf-1 to inhibit its activation in response to Cytochrome c.
- HSP90β: Acts as an Apaf-1 inhibitor, suppressing its oligomerization, particularly in tyrosine kinase-induced leukemias.
- Transcriptional Regulation: Apaf-1 is a key transcriptional target for p53 and E2F1.

## Apoptosome Assembly
The Apaf-1 heptamer recruits pro-Caspase-9 molecules through CARD-CARD domain interactions. This clustering of pro-caspase-9 leads to its auto-activation, initiating the caspase cascade.

nodes.label: Caspase-3
nodes.description:
Caspase-3 is the primary executioner (effector) caspase in apoptosis, responsible for cleaving the majority of apoptotic substrates. It sits at the convergence of the intrinsic (Caspase-9-dependent) and extrinsic (Caspase-8-dependent) pathways and is the most widely used marker of apoptotic cell death (via cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining).

## Structure & Activation
Procaspase-3 is a ~32 kDa zymogen containing a prodomain and a catalytic domain. It is activated by proteolytic cleavage at Asp175 by initiator caspases:
- Intrinsic pathway: Caspase-9 cleaves procaspase-3 at the apoptosome
- Extrinsic pathway: Caspase-8 directly cleaves procaspase-3 (type I cells) or indirectly via Bid→MOMP→Caspase-9 (type II cells)

Active Caspase-3 is a heterotetramer (p17/p12)₂ with broad substrate specificity.

## Mechanism of Action & Pathways
Active Caspase-3 cleaves >1000 cellular substrates, including:
- DNA repair: PARP (inactivates repair)
- DNA fragmentation: ICAD/CAD (activates DNase to fragment DNA)
- Nuclear structure: Lamin B1 (disassembles nuclear envelope)
- Cytoskeleton: Actin, fodrin (cell shrinkage)
- Signaling: Akt, RIPK1, FLIP (amplifies death signaling)

> [!info] Convergence Point of Apoptotic Pathways
> Caspase-3 integrates signals from both the extrinsic pathway (via Caspase-8) and the intrinsic pathway (via Caspase-9). Its activation marks the irreversible commitment to apoptotic cell death.

nodes.label: Fas
nodes.description:
Fas (also known as CD95, APO-1, or DR2) is a key death receptor belonging to the tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) superfamily. It plays a central role in the Extrinsic Pathway of Apoptosis.

## Mechanism
Binding of the ligand FasL (Fas ligand) to the Fas receptor induces receptor trimerization. This leads to the recruitment of the adaptor protein FADD (Fas-associated death domain) and pro-Caspase-8 to form the Death-Inducing Signaling Complex (DISC).

## Role in Cancer
- Downregulation: Loss of Fas expression or mutations in the FAS gene are common mechanisms by which cancer cells (e.g., in leukemia and cervical cancer) evade immune-mediated apoptosis.
- Resistance: Reduced membrane expression of Fas is linked to acquired drug resistance in many tumors.

## Documents
