This buffering is a front-line antioxidant defense. The directionality is iron chelation to suppressed radical formation. A caveat is that ferritin can be released or degraded during inflammation and hemorrhage, liberating iron that then becomes pro-oxidant.

nodes.label: Iron accumulation in Substantia Nigra
nodes.description: Iron accumulation in the substantia nigra promotes the Fenton reaction because elevated redox-active iron there catalyzes conversion of H2O2 to hydroxyl radicals near dopaminergic neurons. The iron burden correlates with oxidative damage markers in Parkinson's disease. The directionality is iron accumulation to radical generation. A caveat is that iron accumulation may also be a downstream consequence of oxidative damage and impaired iron export, so the relationship is partly bidirectional.

nodes.label: Redox Imbalance
nodes.description: Oxidative stress is a redox imbalance in which reactive oxygen (and nitrogen) species production exceeds the capacity to detoxify them or repair the resulting damage. This definition frames oxidative stress as a dynamic disequilibrium rather than a single molecule. The directionality is imbalance between oxidants and defenses. A caveat is that transient oxidative shifts are physiological signaling events, so 'stress' specifically denotes sustained or excessive imbalance.

nodes.label: Antioxidant Response
nodes.description: NRF2 is the master regulator of the antioxidant response, inducing more than 200 cytoprotective genes including those for glutathione synthesis, thioredoxin, heme oxygenase, and drug detoxification. It integrates signals from KEAP1, redox status, and electrophiles. The directionality is NRF2 activation to coordinated defense transcription. A caveat is that excessive or chronic NRF2 activation can support tumor cell survival, so its regulation is finely balanced.

nodes.label: Low-level oxidative stress
nodes.description: Low-level oxidative stress activates mitohormesis, a beneficial adaptive response in which transient ROS upregulate DNA repair, antioxidant defenses, and autophagy to improve resilience. This explains the paradoxical benefits of mild mitochondrial stress. The directionality is mild oxidant to adaptive reprogramming. A caveat is that the benefit is strictly dose-dependent; higher oxidative stress overwhelms the response and becomes damaging, the classic hormetic inverted-U.

nodes.label: Adrenochrome Formation
nodes.description: Oxidative stress drives adrenochrome formation because high levels of superoxide and H2O2 favor oxidation and cyclization of adrenaline to the neurotoxic quinone adrenochrome. This pathway has been implicated in psychosis models and redox-linked neuronal injury. The directionality is catecholamine oxidation to adrenochrome. A caveat is that adrenochrome formation in vivo is contested, and adrenochrome can also be detoxified or further metabolized, so its pathological relevance remains debated.

nodes.label: Telomere Attrition
nodes.description: Progressive telomere shortening with each cell division eventually exposes chromosome ends that are recognized as DNA double-strand breaks, triggering replicative senescence at the Hayflick limit. Critically short or dysfunctional telomeres activate the ATM/p53 and ATR/p21 DDR cascades, halting proliferation to prevent chromosomal instability. This mechanism is the canonical explanation for the finite replicative capacity of primary human cells in culture. The directionality is one-way in normal cells, though telomerase reactivation can bypass the arrest -- a hallmark of cancer.

nodes.label: Oncogene Activation
nodes.description: Activated oncogenes such as RAS, BRAF, and MYC drive hyperproliferation and replication stress, which in turn elicit oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) as an intrinsic tumor-suppressive failsafe. The unscheduled S-phase entry generates DNA replication stress and DNA damage that stabilize p53 and derepress the CDKN2A/p16INK4a locus, locking cells in arrest. OIS is observed in benign lesions such as melanocytic nevi and is a major barrier to tumor progression. The paradox is that OIS cells secrete a SASP that, while recruiting immune clearance, can also promote tumorigenesis in neighboring cells.

nodes.label: p53/p21 Pathway
nodes.description: The p53/p21 axis is a primary enforcement mechanism of senescence, especially in damage- and stress-induced forms. DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor p21CIP1; p21 inhibits cyclin E/A-CDK2, preventing phosphorylation of Rb and blocking S-phase entry. This pathway provides a rapid, p53-dose-dependent G1/S arrest that can be engaged acutely after genotoxic insult. A caveat is that the p53 pathway is frequently disabled in cancer, and p53 also restrains the SASP, so its loss reshapes rather than simply abolishes senescence.

nodes.label: p16/Rb Pathway
nodes.description: The p16INK4a/Rb pathway enforces the long-term, irreversible phase of senescence independently of p53. p16 inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, keeping Rb hypophosphorylated and bound to E2F, thereby preventing expression of S-phase genes; this locks in a durable growth arrest. Unlike the p53/p21 arm, which can be transient, p16/Rb-mediated arrest is typically sustained for the life of the cell and is the stronger correlate of in vivo senescent burden with age. Its engagement is a key determinant of why senescence is considered irreversible rather than a quiescent state.

nodes.label: E2F
nodes.description: Both the p53/p21 and p16/Rb axes converge on suppression of the E2F family of transcription factors, which are master regulators of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase progression. Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F and, together with SAHF-mediated heterochromatinization, represses E2F target loci; p21 additionally blocks CDK-mediated release of this repression. Inhibition of E2F is therefore the final common effector of the senescent growth arrest. This directed, downstream suppression is a defining mechanistic feature shared across senescent cell types.

nodes.label: Lamin B1
nodes.description: Senescent cells characteristically show reduced expression of lamin B1 (encoded by LMNB1), a structural component of the nuclear lamina. Lamin B1 loss detaches lamina-associated domains (LADs) from the nuclear periphery, spatially reorganizing chromatin and contributing to the altered gene expression and genomic instability of senescence. This marker is relatively conserved across cell types and tissues, making it a practical histological and molecular signature of senescent cells in vivo. A caveat is that lamin B1 loss can also occur in certain differentiation and disease states, so it is best used in combination with other markers.

nodes.label: Secretory Phenotype
nodes.description: The SASP is a hypersecretory state -- a specialized secretory phenotype -- in which senescent cells upregulate and release hundreds of factors including interleukins, chemokines, growth factors, proteases, and extracellular vesicles. This secreted output contrasts with the quiescent, low-turnover secretome of non-senescent cells and is a defining non-cell-autonomous feature of the senescent state. The composition of the SASP is variable, shaped by the senescence inducer, cell type, and tissue context. Its classification as a secretory phenotype emphasizes that senescence exerts its effects largely through communication with the microenvironment.

nodes.label: JAK-STAT3
nodes.description: The JAK-STAT3 signaling axis promotes a pro-inflammatory SASP by interacting with p38 MAPK and mTOR and by transducing cues from SASP cytokines such as IL-6. STAT3 activation contributes to age-related frailty and to the immune-modulatory and tumor-promoting facets of the secretome. JAK1/2 inhibitors (e.g., ruxolitinib) reduce SASP cytokines IL-6 and IL-8, validating the axis as a senomorphic target. The pathway is especially important for the feed-forward, self-reinforcing inflammation characteristic of chronic senescence.

nodes.label: Apigenin
nodes.description: Apigenin, a flavonoid, reduces SASP-driven breast cancer aggressiveness by inhibiting NF-κB-dependent SASP factors and the chemokine CXCL10. It also blocks the ASAP-to-SASP transition by disrupting ATM-HSPA8 and HSPA8-p38 MAPK crosstalk, and binds PRDX6 to inhibit its iPLA2 activity. These actions place apigenin at both the early stress-response and the established-secretome levels. Its effects are documented in specific cancer and fibroblast models, supporting a medium-to-high confidence senomorphic role.

nodes.label: Nutlin 3a
nodes.description:
Nutlin-3a is a cis-imidazoline small molecule that inhibits MDM2 and stabilizes p53, with context-dependent senolytic, senescence-inducing, and senomorphic effects on the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype.

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

Nutlin-3a binds the p53-binding pocket of the E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2, disrupting the MDM2–p53 interaction and preventing p53 ubiquitination and degradation (Vassilev et al., 2004, PMID 15790651). Stabilized p53 accumulates and activates target genes including p21, driving cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis. Crucially, p53 also represses the SASP: elevated p53 antagonizes the NF-κB and C/EBPβ arms that drive SASP transcription (Freund et al., 2010, PMID 20357755). Thus nutlin-3a can silence the pro-inflammatory secretome independently of cell killing.

## Role in Senescence / SASP

Nutlin-3a has a dual senescence role. (1) As a senescence inducer: by enforcing p53 it drives arrest or apoptosis in tumor cells, and p53-dependent apoptosis makes it a candidate senolytic in p53-wild-type contexts. (2) As a senomorphic suppressor: p53 represses the SASP, so nutlin-3a dampens the inflammatory secretome of already-senescent cells. The balance depends on cell type, p53 status, and dose. Nutlin-3a is a widely used tool compound for dissecting p53-mediated senescence and SASP control.

## Clinical / Pathological Relevance

Clinical derivatives (RG7112, idasanutlin) advanced in trials for MDM2-amplified cancers (e.g., AML, liposarcoma). Effica

nodes.label: Paracrine Senescence
nodes.description:
Paracrine senescence (also called bystander senescence or secondary senescence) is the process by which Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype secreted by senescent cells induce Senescence in neighbouring healthy cells, spreading the senescence phenotype through tissues. It explains why small numbers of senescent cells can drive disproportionate tissue dysfunction and why local senescent-cell burden amplifies with age (Acosta et al., 2013; PMID 23636316; Nelson et al., 2018, PMID 29902437).

## Mechanism

In OIS cells, SASP components — including IL-1α, TGFβ, VEGF, CCL2, and CCL20 — autocrinally reinforce senescence-associated growth arrest and additionally induce paracrine proliferation arrest by binding their specific receptors on receiving cells, activating secondary DDR-independent arrest pathways.

Notch signalling is essential for establishing paracrine senescence and weakens the SASP produced by secondary senescent cells, thereby preventing runaway continuous senescence induction. TGF-β and IGFBP3 from the SASP reinforce arrest in neighbours via Smad and PI3K/Akt suppression.

### SASP Components Mediating Paracrine Senescence

> [!info] Source: Acosta et al., 2013 (PMID 23636316)
> Coupling SILAC-based quantitative proteomics with a 78-compound drug library screen, Acosta et al. identified multiple SASP components mediating paracrine senescence. The top mediators were TGFβ family ligands, VEGF, CCL2, and CCL20. Drug inhibitors targeting VEGFR2/FLT3, TGFBR1, and CCR

nodes.label: Natural Killer Cells
nodes.description:
Natural killer (NK) cells are innate lymphoid cells that provide rapid cytotoxic responses against virus-infected cells and tumour cells without prior antigen sensitisation. They are part of the innate immune system's first line of defence, complementing the adaptive immune system (T and B cells). NK cells recognise target cells through a balance of activating and inhibitory receptors, and they kill via perforin/granzyme-mediated apoptosis and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).

## Ontogeny & Subsets

- Origin: NK cells develop from common lymphoid progenitors in the bone marrow, with maturation occurring in secondary lymphoid tissues (lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils).
- Development: NK cell development requires IL-15, IL-7, and Flt3 ligand. The transcription factor T-bet and Eomes are essential for terminal maturation.
- Subsets:
- CD56^bright CD16− NK cells: ~90% of NK cells in lymph nodes. High cytokine production (IFN-γ, TNF-α), low cytotoxicity. Regulatory function.
- CD56^dim CD16+ NK cells: ~90% of NK cells in blood. High cytotoxicity, lower cytokine production. Main effector population for target cell killing.
- Tissue-resident NK cells: Found in liver, uterus, lungs, and skin. Distinct transcriptional profiles and functions.

## Recognition & Activation

NK cell activity is determined by the integration of signals from activating and inhibitory receptors:

- Inhibitory receptors:
- KIR (Killer Immunoglobulin-like Receptors): Recognise classical MHC-I molec

nodes.label: Macrophages
nodes.description:
Overview: Macrophages are specialized immune cells derived from monocytes that play critical roles in tissue homeostasis, immune surveillance, and inflammation. In Atherosclerosis, macrophage cholesterol accumulation and Foam Cells formation are hallmarks of early atherogenesis.

> [!info] Source: Berrougui et al., Atherosclerosis 2009
> Macrophages (J774, THP-1, and mouse peritoneal macrophages) take up and oxidize LDL, leading to significant cholesterol accumulation. Oxidative stress (Fe/ascorbate) impairs ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux. Resveratrol (0–25 µM) restores HDL3-mediated cholesterol efflux under oxidative stress in a dose-dependent manner.

## Cholesterol Homeostasis in Macrophages

- Cholesterol accumulation: Macrophages accumulate cholesterol via LDL uptake, oxidation, and increased biosynthesis
- Foam cell formation: Excessive cholesterol accumulation transforms macrophages into foam cells — the hallmark of early atherosclerotic lesions
- Cholesterol efflux: The protective mechanism by which HDL removes excess cholesterol from macrophages; occurs via three pathways:
1. Aqueous diffusion
2. SR-BI-mediated bidirectional flux
3. ABCA1-mediated transfer to lipid-poor apoA-1
- Oxidative stress effects: Fe/ascorbate impairs ABCA1 expression and cholesterol efflux; Resveratrol restores this function

## Cell Lines Used in Research

- J774: Mouse macrophage cell line; commonly used for cholesterol efflux studies

nodes.label: Fibrosis
nodes.description:
Fibrosis is a pathological biological process defined by the excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components — principally Collagen, fibronectin, and proteoglycans — within tissues, resulting in scarring and progressive architectural distortion. It is the common终点 of chronic injury across virtually every organ system, including the liver (cirrhosis), lung (pulmonary fibrosis), kidney (nephrosis), heart (myocardial fibrosis), and skin (keloids/scleroderma). Rather than being a single disease, fibrosis represents a conserved wound-healing response that has failed to resolve, shifting from physiological repair toward maladaptive tissue remodeling.

## Mechanism and Cellular Basis

The central effector cell is the activated Fibroblast, and its transdifferentiated derivative, the myofibroblast, which expresses α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and is the principal source of Extracellular Matrix. Myofibroblasts arise not only from resident fibroblasts but also through Epithelial-to-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) of epithelial cells, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), and recruitment of fibrotic progenitor cells. The master profibrotic cytokine is TGF-β, which drives collagen synthesis, inhibits ECM degradation by suppressing matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and stimulates tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs). Additional mediators include PDGF, CTGF, IL-13, and angiotensin II.

## Physiological vs. Pathological Function

nodes.label: MMP-3
nodes.description:
Matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3), also known as stromelysin-1, is a zinc-dependent endopeptidase secreted as a component of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype. It is a broad-spectrum ECM-degrading enzyme that promotes tissue remodelling, EMT and cancer progression.

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

MMP-3 is a secreted zinc metalloproteinase whose catalytic domain bears the conserved HEXXHXXGXXH zinc-binding motif. Its substrate range is unusually broad: it degrades Collagen types III, IV, V, IX and X, fibronectin, laminin, proteoglycans and Elastin, and—importantly—it proteolytically activates latent pro-MMPs (pro-MMP-1, -7, -8, -9, -13), positioning MMP-3 as an upstream "trigger" of collagenolysis cascades (PMID 10545505). Its expression is transcriptionally driven by the SASP transcription factors NF-κB and AP-1 and restrained by tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMP3). A common functional polymorphism (rs3025058, 5A/6A) modulates MMP-3 promoter activity and associates with arthritis and cancer risk.

## Role in Senescence / SASP

Senescent Fibroblasts and epithelial cells secrete MMP-3 as part of the pro-inflammatory, matrix-remodelling SASP. By activating collagenases and releasing matrix-bound growth factors, MMP-3 reshapes the Extracellular Matrix and potentiates paracrine senescence. A landmark finding is that MMP-3 can itself induce EMT in mammary epithelial cells by cleaving E-cadherin and triggering mesenchymal reprogramming (Sternlicht et al

nodes.label: CCL2
nodes.description:
CCL2 (C-C motif chemokine ligand 2), also known as MCP-1 (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1), is a CC chemokine that binds the receptor CCR2 and is the principal recruiter of monocytes and macrophages to sites of inflammation. It is one of the most conserved and well-characterized components of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (Coppé et al., 2008, PMID 18948995; 2010, PMID 20723158).

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

- Receptor binding: CCL2 signals chiefly through CCR2 (a Gαi-coupled GPCR), with minor activity at CCR4; it activates PI3K/Akt, p38 MAPK/ERK, and Ca2+ flux to drive chemotaxis and adhesion of monocytes.
- Cell sources: Released by senescent fibroblasts, endothelial cells, macrophages, and epithelial cells under stress.
- Transcriptional regulation: Transcription is driven by NF-κB, AP-1, STAT1/STAT3, and the C/EBP family, and is potently induced by the SASP cytokines IL-1α and IL-1β — a feed-forward loop because recruited macrophages further inflame tissue.
- Downstream cellular effects: Recruits classical monocytes, macrophages, memory T cells, and dendritic cells; promotes M2-like polarization and tissue remodeling.

## Role in Senescence / SASP

- CCL2 is a core SASP chemokine whose expression is tightly linked to the IL-1α/IL-1β arm of the secretome.
- It mediates immune recruitment to senescent cells that can be beneficial (macrophage-mediated clearance, immune surveillance) or detrimental (chronic monocyte infiltration, tissue damage).

nodes.label: TNFalpha
nodes.description: Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha) is a pro-inflammatory SASP cytokine that contributes to immune modulation, NF-κB reinforcement, and inflammaging. It can act in an autocrine loop to amplify the secretome and in a paracrine manner to affect neighboring cells. TNFalpha is less universally dominant than IL-6 in the SASP but is consistently present in many models. Its pleiotropic inflammatory actions solidify its status as a canonical SASP component.

nodes.label: GATA4
nodes.description:
GATA4 is a zinc-finger transcription factor of the GATA family, best known for governing cardiac and endodermal development. In the context of cellular senescence, GATA4 is a stress-inducible factor that functions as a regulator of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype, acting alongside NF-κB, C/EBPβ, and DNA-damage signaling to sustain inflammatory secretome expression.

## Overview

GATA4 binds the consensus motif (A/T)GATA(A/G) via two zinc fingers and activates or represses target genes involved in differentiation, stress response, and survival. It is stabilized under cellular stress and is a nodal mediator linking tissue injury and inflammatory gene programs.

## Structure & Function

The two C4 zinc fingers of GATA4 mediate DNA binding and protein interactions; an N-terminal transcriptional activation domain and regulatory serines govern its activity. GATA4 can be degraded by autophagy (e.g., upon nutrient stress via FOXO/autophagy) and stabilized by stress, making its protein level a sensor of cellular damage.

## Role in Senescence / SASP

The review lists GATA4 among the transcription factors and upstream regulators — together with DNA-damage signaling, C/EBPβ, p38 MAPK, mTOR, JAK-STAT, and Notch — that control SASP expression. GATA4 contributes to the NF-κB- and C/EBPβ-driven inflammatory program, helping maintain expression of SASP cytokines and chemokines. Its induction under genotoxic and oncogenic stress positions GATA4 as a stress-integrating transcript

nodes.label: METTL3/METTL14
nodes.description: The METTL3-METTL14 m6A methyltransferase complex promotes SASP factor expression by installing N6-methyladenosine marks that facilitate enhancer-promoter looping and stabilize SASP transcripts. This epitranscriptomic layer adds post-transcriptional control to the secretome. The relationship is mechanistically plausible and supported by knockout studies, but the field is newer and less consolidated than the NF-κB/mTOR axes. Confidence is therefore moderate.

nodes.label: Ruxolitinib
nodes.description:
Ruxolitinib (INCB018424) is a selective ATP-competitive inhibitor of Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) and JAK2, and the first JAK inhibitor approved by the FDA (2011 for myelofibrosis; 2014 for polycythemia vera). It is a senomorphic therapy that targets the JAK–STAT3 pathway to suppress the pro-inflammatory SASP.

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

Ruxolitinib inhibits JAK1 and JAK2, the tyrosine kinases that transduce signals from interferon, hematopoietic, and many cytokine receptors. By blocking JAK catalytic activity it prevents phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of downstream STAT3 (and STAT5), shutting off transcription of inflammatory target genes. In senescent cells, JAK–STAT is a major amplifier of the SASP; ruxolitinib abrogates secretion of IL-6 and IL-8 and blunts the broader pro-fibrotic and immunomodulatory secretome without killing the cells.

## Role in Senescence / SASP

Ruxolitinib is a prototypic senomorphic agent: it does not eliminate senescent cells but suppresses their inflammatory output via JAK–STAT blockade. By quelling the SASP it reduces the senescence-associated chronic inflammation that drives Inflammaging and age-related tissue dysfunction, and it has been used experimentally to "rejuvenate" aspects of the aged phenotype in several models.

## Clinical / Pathological Relevance

FDA-approved for myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, and steroid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease; a topical formulation (ruxolitinib cream, Opzelura) is approved f

nodes.label: Lamivudine
nodes.description:
Lamivudine (3TC) is a nucleoside analog and competitive inhibitor of reverse transcriptase, developed as an antiretroviral for HIV and as a therapy for chronic hepatitis B. In the senescence literature it has been repurposed as a senomorphic agent: rather than killing senescent cells, it dampens their pro-inflammatory secretome (the SASP) by interfering with the retrotransposon arm of SASP induction. The key mechanistic insight is that lamivudine blocks reverse transcription of the LINE-1 (L1) retroelement, lowering the burden of cytosolic retroelement cDNA that would otherwise trigger innate immune signaling.

## Mechanism / Structure

Lamivudine is a cytidine analog in which the normal 2'-deoxyribose ring is constrained into a oxathiolane (five-membered) ring. After intracellular phosphorylation to its triphosphate form, it competes with natural dCTP for incorporation by reverse transcriptase, terminating viral cDNA chain elongation. The same inhibitory principle applies to the endogenous reverse transcriptase activity encoded by autonomous LINE-1 elements.

> [!info] Retrotransposon–SASP linkage
> Senescent cells experience derepression of normally silenced repetitive elements. LINE-1 retrotransposition produces cytosolic cDNA, which is sensed by the cGAS-STING Pathway and reinforces NF-κB–driven inflammation, feeding the SASP. By suppressing L1 reverse transcription, lamivudine reduces this cDNA pool and the downstream inflammatory cascade.

The inhibition of cGAS-STING P

nodes.label: SAMD
nodes.description: Senescent cells exhibit senescence-associated mitochondrial dysfunction (SAMD), characterized by reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity, altered mitochondrial morphology, and elevated ROS production. SAMD is not merely a bystander but an active driver: mitochondrial stress releases mtDNA via minority MOMP, activating cGAS-STING and reinforcing the SASP. The dysfunctional mitochondria also elevate ROS that cause further DNA damage, amplifying arrest. SAMD thus couples metabolic remodeling to the inflammatory secretome.

nodes.label: Dasatinib
nodes.description: Dasatinib, a multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is a component of the foundational D+Q (dasatinib + quercetin) senolytic combination. It is proposed to act by inhibiting pro-survival kinases in senescent cells, lowering their apoptotic threshold. Dasatinib has established clinical use in chronic myeloid leukemia, aiding its repurposing. Its senolytic activity is well demonstrated in vitro and in vivo, though tissue selectivity varies.

nodes.label: Navitoclax
nodes.description: Navitoclax (ABT-263) is a potent BCL-2/BCL-XL/BCL-W inhibitor with strong senolytic activity, effectively inducing apoptosis in senescent cells. It is limited clinically by on-target thrombocytopenia due to BCL-XL dependence of platelets, spurring the development of more selective derivatives. Its senolytic efficacy is well established in multiple models. The toxicity caveat shapes its use toward intermittent or tissue-targeted regimens.

nodes.label: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
nodes.description: Senolytic therapy (D+Q) has been tested for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in a pilot clinical trial (NCT02874989), where it improved physical function. The rationale is that senescent cell accumulation and SASP-driven fibrosis contribute to IPF pathogenesis. Results support further evaluation of senolytics in fibrotic lung disease. This is among the most advanced clinical indications for senolytic therapy.

nodes.label: Diabetic Kidney Disease
nodes.description: Senolytic therapy (D+Q) has been tested in a pilot/phase trial for diabetic kidney disease (NCT02848131), based on evidence that senescent cells and SASP drive renal fibrosis and dysfunction in diabetes. The trial assesses feasibility, safety, and biomarkers of renal senescence. Early data inform the potential of senolytics in metainflammation and nephropathy. Clinical confidence remains preliminary pending larger trials.

nodes.label: Osteoarthritis
nodes.description: Senolytic therapy is being tested for osteoarthritis (e.g., NCT04210986) to reduce pain and improve joint function by clearing senescent chondrocytes and synovial cells. Preclinical studies show senolytics alleviate OA pathology and improve cartilage integrity. The SASP from senescent joint cells is implicated in cartilage degradation and inflammation. This represents a leading musculoskeletal application of senolytics.

nodes.label: Senotherapeutic
nodes.description: The term 'senotherapeutic' is an umbrella encompassing both senolytics (which eliminate senescent cells) and senomorphics (which suppress the SASP). Senolytics act on the cellular driver, while senomorphics act on the secretory effector, together spanning the intervention space against senescence. This inclusive definition reflects the field's two-pronged therapeutic philosophy. Recognizing both under one term aids classification of anti-senescence strategies.

nodes.label: Healthspan
nodes.description:
Healthspan refers to the period of life during which an individual remains generally healthy and free from serious disease, disability, or functional decline. It is distinguished from Lifespan — total years lived — as a primary metric for Aging Research and Gerontology.

## Metrics

Healthspan is assessed by:
- Morbidity — absence of Chronic Disease (Cardiovascular Disease, Cancer, Diabetes Mellitus, Neurodegenerative Disease)
- Functional Status — Mobility, Cognition, Activities of Daily Living
- Frailty Index — accumulation of deficits and Frailty measures
- Biological Age — Epigenetic Clocks, Biomarkers of Aging

## Interventions

Evidence-based strategies for extending healthspan:
- Caloric Restriction — extends healthspan across model organisms
- Exercise — preserves Muscle Mass, Cardiovascular Function, and Cognition
- Rapamycin — mTORC1 inhibitor; extends healthspan in mice
- Metformin — anti-diabetic drug; putative geroprotector
- NAD+ precursors — Nicotinamide Mononucleotide, Nicotinamide Riboside
- Senolytics — Dasatinib + Quercetin; clears senescent cells
- Dietary Restriction — Intermittent Fasting, Mediterranean Diet

## Compression of Morbidity

The Compression of Morbidity hypothesis (Fries, 1980) posits that extending healthspan while delaying the onset of chronic disease compresses the period of end-of-life disability into a shorter timeframe, reducing healthcare burden and improving Quality of Life.

nodes.label: Senotherapy
nodes.description: Senotherapy encompasses senolytics, the cell-elimination arm that selectively induces apoptosis in senescent cells by disabling SCAPs. This is one of the two principal divisions of senotherapy, the other being senomorphics. The term captures the spectrum of interventions aimed at the senescent cell. Encompassing senolytics underscores the elimination-based strategy's centrality to the field.

nodes.label: Notch
nodes.description: Notch signaling is essential for establishing paracrine senescence and, paradoxically, weakens the secondary SASP in receiving cells. Notch integrates cues from the SASP to reinforce arrest in neighbors while modulating their secretory output. Its role indicates that paracrine senescence is an active, regulated program rather than passive factor exposure. The precise directionality (establish vs. dampen SASP) reflects context-dependent Notch outputs.

nodes.label: IFITM3
nodes.description: IFITM3 is enriched in exosomes released from senescent cells and mediates paracrine senescence by transmitting senescence signals to recipient cells. As an exosomal cargo, it represents a vesicle-based, rather than soluble-factor, route of spread. Its inclusion highlights that paracrine senescence is not solely cytokine-driven. The mechanism adds a non-classical communication modality to the SASP paradigm.

nodes.label: Immunosenescence
nodes.description: Senescence surveillance is impaired by immunosenescence -- the age-related decline in immune competence -- which compromises NK, macrophage, and T-cell mediated clearance of senescent cells. Elevated MDSCs and immune suppression further blunt surveillance. The result is permissive accumulation of senescent cells and increased tumor and inflammatory risk. This positions immunosenescence as both cause and consequence of senescence pathology.

nodes.label: PI3K/Akt
nodes.description: PI3K/Akt survival kinase signaling is a major pro-growth, anti-apoptotic cascade within SCAPs that promotes senescent-cell persistence. Akt phosphorylates substrates that inhibit pro-apoptotic proteins and sustain metabolic fitness. Its inhibition (e.g., by quercetin) lowers the apoptotic threshold of senescent cells. PI3K/Akt thus represents both a survival支柱 and a senolytic target.

nodes.label: mtDNA
nodes.description:
Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is the ~16.6 kb circular genome encoding subunits of the electron-transport-chain complexes and rRNAs/tRNAs. While essential for oxidative phosphorylation, mtDNA can act as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) when released from mitochondria into the cytosol or extracellular space, triggering innate immune activation.

## Release Mechanisms

- Major Mitochondrial Outer Membrane Permeabilization (MOMP): Typically associated with Apoptosis; massive BAX/BAK pore formation releases mtDNA and apoptogenic factors.
- Minority MOMP (miMOMP): Sublethal permeabilization by BAX/BAK that releases mtDNA without triggering cell death — the principal route in senescent cells (McArthur et al., 2018; PMID 30257233).
- Vacuole-like structures / mitophagy defects: Impaired Mitophagy allows damaged mitochondria to leak mtDNA.
- Extracellular export: mtDNA is found in extracellular vesicles and cell-free in plasma as an ageing biomarker.

## Role in Senescence

In Senescent Cells, mitochondrial dysfunction and miMOMP cause cytosolic mtDNA accumulation. This activates the cGAS-STING innate-immune sensor (cGAS binds mtDNA, generating cGAMP that activates STING → TBK1/IRF3 and NF-κB), driving type I interferons and pro-inflammatory cytokines that are core components of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (Dougherty et al., 2019/2020; PMID 31624094; Glück et al., 2020).

nodes.label: HIRA/ASF1a
nodes.description: SAHF are assembled by the HIRA-ASF1a histone chaperone complex, which deposits macroH2A and core histones to establish H3K9me3-marked heterochromatin at SAHF. This chaperone-driven deposition is required for the formation of the DAPI-dense foci. The process links histone dynamics directly to senescence-specific chromatin reorganization. HIRA/ASF1a thus provide the assembly machinery for the repressive structures.

nodes.label: SADS
nodes.description: SADS (senescence-associated distal satellite) is a form of heterochromatin decompaction in senescent cells, specifically the relaxation of constitutive pericentromeric and pericentrosomal satellite heterochromatin. Unlike SAHF (which compacts facultative heterochromatin), SADS decompacts constitutive repeats. This structural change alters the nuclear architecture and chromatin accessibility of repetitive regions. SADS represents a distinct, counterintuitive chromatin reorganization during senescence.

nodes.label: Heterochromatin Decompaction
nodes.description: SADS (senescence-associated distal satellite) is a form of heterochromatin decompaction in senescent cells, specifically the relaxation of constitutive pericentromeric and pericentrosomal satellite heterochromatin. Unlike SAHF (which compacts facultative heterochromatin), SADS decompacts constitutive repeats. This structural change alters the nuclear architecture and chromatin accessibility of repetitive regions. SADS represents a distinct, counterintuitive chromatin reorganization during senescence.

nodes.label: T Cell
nodes.description:
T cells are lymphocytes central to the Adaptive Immune Response, mediating cellular immunity through antigen-specific recognition by the T cell receptor. Autophagy is unexpectedly indispensable for T cell biology: it supports thymic development, naive-to-effector activation, clonal expansion, memory formation, and the metabolic reprogramming that fuels proliferation. By clearing damaged mitochondria and recycling nutrients, Autophagy preserves T cell proteostasis and bioenergetic flexibility under the stringent demands of immune activation.

## Metabolic Dependence on Autophagy

Upon antigen recognition, T cells shift from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis while also requiring mitochondrial integrity. Mitophagy removes depolarized mitochondria, preventing excess Oxidative Stress and apoptotic priming, and supports the metabolic switch. Autophagy also supplies amino acids and intermediates during the nutrient-limited phases of clonal expansion, sustaining mTORC1-dependent growth. Loss of Atg proteins in T cells impairs survival, skews cytokine output, and diminishes memory generation.

## Roles in Differentiation & Function

Autophagy modulates T cell subset fate: it restrains excessive Inflammation by limiting inflammasome activation and mitochondrial DNA release, and it influences regulatory T cell (Treg) suppressive function and effector CD8+ cytotoxic activity. Selective autophagy of signaling molecules tunes TCR and cytokine receptor downstream pathways, int

nodes.label: DNA-SCARS
nodes.description: Genotoxic stress in TIS generates persistent DNA damage foci termed DNA-SCARS (DNA segments with chromatin alterations reinforcing senescence), which are precursors to cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCF). These structures sustain DDR signaling and the arrested state. DNA-SCARS thereby mechanistically link damage to durable senescence. They are a defining feature distinguishing TIS from transient damage responses.

nodes.label: Glucocorticoids
nodes.description:
Glucocorticoids (cortisol, dexamethasone, prednisolone) are adrenal steroid hormones with potent anti-inflammatory effects. They block pro-inflammatory Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype by impairing IL-1α-mediated NF-κB activity via the glucocorticoid receptor, making them a class of senomorphic therapy.

## Mechanism of Action & Signaling

Glucocorticoids bind the intracellular Glucocorticoid Receptor (GR, NR3C1), a ligand-activated nuclear receptor. The hormone–GR complex translocates to the nucleus, where it both transactivates anti-inflammatory genes and transrepresses pro-inflammatory transcription: it recruits histone deacetylases, competes with NF-κB and AP-1 for coactivators, and directly inhibits NF-κB transcriptional activity. In senescent cells, glucocorticoids specifically blunt the IL-1α–driven arm of the SASP — suppressing IL-1α maturation and the NF-κB–dependent expression of downstream SASP factors (Coppé et al.; SASP review, PMID 20365073).

## Role in Senescence / SASP

Glucocorticoids are classic senomorphic agents: they suppress the pro-inflammatory component of the SASP without eliminating senescent cells. They preferentially dampen the IL-1α/NF-κB limb, leaving some growth-factor SASP components relatively intact. By contrast, chronic endogenous glucocorticoid excess (Cushing phenotype) is associated with accelerated aging features, illustrating that context and dose determine whether GR signaling is protective or detrimental to tissue homeostasi

nodes.label: SB203580
nodes.description: p38 MAPK is inhibited by SB203580, a classical pyridinyl imidazole inhibitor that suppresses p38alpha/beta and thereby reduces SASP from fibroblasts of older donors. By blocking p38, SB203580 lowers NF-κB activation and SASP transcript stabilization. This provides a tool compound validating p38 as a senomorphic target. The inhibition is specific and well characterized in cellular models.

nodes.label: p21 CIP1
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor p21CIP1; p21 binds and inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes (notably CDK2), enforcing a G1/S arrest. This p53 to p21 axis is a primary, rapid enforcement mechanism of senescence and quiescence. The induction is dose-dependent and reversible in the short term but locks arrest when sustained. It exemplifies tumor-suppressive cell-cycle control.

nodes.label: CDK2
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: p21CIP1 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) by binding the cyclin E/A-CDK2 complex, preventing phosphorylation of Rb and thereby enforcing G1/S arrest. This is a direct enzymatic inhibition central to p53-driven senescence and quiescence. By blocking S-phase entry, p21 locks cells out of the cell cycle. Its inhibitory action is a canonical CDK-inhibitor function.

nodes.label: Early SASP
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Senolytic Treatment With Fisetin Reverses Age‐Related Endothelial Dysfunction Partially Mediated by SASP Factor CXCL12.md
nodes.description: p21 supports an early secretory phenotype -- including factors such as CXCL14 and IGFBP3 -- that places stressed cells under immunosurveillance prior to full senescence. This early p21-associated secretome differs from the later NF-κB-dominated SASP. It suggests p21 contributes to both arrest and the initial communicative state of stressed cells. The relationship is more nuanced than simple arrest enforcement, giving moderate confidence.

nodes.label: CDK4
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: p16INK4a inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 4 (CDK4) by binding the cyclin D-CDK4 complex, preventing Rb phosphorylation and maintaining the growth-suppressive, hypophosphorylated state of Rb. This is a primary mechanism by which p16 enforces the durable, p53-independent phase of senescence. Loss of p16 is a common event in cancer, underscoring its tumor-suppressive role. The inhibition is direct and well established.

nodes.label: CDK6
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: p16INK4a also inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase 6 (CDK6), similarly preventing cyclin D-CDK6-mediated Rb phosphorylation and stabilizing the arrested state. This broad inhibition of both CDK4 and CDK6 ensures robust G1 blockade. The dual targeting makes p16 a potent, non-redundant cell-cycle inhibitor. Its action underpins the irreversibility of established senescence.

nodes.label: Senescent Cell Accumulation
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Mitochondrial dysfunction in cellular senescence a bridge to neurodegenerative disease.md
nodes.description: Aging causes senescent-cell accumulation as telomere shortening, cumulative DNA damage, and stem-cell stress increase senescent-cell formation, while declining immune clearance reduces removal. The burden rises across multiple tissues, often described as exponential with age. This accumulation is a cardinal hallmark linking cellular senescence to organismal aging. The causal direction is reinforced by experiments showing that clearing these cells alleviates age-related dysfunction.

nodes.label: Minority MOMP
nodes.description: Minority MOMP refers to sublethal, intermittent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization by BAX/BAK that releases mtDNA into the cytosol without committing the cell to full apoptosis. In senescent cells this leaked mtDNA acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern activating cGAS-STING. The process sustains SASP signaling while SCAPs restrain complete death. It exemplifies how senescent cells walk a fine line between life and death.

nodes.label: SASP Enhancers
nodes.description: H3K27ac marks senescence-activated super-enhancers that drive SASP expression, identifying the enhancer landscape licensed during senescence. These acetylated, active enhancers recruit BRD4 and transcription factors such as AP-1 and NF-κB to SASP loci. The mark thus charts the chromatin basis of the secretome. Targeting these enhancers (e.g., with BET inhibitors) suppresses SASP.

nodes.label: Activin A
nodes.description: Activin A is a homodimer of inhibin beta-A (INHBA) subunits and a member of the TGFβ superfamily of cytokines. Like other family members it signals through serine/threonine kinase receptors to regulate cell fate and inflammation. Its classification within the TGFβ superfamily situates it among the SASP factors with paracrine arrest-inducing capacity. Activin A is a structurally defined ligand distinct from TGFβ1 but functionally overlapping.

nodes.label: TGFβ Superfamily
nodes.description: Activin A is a homodimer of inhibin beta-A (INHBA) subunits and a member of the TGFβ superfamily of cytokines. Like other family members it signals through serine/threonine kinase receptors to regulate cell fate and inflammation. Its classification within the TGFβ superfamily situates it among the SASP factors with paracrine arrest-inducing capacity. Activin A is a structurally defined ligand distinct from TGFβ1 but functionally overlapping.

nodes.label: ALK4
nodes.description: Activin A signals through the type I receptor ALK4 and type II receptors activin RIIA/RIIB, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3 to transmit signals to the nucleus. This receptor architecture is canonical for activin/nodal signaling within the TGFβ superfamily. The ALK4-SMAD2/3 axis is required for Activin A's biological effects in senescence. It links ligand binding directly to transcriptional reprogramming of recipient cells.

nodes.label: SMAD2
nodes.description: Phosphorylated SMAD2 (with SMAD3) complexes with SMAD4 and translocates to the nucleus to regulate target gene transcription downstream of Activin A-ALK4 signaling. This SMAD-dependent transduction is the principal route by which Activin A alters gene expression in receiving cells. It drives expression of cell-cycle inhibitors that reinforce arrest. The pathway is a standard TGFβ-superfamily output mechanism.

nodes.label: CDKN2B
nodes.description:
CDKN2B encodes p15^INK4b^ (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2B), a member of the INK4 family of CDK inhibitors that specifically binds and inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, preventing their association with D-type cyclins. This maintains Rb in its hypophosphorylated, growth-suppressive state, enforcing G1 cell cycle arrest. CDKN2B is a key effector of TGFβ-mediated growth arrest and plays a critical role in paracrine senescence.

## Mechanism of Action

- CDK4/6 inhibition: p15^INK4b^ binds CDK4 and CDK6, preventing cyclin D–CDK complex formation and Rb phosphorylation.
- G1 arrest: By maintaining hypophosphorylated Rb, p15^INK4b^ sequesters E2F transcription factors, silencing genes required for S-phase entry.
- TGF-β target: CDKN2B is a direct transcriptional target of TGFβ signaling via SMAD3/SMAD4 complexes binding to SMAD-binding elements in the CDKN2B promoter.
- Epigenetic regulation: The CDKN2B locus is subject to DNA Methylation and PRC2-mediated H3K27me3 silencing; its derepression is a hallmark of senescence.

> [!info] p15^INK4b^ in the INK4 Family
> The INK4 family comprises four members: p16^INK4a^ (CDKN2A), p15^INK4b^ (CDKN2B), p18^INK4c^ (CDKN2C), and p19^INK4d^ (CDKN2D). All specifically inhibit CDK4/6 but have distinct expression patterns and regulatory mechanisms. p15^INK4b^ is the primary CDK inhibitor induced by TGF-β, while p16^INK4a^ is the primary senescence-associated CDK inhibitor induced by oncogenic stress.

nodes.label: Follistatin
nodes.description: Follistatin binds and neutralizes Activin A extracellularly, acting as a soluble antagonist that can block its paracrine senescence-inducing activity. This provides a natural brake on Activin A signaling and a potential therapeutic route to limit SASP-mediated arrest spread. The follistatin-Activin A axis is a classic antagonistic ligand-binding pair. Neutralization experiments confirm its functional relevance in paracrine senescence.

nodes.label: Acute Stress-Associated Phenotype
nodes.description: The acute stress-associated phenotype (ASAP) is the early, prompt cellular response mounted upon stress before full senescence markers become evident; it can transition into the chronic SASP. ASAP represents a pre-secretome state that licenses subsequent inflammatory output. Its precedence establishes a temporal hierarchy: stress sensing first, then durable secretome. Understanding ASAP helps separate acute protective responses from chronic, deleterious senescence.

nodes.label: ATM
nodes.description: The ASAP is characterized by phosphorylation and nucleus-to-cytoplasm translocation of ATM, TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination, and TAK1 activation, marking an early DDR- and innate-immune-primed state. ATM acts as an upstream gate that senses stress and initiates the signaling cascade toward SASP. These features distinguish ASAP from the fully established senescent secretome. The involvement of ATM/TRAF6/TAK1 places ASAP at the crossroads of DNA damage and inflammation.

nodes.label: PRDX6
nodes.description: The PRDX6 to HSPA8 axis controls the ASAP to SASP transition; apigenin binds PRDX6 inhibiting its iPLA2 activity and thereby restraining secretome maturation. PRDX6 thus operates as a gatekeeper linking redox/lipid signaling to inflammatory progression. Its role adds a peroxide/phospholipase dimension to senescence initiation. Confidence is moderate as the axis is mechanistically documented but less consolidated than ATM/p38.

nodes.label: HSPA8
nodes.description: HSPA8 (HSC70) activation and its interactions with ATM and p38 MAPK mediate ASAP maturation into the SASP, acting as a chaperone node that integrates stress signals. By bridging early DDR to kinase cascades, HSPA8 helps decide commitment to the secretory phenotype. Its gating role is supported by apigenin-disruption studies. Confidence is moderate given the emerging nature of the chaperone-senescence link.

nodes.label: CCL20
nodes.description: CCL20 (MIP-3alpha) is a CC chemokine that signals exclusively through the receptor CCR6, belonging to the broader chemokine family that directs leukocyte trafficking. Its classification as a chemokine situates it among the SASP components that recruit immune cells. As a SASP factor, CCL20 extends the communicative reach of senescent cells to adaptive immunity. Its restricted receptor usage gives it a focused recruitment profile.

nodes.label: Chemokine
nodes.description: CCL20 (MIP-3alpha) is a CC chemokine that signals exclusively through the receptor CCR6, belonging to the broader chemokine family that directs leukocyte trafficking. Its classification as a chemokine situates it among the SASP components that recruit immune cells. As a SASP factor, CCL20 extends the communicative reach of senescent cells to adaptive immunity. Its restricted receptor usage gives it a focused recruitment profile.

nodes.label: CCR6
nodes.description: CCL20 is the sole ligand for CCR6, a Gai-coupled GPCR that drives chemotaxis via PI3K/Akt, p38 MAPK, and Ca2+ flux in target cells. This exclusive pairing directs recruitment of CCR6+ cells such as TH17 lymphocytes and dendritic cells. In the senescence context, CCL20-CCR6 links the SASP to adaptive immune infiltration. The signaling mechanism is well characterized in lymphocyte biology.

nodes.label: TH17
nodes.description: The CCL20-CCR6 axis links the SASP to adaptive immunity by recruiting TH17 cells, which express CCR6 and are drawn to CCL20-rich senescent foci. TH17 recruitment can amplify local inflammation and shape the immune milieu around senescent cells. This connects the secretome to a distinct T-cell subset with pro-inflammatory roles. The relationship expands the immunological consequences of the SASP.

nodes.label: p15INK4b
nodes.description:
p15INK4b is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor of the INK4 family, the protein product of the CDKN2B tumor-suppressor locus. It binds and inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, preventing formation of the cyclin D–CDK complex and the phosphorylation of the Retinoblastoma Protein (Rb). By keeping Rb hypophosphorylated, p15INK4b enforces a durable G1 cell-cycle block that is central to senescence and growth suppression.

### Mechanism / Structure

p15INK4b belongs to the INK4 (INhibitor of Kinase 4) family of small ankyrin-repeat proteins, structurally and functionally parallel to p16INK4a. Its mechanism is direct:

- It occupies the ATP-binding cleft of CDK4/6, blocking cyclin D association and catalytic activity.
- Loss of CDK4/6 activity leaves Rb unphosphorylated, so Rb remains bound to and represses E2F target genes required for S-phase entry.
- The result is a canonical INK4–Rb axis-mediated G1 arrest.

> [!info] Redundant CDK inhibition
> p15INK4b provides redundant CDK inhibition alongside p16INK4a. Both INK4 proteins can independently lock cells out of the cycle, making the CDKN2A/B locus a robust gatekeeper of cell-cycle exit.

### Role in Senescence

Induction of CDKN2B is a key event in paracrine and TGFβ-driven senescence. p15INK4b acts cooperatively with p21 CIP1: p15 blocks CDK4/6 while p21 inhibits CDK2, producing a robust, redundant blockade that durably locks receiving cells out of the cell cycle. This cooperativity strengthens the arrest against mitogenic escape and is a r

nodes.label: HLA-E
nodes.description: HLA-E is a non-classical (class Ib) major histocompatibility complex molecule with limited polymorphism, presenting a restricted set of peptides (often leader peptides) to innate lymphoid receptors. Its classification distinguishes it from classical MHC class Ia molecules. In senescence, HLA-E upregulation becomes a mechanism of immune evasion. The class Ib identity underpins its specialized ligand-receptor interactions.

nodes.label: MHC Class Ib
nodes.description: HLA-E is a non-classical (class Ib) major histocompatibility complex molecule with limited polymorphism, presenting a restricted set of peptides (often leader peptides) to innate lymphoid receptors. Its classification distinguishes it from classical MHC class Ia molecules. In senescence, HLA-E upregulation becomes a mechanism of immune evasion. The class Ib identity underpins its specialized ligand-receptor interactions.

nodes.label: NKG2A
nodes.description:
NKG2A is an inhibitory receptor encoded by KLRC1 and expressed as a heterodimer with the invariant signaling partner CD94 on natural killer (NK) cells and a minority of CD8+ T cells. The complex recognizes HLA-E — the non-classical MHC class Ib molecule that presents leader peptides derived from classical HLA-A/B/C molecules. Engagement of HLA-E by CD94/NKG2A recruits SHP-1 via immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIMs), delivering a potent "stop" signal that overrides activating receptors and prevents cytotoxicity.

## Structure and Signaling

- NKG2A is a type II transmembrane C-type lectin-like protein; it lacks an intracellular signaling domain and depends on CD94 for cell-surface expression and ITIM transduction.
- Upon HLA-E binding, NKG2A ITIMs are phosphorylated and recruit SHP-1, dephosphorylating downstream activation pathways (e.g., Syk/ZAP70-linked cascades) in NK cells.

> [!important] Because HLA-E is stabilized by peptides from other HLA molecules, NKG2A effectively reports on the overall HLA expression of a target cell: low HLA-I ("missing-self") reduces HLA-E surface levels, relieving NKG2A inhibition and permitting NK killing.

## Role in Immune Evasion

Elevated HLA-E is a recurring immune-escape strategy. In senescence and malignancy, HLA-E up-regulation engages CD94/NKG2A on NK cells and CD8+ T cells, blunting their cytotoxic function. This is a major axis of Immune Evasion, operating in parallel with PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint engagement.

nodes.label: CD8 T Cells
nodes.description:
CD8 T cells (cytotoxic T lymphocytes) recognize peptide–MHC I complexes to kill infected or malignant cells. They form long-lived memory cells that underpin durable protective immunity.

## Rapamycin and CD8 T cells

Inhibition of mTORC1 by Rapamycin can improve immune responses to infection and vaccination by increasing CD8⁺ memory lymphocyte counts and Dendritic cells activity. Low-dose mTOR inhibition is immunostimulatory and potentiates vaccine efficacy, whereas higher doses are immunosuppressive ([Zerdka et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12766144/)). Human trials show improved influenza vaccine responses with everolimus.

> [!tip] Vaccine potentiation
> Brief mTORC1 inhibition raises CD8⁺ memory and antiviral proteins, translating to better vaccine responses and fewer infections in the elderly.

## Documents

List of documents in the wiki that mention this entity

- mTOR Pathway as Target of Anti-aging Therapies (Zerdka et al., 2025)
- Notes rapamycin increases CD8⁺ memory lymphocytes and dendritic cell activity.

## Connections

- Rapamycin — low-dose boosts CD8 memory
- mTORC1 — inhibition enhances vaccine responses
- Dendritic cells — antigen presentation partner
- Regulatory T cells — counterbalancing subset

## Linking Summary

nodes.label: Inflammasome
nodes.description: Inflammasomes are cytosolic supramolecular complexes of the innate immune system that assemble in response to pathogens or sterile danger signals to activate inflammatory caspases. They are not antibodies (immune complexes) but rather multiprotein scaffolds; the original classification here as an immune complex is loose, though inflammasomes are innate immune signaling platforms. They serve as a key intersection between senescence, DAMPs, and inflammation. Their activation links cellular damage to IL-1 family cytokine release.

nodes.label: Immune Complex
nodes.description: Inflammasomes are cytosolic supramolecular complexes of the innate immune system that assemble in response to pathogens or sterile danger signals to activate inflammatory caspases. They are not antibodies (immune complexes) but rather multiprotein scaffolds; the original classification here as an immune complex is loose, though inflammasomes are innate immune signaling platforms. They serve as a key intersection between senescence, DAMPs, and inflammation. Their activation links cellular damage to IL-1 family cytokine release.

nodes.label: Noncanonical Inflammasome
nodes.description: Senescent cells activate the noncanonical inflammasome (caspase-5/11), which cleaves IL-1α and drives SASP establishment. This provides a caspase-5-dependent route to the secretome that is distinct from the canonical NLRP3/caspase-1 pathway. The noncanonical activation is increasingly recognized as a core SASP licensing mechanism. It links intracellular LPS/cytosolic sensing to senescence inflammation.

nodes.label: MyD88
nodes.description: MyD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor protein serving as the central hub of Toll-like receptor (TLR) and IL-1R signaling, linking receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. Its classification as an adaptor reflects its role in assembling signaling complexes rather than enzymatic catalysis. In senescence, MyD88 transduces IL-1α signals that sustain the SASP. It is a foundational innate immune signaling scaffold.

nodes.label: Adaptor Protein
nodes.description: MyD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor protein serving as the central hub of Toll-like receptor (TLR) and IL-1R signaling, linking receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. Its classification as an adaptor reflects its role in assembling signaling complexes rather than enzymatic catalysis. In senescence, MyD88 transduces IL-1α signals that sustain the SASP. It is a foundational innate immune signaling scaffold.

nodes.label: IL-1R
nodes.description:
The Interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R) is the cell-surface receptor that binds the pleiotropic pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β (and IL-1α). Ligation of IL-1R by IL-1β recruits the adaptor MyD88 and the kinase IRAK (interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase), ultimately activating TRAF6 and the NF-κB signaling cascade. This drives transcription of downstream inflammatory mediators such as TNF-α, IL-6, and additional IL-1β, placing IL-1R at the apex of a feed-forward inflammatory loop.

## Relevance to the Sirtuin System

Sirtuins broadly exert anti-inflammatory effects by suppressing the NF-κB limb that IL-1R engages:
- SIRT1 and SIRT6 deacetylate the RelA/p65 subunit of NF-κB, blunting transcriptional activation downstream of IL-1R stimulation and reducing secretion of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6.
- SIRT1 counteracts IL-1β-mediated stress (e.g., in chondrocytes and vascular cells) through the TLR2/SIRT1/NF-κB axis.
- SIRT3 deficiency amplifies macrophage inflammatory responses to LPS/IL-1R-family stimuli, with elevated IL-1β and inflammasome activation.

Thus IL-1R-dependent signaling represents a major upstream trigger whose output is tuned by sirtuin-mediated deacetylation of NF-κB components.

## Connections

- IL-1β: Primary ligand that activates IL-1R.
- MyD88, IRAK: Adaptor and kinase in the IL-1R proximal complex.
- NF-κB: Central transcription factor activated downstream of IL-1R.

nodes.label: IRAK4
nodes.description:
IRAK4 (interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 4) is the proximal kinase of MyD88-dependent IL-1R/TLR signaling, recruiting and activating IRAK1 to drive NF-κB and MAPK activation.

## Role in Apigenin's SASP Suppression

> [!info] Source: Repurposing apigenin for senomorphic effect in antiaging pipelines
> Apigenin suppresses the SASP partly by inhibiting IL-1α signaling via IRAK1, IRAK4, p38 MAPK, and NF-κB, reducing breast cancer cell aggressiveness[25].

## Connections

- IL-1α — Upstream ligand.
- IRAK1 — Downstream IRAK family kinase.
- NF-κB — Downstream transcription factor.
- Apigenin — Inhibits IRAK4-dependent SASP.
- SASP — Suppressed output.

## Linking Summary

- New links added: IL-1α, IRAK1, NF-κB, Apigenin, SASP
- Suggested new entity notes to create: (none)
- Strong connections to strengthen: IRAK4 ↔ IRAK1

nodes.label: IRAK1
nodes.description: Active IRAK4 phosphorylates IRAK1, which then recruits TRAF6 through its C-terminal TRAF6-binding motifs, extending the myddosome signaling complex. This step connects the receptor-proximal kinases to E3 ubiquitin ligase activity and TAK1 activation. In senescence, IRAK1 is required for full SASP establishment. The relationship is a standard component of IL-1R/TLR signal propagation.

nodes.label: Myddosome
nodes.description: MyD88 assembles into the helical oligomeric myddosome with IRAK4 and IRAK1/2, serving as the scaffolding platform that activates downstream kinases (e.g., TAK1) and transcription factors (NF-κB). This supramolecular complex is the mechanistic core of IL-1R/TLR signaling. In senescence, myddosome formation underlies IL-1α-driven SASP. The assembly is a defining structural feature of MyD88-dependent signaling.

nodes.label: Senescent Cells to Macrophages
nodes.description: Senescent-cell surface IL-1α engages IL-1R on macrophages, recruiting MyD88 to activate NF-κB and amplify SASP both in the sender (autocrine) and in recruited immune cells (paracrine). This bridges the senescent cell and the macrophage through IL-1R/MyD88 signaling, propagating inflammation. The relationship situates MyD88 at the interface of senescence and innate immunity. It explains how local senescence ignites broader inflammatory responses.

nodes.label: Myeloid-Derived Suppressor Cells
nodes.description: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are a heterogeneous population of immature myeloid cells with potent immunosuppressive activity, expanded under pathological stress including cancer and chronic inflammation. Their classification reflects an arrested differentiation state rather than a single lineage. In senescence contexts, MDSCs are recruited by SASP factors and blunt anti-tumor and anti-senescence immunity. They represent a key immunosuppressive cell type in aging and cancer.

nodes.label: Immature Myeloid Cell
nodes.description: Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are a heterogeneous population of immature myeloid cells with potent immunosuppressive activity, expanded under pathological stress including cancer and chronic inflammation. Their classification reflects an arrested differentiation state rather than a single lineage. In senescence contexts, MDSCs are recruited by SASP factors and blunt anti-tumor and anti-senescence immunity. They represent a key immunosuppressive cell type in aging and cancer.

nodes.label: GM-CSF
nodes.description: The SASP factor GM-CSF stimulates myeloid expansion and biases differentiation toward immunosuppressive MDSCs, recruiting them into senescent and tumor tissues. GM-CSF thereby shapes the myeloid compartment to be tolerogenic and arrest-promoting. The relationship links a specific SASP cytokine to myeloid suppressor accumulation. It is a recognized driver of MDSC expansion in inflammation and cancer.

nodes.label: Caspase-5
nodes.description: Caspase-5 (human) is the inducible noncanonical effector caspase that cleaves IL-1α and gasdermin D to drive SASP and pyroptosis. Its activation is essential for the noncanonical inflammasome's role in senescence. The relationship positions caspase-5 as the enzymatic executor of the pathway in human cells. It is supported by cleavage-site and loss-of-function studies.

nodes.label: Caspase-11
nodes.description: Caspase-11 (mouse) is the noncanonical effector caspase that cleaves IL-1α and gasdermin D, paralleling human caspase-4/5. It is activated by cytosolic LPS and drives SASP establishment in murine senescence models. The relationship establishes the species-specific executor of the noncanonical pathway. It is a well-supported component of senescence inflammasome biology.

nodes.label: LPS
nodes.description: The hexa-acylated lipid A of LPS binds directly to the CARD domain of caspase-4/5/11, inducing their dimerization and activation -- the defining trigger of the noncanonical inflammasome. While classically microbial, this mechanism can be engaged in senescence-associated inflammatory contexts. The relationship is the canonical activation mode of the pathway. It links Gram-negative sensing to caspase-11/4/5 activation.

nodes.label: Paracrine Reprogramming
nodes.description: Paracrine reprogramming is the biological process by which SASP factors alter the differentiation status and fate of neighbouring cells, pushing them toward stemness, EMT, or altered lineage commitment. Distinct from paracrine senescence (which induces arrest), it remodels recipient identity. The process is mediated by cytokines such as IL-6, TGFβ, and VEGF family members. It expands the non-cell-autonomous influence of senescent cells beyond growth arrest.

nodes.label: Stemness
nodes.description: IL-6 is a central driver of in vivo reprogramming toward pluripotency and stemness via JAK/STAT3 signaling, promoting a dedifferentiated, stem-like state in recipient cells. This underlies both wound-healing plasticity and, pathologically, cancer stemness. The relationship links a core SASP cytokine to cell-fate reprogramming. It is supported by reprogramming and cancer-stemness studies.

nodes.label: Chronic SASP
nodes.description: Chronic SASP (IL-6, IL-8 via JAK/STAT3) promotes cancer stem-cell traits and expands the CSC pool in neighbouring epithelial and tumour cells, enhancing tumour initiation and relapse potential. By driving stemness and survival, the persistent secretome fosters malignant progression. The relationship is a key mechanism by which senescence can become tumor-promoting. It is supported by cancer-stemness and senescence co-culture studies.

nodes.label: Myeloid Differentiation
nodes.description: GM-CSF and CCL2 skew myeloid differentiation toward immunosuppressive MDSCs and specific macrophage phenotypes, reshaping the myeloid compartment in senescence and cancer. This biases haematopoiesis away from inflammatory resolution toward tolerance and suppression. The relationship links SASP factors to myeloid lineage outcomes. It is supported by myeloid-differentiation and tumor-immunology studies.

nodes.label: VEGFc
nodes.description: VEGF-C is a member of the VEGF family of cysteine-knot growth factors, structurally related to VEGF-A but with distinct receptor usage and lymphatic specificity. Its classification situates it among the growth-factor arm of the SASP. In senescence, VEGF-C is an early-induced angiogenic/lymphangiogenic factor. The family membership underpins its receptor interactions.

nodes.label: VEGF Family
nodes.description: VEGF-C is a member of the VEGF family of cysteine-knot growth factors, structurally related to VEGF-A but with distinct receptor usage and lymphatic specificity. Its classification situates it among the growth-factor arm of the SASP. In senescence, VEGF-C is an early-induced angiogenic/lymphangiogenic factor. The family membership underpins its receptor interactions.

nodes.label: VEGFR3
nodes.description: VEGF-C signals primarily through VEGFR-3 on lymphatic endothelium, promoting lymphangiogenesis and lymphatic vessel sprouting. This receptor usage distinguishes VEGF-C from VEGF-A's preferential VEGFR2 engagement. In the SASP, VEGF-C-VEGFR3 signaling contributes to lymphatic remodeling around senescent tissue. The relationship is a canonical VEGF-C function.

nodes.label: VEGFR2
nodes.description: At higher concentrations or after proteolytic processing, VEGF-C also engages VEGFR2 on blood vascular endothelium, supporting angiogenesis in addition to its lymphatic actions. This dual receptor usage broadens its angiogenic potential within the SASP. The relationship explains how VEGF-C can drive both blood- and lymphatic-vessel formation. It is supported by receptor-binding and processing studies.

nodes.label: Lymphangiogenesis
nodes.description: Full-length VEGF-C preferentially activates VEGFR-3 and promotes lymphatic vessel sprouting, driving lymphangiogenesis. In senescence, this contributes to lymphatic remodeling and potentially to immune cell trafficking routes. The relationship is the canonical lymphangiogenic function of VEGF-C. It expands the vascular consequences of the SASP beyond blood vessels.

nodes.label: DNA Replication Stress
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: Constitutive oncogenic RAS signaling pushes cells into hyper-replication, where DNA replication forks are initiated at excessive frequency and become stalled or collapsed. This generates single-stranded DNA gaps and replication stress that activate checkpoint kinases. The relationship is a central mechanism linking oncogene activation to senescence-inducing damage. It is well established in OIS biology.

nodes.label: ATR
nodes.source_file: _document_ - Small molecule compounds that induce cellular senescence.md
nodes.description: Stalled or collapsed replication forks generate single-stranded DNA gaps that engage the ATR-CHK1 cascade, activating a checkpoint that senses replication stress. In OIS, ATR signaling contributes to arrest and senescence establishment. The relationship is a canonical DNA-damage-checkpoint response. It links oncogene-driven hyper-replication to cell-cycle enforcement.

nodes.label: CDKN2A
nodes.description: The CDKN2A locus encoding p16INK4a is derepressed in OIS via loss of PRC1/2-mediated H3K27me3 repression, allowing p16 accumulation that enforces durable arrest. This epigenetic switch is a hallmark of the p53-independent senescence phase. The relationship couples oncogene signaling to stable CDK-inhibitor expression. It is a well-characterized epigenetic event in OIS.

nodes.label: Sir2 (yeast)
nodes.description: Sir2 (silent information regulator 2) is the founding member of the sirtuin family, first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a regulator of mating-type locus silencing and replicative lifespan. The seven mammalian paralogues SIRT1–SIRT7 evolved from this ancestral NAD+-dependent deacetylase, retaining the conserved catalytic core while diversifying in subcellular localization and substrate repertoire. This phylogenetic continuity means insights from yeast Sir2 historically informed mammalian sirtuin biology, although the mammalian enzymes acquired lineage-specific regulatory domains. The relationship is directional: yeast Sir2 is the evolutionary precursor, not a downstream effector, of the SIRT1–7 family.

nodes.label: Sirtuins (SIRT1–7)
nodes.description: Sir2 (silent information regulator 2) is the founding member of the sirtuin family, first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a regulator of mating-type locus silencing and replicative lifespan. The seven mammalian paralogues SIRT1–SIRT7 evolved from this ancestral NAD+-dependent deacetylase, retaining the conserved catalytic core while diversifying in subcellular localization and substrate repertoire. This phylogenetic continuity means insights from yeast Sir2 historically informed mammalian sirtuin biology, although the mammalian enzymes acquired lineage-specific regulatory domains. The relationship is directional: yeast Sir2 is the evolutionary precursor, not a downstream effector, of the SIRT1–7 family.

nodes.label: Mono-ADP-ribosyl transferases
nodes.description: Beyond deacetylation, several sirtuins catalyze mono-ADP-ribosylation, transferring the ADP-ribose moiety of NAD+ onto target proteins without removing an acetyl group. SIRT4 and SIRT6 prominently display this mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase activity, with SIRT6 using it to recruit heterochromatin proteins such as KAP1/HP1α. The directionality is that NAD+ is the donor and the target lysine (or other residue) is the acceptor, producing a mono-ADP-ribosylated product rather than free OAADPr. Biologically, ADP-ribosylation allows sirtuins to regulate processes—such as DNA repair and LINE-1 repression—distinct from their deacetylase functions.

nodes.label: Sirtuin deacetylation reaction
nodes.description: During the sirtuin-catalyzed deacetylation of a lysine, NAD+ is cleaved between its nicotinamide and ADP-ribose moieties, and the acetyl group is transferred to the ADP-ribose to generate 2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose (OAADPr) plus free nicotinamide. OAADPr is a stoichiometric by-product, released in equimolar amounts with the deacetylated substrate on every catalytic cycle. This molecule is not merely waste: it binds and activates the TRPM2 cation channel, linking sirtuin activity to calcium signaling and cellular stress responses. A caveat is that OAADPr accumulation can itself feed back on cellular metabolism, and its levels reflect the integrated deacetylase flux of the cell.

nodes.label: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose)
nodes.description: During the sirtuin-catalyzed deacetylation of a lysine, NAD+ is cleaved between its nicotinamide and ADP-ribose moieties, and the acetyl group is transferred to the ADP-ribose to generate 2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose (OAADPr) plus free nicotinamide. OAADPr is a stoichiometric by-product, released in equimolar amounts with the deacetylated substrate on every catalytic cycle. This molecule is not merely waste: it binds and activates the TRPM2 cation channel, linking sirtuin activity to calcium signaling and cellular stress responses. A caveat is that OAADPr accumulation can itself feed back on cellular metabolism, and its levels reflect the integrated deacetylase flux of the cell.

nodes.label: OAADPr
nodes.description: OAADPr (2'-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose) binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminal domain of the TRPM2 non-selective cation channel, promoting its opening and calcium influx into the cytosol. Because OAADPr is generated directly by sirtuin deacetylase activity, TRPM2 activation acts as a sensor of cellular sirtuin flux and NAD+ utilization. The directionality is unidirectional under basal conditions: sirtuin activity produces OAADPr, which then gates TRPM2, rather than TRPM2 regulating sirtuins. This coupling provides a mechanistic link between metabolic state, redox stress, and calcium-dependent processes such as insulin secretion and apoptotic signaling.

nodes.label: TRPM2
nodes.description:
TRPM2 (Transient Receptor Potential Melastatin-Related Channel 2) is a calcium-permeable non-selective cation channel. It is expressed highly in the Brain, immune system, and cardiovascular system. TRPM2 functions as an oxidative stress sensor, and its prolonged activation leads to intracellular calcium overload and subsequent cell death (apoptosis). TRPM2 is unique among ion channels because it is directly gated by a metabolite of sirtuin catalysis — providing a rare, direct coupling between the Sirtuins and membrane excitability.

## Structure and Gating Mechanism

TRPM2 is a ~170 kDa subunit forming tetrameric channels. It contains an N-terminal MHR (Meltastatin Homology Region) domain, six transmembrane segments with a pore loop, and a remarkable C-terminal extension bearing an enzymatic NUDT9-H homology domain. This domain lacks catalytic activity but serves as a ligand-binding site for ADP-ribose derivatives. TRPM2 opens in response to intracellular ADP-ribose, and its sensitivity is dramatically potentiated by OAADPr (2′-O-acetyl-ADP-ribose) and by warm temperatures and cytosolic Ca2+. H2O2 and other oxidants elevate the intracellular ADP-ribose/NAD+ metabolic pool, engaging TRPM2 as a heat- and redox-coupled cation channel.

TRPM2 is unique among ion channels because it is directly gated by sirtuin reaction metabolites:
